# Second order estimates on transition layers for the Allen–Cahn equation with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions: Part I – Boundary-orthogonal transition layers

**Authors:** Akashdeep Dey Address: Chennai Mathematical Institute, H1, SIPCOT IT Park, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 603103, India Email address: akashdeep@cmi.ac.in , Wenkui Du Address: School of Mathematics, Hunan University, Changsha, Hunan Province, 410082, China Email address: duwenkui@hnu.edu.cn , Davide Parise Address: Department of Mathematics, Zeeman Building, University of Warwick, Gibbet Hill Road, Coventry CV4 7AL, UK Email address: Davide.Parise@warwick.ac.uk and Lorenzo Sarnataro Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Toronto, 40 St. George Street, Toronto, ON M5S 2E4 Canada Email address: lorenzo.sarnataro@utoronto.ca

## Abstract

We study stable solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition on Riemannian manifolds with boundary, in the regime where the transition layers meet the boundary orthogonally. Under an a priori bound for the enhanced second fundamental form in the transition region, we establish uniform second-order Hölder estimates and quantitative mean curvature decay for the nodal hypersurfaces up to the boundary in ambient dimensions at most 10. The proof adapts the technique pioneered by Wang–Wei [28, 29], adding a further correction determined by the geometry of the ambient boundary. Its leading contribution to mean curvature cancels on the nodal set but survives on non-zero level sets in the transition region, whose mean curvature need not decay uniformly. This phenomenon has no interior analogue and is exhibited by stable solutions constructed by Kowalczyk [18].

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction

- 2 Basic definitions and notation

- I Derivation of the Toda system 3 Preliminary setup 4 Geometric setup and twisted Fermi coordinates 5 An optimal approximate solution 6 Equation for the error and mean curvature approximation by Toda system 7 Inner-outer gluing estimates for the error function $\phi$ 8 Improved horizontal estimates for $\phi_{y_{i}}$ and improved Toda system

- II Stability of Toda system implies curvature estimates 9 Stability inequality for Toda system 10 A separation estimate from local bounds for the Emden equation 11 Final estimates and the boundary correction on nonzero levels

- III Appendices A Proof of derivative estimates for enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}$ in Proposition B Proof of geometric approximation estimates and mean curvature expansion in Proposition C The one-dimensional heteroclinic solution $\mathbb{H}$ D Proofs of exponential interaction decay estimates in Lemmas and Lemma E Some classical elliptic regularity estimates F Liouville theorems and a priori estimates in gluing procedure References

### 1. Introduction

In this paper we establish second-order estimates for stable solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions on compact Riemannian manifolds with boundary, in the situation where the transition layers of the solution meet the boundary orthogonally. Together with the estimates in the forthcoming paper [10], which deal with the situation where the transition layers of the solution approach the boundary parallelly from one side, they fully extend the regularity theory developed by Wang–Wei [28, 29] to the case of Neumann solutions on manifolds with boundary. In [11], we shall use the estimates in Theorem 1.1 and those in [10] to obtain a min-max construction of free boundary geodesics and geodesic billiards in compact Riemannian surfaces with boundary, and free boundary minimal hypersurfaces in compact Riemannian manifolds with boundary of dimensions 3 and 4, entirely based on solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation. Moreover, we shall obtain a characterisation of curves realising the (phase-transition) $p$ –widths of the length functional on a Riemannian surface with boundary similar to the one obtained by Chodosh–Mantoulidis in the closed case [6].

The estimates in this paper differ from the interior ones of [29] (and the corresponding interior estimates in Riemannian 3-manifolds due to Chodosh–Mantoulidis [5]) in two key aspects caused by the geometry of the boundary: a logarithmic loss in the mean curvature decay and the quantitative separation estimates, and a distinction between the zero level set and the other level sets in the transition layer. While it is unclear whether the first difference is a feature of our proof and whether it could potentially be overcome, the second one reflects a genuine boundary phenomenon, as the stable solutions constructed by Kowalczyk in [18] show (see Section 1.2 for a careful discussion of these differences). This shows the subtleness of the boundary problem, and highlights a phenomenon that has no interior counterpart.

#### 1.1. Setup and main result

Let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth compact Riemannian manifold with boundary. We consider solutions $u:M\to(-1,1)$ of Allen–Cahn equation with vanishing Neumann boundary condition

$$ \begin{cases}\varepsilon^{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}u=W^{\prime}(u)&\text{in }M,\\
\partial_{\nu}u=0&\text{on }\partial M,\end{cases} $$

where $\nu$ is the inward-pointing unit normal to $\partial M$ . Throughout the paper, $W$ is a smooth even double-well potential, positive in $(-1,1)$ , with

$$ W(\pm 1)=W^{\prime}(\pm 1)=0,\qquad W^{\prime\prime}(\pm 1)=1, $$

and with $0$ as its unique critical point in $(-1,1)$ , satisfying $W^{\prime\prime}(0)<0$ . Model examples include $W(t)=\frac{(1-t^{2})^{2}}{8}$ and $W(t)=\frac{1+\cos(\pi t)}{\pi^{2}}$ .

Equation (1.1) is the Euler–Lagrange equation for the Allen–Cahn energy

$$ E_{\varepsilon}(u)=\int_{M}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{g}}. $$

If $S\subset\partial M$ is relatively open, stability in $M\cup S$ means that

$$ \int_{M}\left(\varepsilon^{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\psi^{2}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{g}}\geq 0\quad\text{for every }\psi\in C_{c}^{1}(M\cup S). $$

In particular, these test functions need not vanish on $S$ .

At a point where $\nabla u\neq 0$ , the enhanced second fundamental form is defined to be

$$ \mathcal{A}(u)=\nabla\!\left(\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|}\right). $$

We use the conventions and notation of Section 2.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Boundary second-order estimates for stable transition layers).

Let $2\leq n+1\leq 10$ and let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold with boundary. Let $S\subset\partial M$ be relatively open, and let $M^{\prime}\Subset M\cup S$ . Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $0<b<1$ . For every $\Lambda>0$ , there are constants $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ and $C<\infty$ with the following property.

Suppose that $0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ and that $u_{\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}(M\cup S,(-1,1))$ is stable in $M\cup S$ and satisfies

$$ \varepsilon^{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}u_{\varepsilon}=W^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\quad\text{in }M,\qquad\partial_{\nu}u_{\varepsilon}=0\quad\text{on }S, $$

together with

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|\leq\Lambda\quad\text{on }\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b\}\cap\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\neq 0\}. $$

Then every component $\Gamma$ of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}$ meeting $S$ satisfies

$$ \|H_{\Gamma}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Gamma\cap M^{\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad[H_{\Gamma}]_{C^{\theta}(\Gamma\cap M^{\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

and

$$ \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma}\|_{C^{\theta}(\Gamma\cap M^{\prime})}\leq C, $$

where $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma}$ denotes the second fundamental form of the hypersurface $\Gamma$ , and $H_{\Gamma}$ its mean curvature. The constants depend only on $M^{\prime}$ , the fixed geometry near $M^{\prime}$ , $W$ , $b$ , $\theta$ , and $\Lambda$ , and are independent of the number of transition layers.

#### Remark 1.2.

Notice that, if $n+1=2$ , then the level set $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}$ is a union of embedded curves, and the norm of its second fundamental form is simply the absolute value of its geodesic curvature $k_{\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}}$ , which is clearly the same as the mean curvature of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}$ . Therefore, in ambient dimension 2, (1.3) gives

$$ \|k_{\Gamma}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Gamma\cap M^{\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad[k_{\Gamma}]_{C^{\theta}(\Gamma\cap M^{\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

for every component $\Gamma$ of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}$ meeting $S$ . On the other hand, unlike in the interior case of [28, Theorem 3.6] and [6, Proposition C.4], it is not possible to obtain decay estimates (in $\varepsilon$ ) for the enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})$ . Indeed, at a point $p\in\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}\cap S$ , by (2.2),

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|^{2}=|k_{\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}}|^{2}+|\partial_{\nu}\log|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}||^{2}, $$

and an easy computation (see Remark 11.8) gives $|\partial_{\nu}\log|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}||^{2}=|k_{S}|^{2}$ , where $k_{S}$ denotes the geodesic curvature of the boundary at $p\in\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}\cap S$ . In particular, $k_{S}$ is independent of $\varepsilon$ . See also Remark 11.10 for a more detailed discussion of this issue.

#### Remark 1.3.

If $S$ is totally geodesic on a neighbourhood of $M^{\prime}\cap S$ , the estimates improve and extend to all transition levels. More precisely, if $0<b<b^{\prime}<1$ , then uniformly for $t\in[-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime}]$ , every component $\Gamma_{t}$ of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}$ meeting $S$ satisfies, on $M^{\prime}$ ,

$$ \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma_{t}}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C,\qquad\|H_{\Gamma_{t}}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|,\qquad[H_{\Gamma_{t}}]_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|, $$

where the constant $C$ (in addition to the geometry of $M^{\prime}$ , $W$ , $b$ , $\theta$ , $\Lambda$ ) also depends on $b^{\prime}$ . If, in addition, $n+1=2$ , then

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|\quad\text{on }M^{\prime}\cap\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}. $$

At regular boundary points, the Neumann condition implies that the nodal set meet $S$ orthogonally. The nodal estimates therefore give local $C^{2,\theta}$ control of the second fundamental form of the nodal set up to the boundary. In ambient dimension two, the norm of the second fundamental form of a curve equals the absolute value of its geodesic curvature, so (1.3) gives decay (and not simply boundedness) of curvature.

Like the main result in [29], Theorem 1.1 is a conditional result, in the sense that it assumes the initial $C^{2}$ bound (1.2) and improves it to the $C^{2,\theta}$ estimates (1.3) and (1.4). In order to upgrade this conditional result to a full unconditional curvature estimate on a compact Riemannian manifold with boundary as in [5, Theorem 3.4], two further ingredients are needed: the boundary-parallel estimates of [10], and the classification result for entire stable solutions in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with uniform Euclidean energy growth, which is now available in dimensions $n+1=2,3,4$ by [14, 1, 13]. Notice that in dimensions $n+1=2,3$ , by [14, 21, 3], the same classification result holds without the additional assumption of uniform Euclidean energy growth.

On the other hand, similarly to [29], no bound on the number of layers is a priori imposed and the dimensional restriction comes from the stability estimates for the scalar equation (i.e. the two component Toda system) to which stability is reduced in Section 10. Nonetheless, as far as geometric applications relying on an unconditional curvature estimate are concerned, one cannot hope to go beyond ambient dimension 7, since the rigidity result for entire stable solutions in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is bound to fail there, as shown in [24]. Notice here the analogy with rigidity results for stable minimal surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with Euclidean area growth [25, 2].

#### 1.2. Comparison with the interior estimates.

Our analysis builds on the reduction of stable Allen–Cahn transition layers to an approximately stable Toda system developed by Wang and Wei in [29]. However the estimates proven in Theorem 1.1 differ from those of [29] in two important respects:

- (i) our estimates yield an $O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2})$ bound for the zero level mean curvature, instead of the Euclidean $O(\varepsilon)$ rate, or the interior Riemannian $o(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|)$ rate (see [29, Remark 10.9]);

- (ii) our estimates only show decay of the mean curvature for the zero level set, and not for all level sets $\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}$ for $t\in[-1+b,1-b]$ .

Let us briefly discuss where these differences come from, and where the theorem could conceivably be strengthened and where it is essentially sharp.

Let us begin with (i). As noticed in [29, Remark 10.9] (see also [5, Corollary 3.3]), it is not surprising that introducing metric errors into the Wang–Wei reduction machinery would lead to a loss in the estimates, and, as the mentioned references show, this is already present in the Riemannian interior theory. It is not known at the moment if the logarithmic loss is a necessary feature of the general Riemannian (interior or boundary) theory, or simply an artefact of the proof strategy. On the other hand, it is worth noticing that the decay rates in (1.3) are strictly weaker than those in Riemannian interior theory of [29] or [5]. Even under the (significantly stronger) assumption that the boundary is totally geodesic, we are not able to recapture the same rates of decay.

This discrepancy comes from the estimates on quantitative separation of neighbouring sheets, rather than from the final elliptic estimates. The loss first occurs in the distance-gap comparison of Claim 10.6, which is used to prove Proposition 10.1. Curvature of the boundary introduces first-order metric terms when the signed Riemannian distance between sheets is compared with the difference of their coordinate heights. The decay estimate of Proposition 10.1 can therefore only be established above the threshold $\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ . Its iteration in Corollary 10.12, followed by the improved Toda equation in Proposition 11.4, gives an $O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2})$ bound, rather than the Euclidean interior rate $O(\varepsilon)$ of [29, Theorem 1.1]. Nonnegative ambient Ricci curvature does not remove the boundary condition for the intrinsic separation function in Remark 11.3. On the other hand, if the boundary is totally geodesic, the first-order metric contribution in the distance comparison disappears, as explained in Remark 10.2 and the separation estimate then improves by one logarithm. Neither this bound nor the general-boundary squared-logarithm bound is claimed to be optimal.

Let us now discuss (ii). The failure to extend the zero-level decay estimate to all transition levels has a different origin. Even though the zero sheets meet the boundary orthogonally, their nearby parallel leaves need not do so. Consequently, a heteroclinic solution depending on signed distance does not by itself satisfy the Neumann condition, and the approximation constructed in Section 5 includes the correction $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ . The evenness of the potential makes this correction $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ odd in its normal variable, so its leading contribution vanishes at the zero level but need not vanish at $s(t)=\mathbb{H}^{-1}(t)$ when $t\neq 0$ . Proposition 11.7 shows that the horizontal Laplacian of the correction $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ enters the mean curvature of the actual level graph. This contribution is only controlled at order $\varepsilon$ in the rescaled metric, corresponding to order one in the original metric. When the boundary is totally geodesic, $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ vanishes identically, and uniform estimates hold for all levels in a fixed compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$ .

Unlike (i), the failure of mean-curvature decay on nonzero levels is demonstrably a feature of the problem in question, as the examples in [18] show. Indeed, Kowalczyk [18] constructs solutions of (1.1) in bounded domains of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with smooth boundary concentrating near nondegenerate straight line segments meeting the boundary orthogonally and computes their Morse indices explicitly. In the regime where Kowalczyk’s solutions are stable, they illustrate why our estimates must distinguish the nodal set from the other transition levels. The level-set geometry obtained from his boundary-layer expansion [18, Section 2.4] shows that, at an endpoint with nonzero boundary curvature, a fixed nonzero level develops an order-one curvature contribution over distances of order $\varepsilon$ . Thus its mean curvature need not tend to zero, and its $C^{\theta}$ curvature seminorm can grow like $\varepsilon^{-\theta}$ , despite a bounded $L^{\infty}$ curvature norm. On the nodal set, on the other hand, the leading boundary correction vanishes by oddness, and the expansion instead gives an $O(\varepsilon)$ bound for the mean curvature. This contrasts with the interior Euclidean estimates of Wang–Wei [29, Theorem 1.1] and the interior Riemannian estimates of Chodosh–Mantouldis [5, Corollary 3.3], which give uniform bounds for $\|H\|_{L^{\infty}}$ and $\|\mathrm{I\!I}\|_{C^{\theta}}$ on all transition levels.

#### 1.3. Outline of the proof.

We follow the overall strategy of Wang–Wei [29] with a few important differences.

By using the assumptions in Theorem 1.1, in Section 3 we reduce the theorem to the local graphical statement in Theorem 3.3. After dilation by $\varepsilon^{-1}$ , the curvature of each sheet of the nodal set becomes $O(\varepsilon)$ , and neighbouring sheets become uniformly separated as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Notice that ordinary Fermi coordinates with respect to a sheet of the nodal set do not in general parametrise a collar neighbourhood of the ambient boundary. To obtain coordinates adapted to both the sheets and the boundary, we use a twisted Fermi coordinates construction inspired by Pacard–Ritoré [23, Section 10]; a closely related construction appears in the work of Kapouleas–Li on free boundary minimal surfaces [17, Definition 2.10 and Lemma 2.12]. The key ingredient in this step is the construction of a vector field $Z$ which is transverse to the sheets (but not necessarily normal to them), tangential to the ambient boundary and satisfies the estimates in Lemma 4.15, which are crucial to control the mixed derivative and commutator terms introduced without destroying the Toda structure of the leading interaction.

In Section 5, we approximate $u$ by alternating translated heteroclinics together with a boundary correction, which is necessary because the one-dimensional heteroclinic solution has a leading order Neumann derivative of order $\varepsilon$ . For each sheet $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ of the nodal set, we cancel this $O(\varepsilon)$ error by solving the linear problem (5.10) on $\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R}$ and then using a cutoff to localise around the sheet. Evenness of the potential $W$ guarantees that this correction $\mathbb{G}$ is odd in the twisted Fermi signed distance variable. Since the translation mode $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ is even, the correction $\mathbb{G}$ is orthogonal to it, and vanishes on the central slice $\{z=0\}$ . The construction of our correction $\mathbb{G}$ is analogous to the improvement of the approximate solution in del Pino–Kowalczyk–Wei [8, Section 5]: in both cases, the $O(\varepsilon)$ leading order in the Neumann derivative is cancelled by adding an odd correction solving a linearized boundary value problem.

For a family of shifts $h=(h_{\alpha})$ , let $\mathbb{H}(\cdot;h)$ denote the alternating superposition of shifted, cut-off heteroclinic profiles, and let $\mathbb{G}(\cdot;h)$ denote the corresponding sum of shifted boundary corrections. Write

$$ \mathbb{H}_{*}=\mathbb{H}(\cdot;h),\quad\mathbb{G}_{*}=\mathbb{G}(\cdot;h),\quad g_{*}=\mathbb{H}_{*}+\mathbb{G}_{*},\qquad\phi=u-g_{*}, $$

so the stars denote the full alternating superposition, evaluated at the selected shifts. As in [29], we choose optimal shifts $h_{\alpha}$ so that, in twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to each sheet,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(y,z)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z)\,dz=0,\quad\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}\!\left((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))\right). $$

This orthogonality condition separates the equations for the layer positions from the coercive equation for the remainder.

Similarly to [29], in Section 6, projection of the Allen–Cahn equation onto the translational mode $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}$ yields a Toda-type relation between the mean curvature, the Laplacian of $h_{\alpha}$ , and the exponential interactions with the two adjacent sheets.

$$ H_{\alpha}(y,0)+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}(y)=\frac{2A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\left(e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|}-e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)|}\right)+E_{\alpha}^{0}(y), $$

where, at this stage, the error $E_{\alpha}^{0}$ has not yet been shown to be .

Section 7 closes these estimates by an inner–outer gluing estimates argument, as in [29, Section 6]. Near a layer, orthogonality removes the translation kernel and gives coercive estimates for the model linearised operator. Away from adjacent layers, the solution is close to $\pm 1$ and $W^{\prime\prime}(u)$ has a uniform positive lower bound. Combining the two estimates, together with the Neumann derivative of $\phi$ , gives

$$ \|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}}+\max_{\alpha}\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}}+\max_{\alpha}\|H_{\alpha}+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{\theta}}\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}+A, $$

where $A$ measures the largest exponential interaction between neighbouring sheets of the nodal set.

This estimate is still insufficient for the final separation argument of Section 10, as $\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}$ could still be of the same order as the leading interaction. Section 8 therefore repeats the inner–outer analysis for the horizontal derivatives of $\phi$ , following [29, Section 7]. Unlike [29], we need to deal with the boundary conditions, which must be treated separately. Derivatives tangent to the boundary have controlled Neumann data, while the inward horizontal derivative has controlled Dirichlet data. As a result the mean curvature is shown to be equal to the difference of the two adjacent interactions, up to an error $O(\varepsilon^{2})+o(A)$ , which is small relative to the interaction scale used in the decay argument of Proposition 10.1.

The Toda equations alone do not force the sheets to separate. In Section 9, we use Allen–Cahn stability with test functions

$$ \varphi=\sum_{\alpha}\eta_{\alpha}\bigl(\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}+\mathbb{G}^{\prime}_{\alpha}\bigr), $$

where $\eta_{\alpha}$ is a function on the sheet $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Unlike [29, Section 8], the boundary correction also enters the linearised equation and we must combine the horizontal and transverse contributions to the diagonal energy by integration by parts before estimating them, and exploit the cancellations supplied by the equation defining the correction $\mathbb{G}$ . A Robin-type boundary term of order $\varepsilon$ still remains, which is controlled by trace estimates with a small loss in the constant in front of the Dirichlet energy and controlled $L^{2}$ errors.

Section 10 combines the Toda equation with the stability inequality to obtain a quantitative lower bound for the distances between neighbouring sheets. The height difference (with respect to the base $\{z=0\}$ ) satisfies a homogeneous Neumann condition, which allows to perform integration by parts without producing additional boundary terms. On the other hand, using height difference rather than sheet separation causes an additional logarithmic loss compared to Wang–Wei, as the first-order metric error in boundary Fermi coordinates limits the iteration to $A\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ . Wang and Wei manage to improve this bound to $A\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}$ in Euclidean space by deriving an equation directly for the separation function on a sheet; however, extending this improvement to our setting would require further work, as the intrinsic separation function does not generally satisfy a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition. Indeed, the normal derivative of this intrinsic separation function contains a term involving the second fundamental form of the ambient boundary whose contribution need not be small after rescaling. Therefore, implementing an intrinsic improvement argument in our setting would require further estimates to control this boundary contribution; these are not established in the present paper.

The proof of the pointwise estimates also differs from [29, Section 9]. Following Farina [12], we first combine the scalar inequality with stability to obtain $L^{p}$ estimates for the normalized exponential interaction, with $p>n/2$ and then obtain local boundedness by a blowup argument. This argument replaces the Green-function and Morrey estimates used in [29, Lemma 9.7-Lemma 9.8] and applies both to interior balls and to boundary half-balls. As stability gives $L^{p}$ control of the interaction for exponents $p<5$ and local boundedness requires $p>n/2$ , this forces $n\leq 9$ , explaining the ambient dimension bound $n+1\leq 10$ .

Finally, in Section 11, we insert this bound into the improved Toda equation and use the oddness of the boundary correction to obtain the nodal mean-curvature estimates. On the other hand, as explained in Section 1.2, for a nonzero transition level, we represent the portion of $\{u=t\}$ near $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ as a graph $z=\ell_{\alpha}(y,t)$ by solving $u(y,\ell_{\alpha}(y,t))=t$ . The boundary correction changes the height of this graph by a quantity proportional to $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,\mathbb{H}^{-1}(t))$ . Differentiating twice along the sheet therefore introduces second horizontal derivatives of this correction. These derivatives vanish on the central profile slice because $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$ , but generally contribute to the mean curvature of nonzero levels, see Lemma 11.6 and Proposition 11.7, giving rise to the difference in behaviour between the nodal set and the other level sets in the transition region, which is the most relevant difference between the boundary problem and the interior one. When the boundary is totally geodesic, the correction vanishes altogether, and the improved separation estimate gives the expected bounds on every transition level.

### 2. Basic definitions and notation

In this section, we present some basic definitions and introduce the notation which we shall use throughout the paper.

Let $W\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ is an even double-well potential, namely $W:\mathbb{R}\to[0,+\infty)$ has the following properties

- (1) $W$ vanishes precisely at $\pm 1$ , and $W^{\prime}(\pm 1)=0$ , $W^{\prime\prime}(\pm 1)=1$ ;

- (2) $0$ is the unique critical point of $W$ in $(-1,1)$ , $W^{\prime}(0)=0$ , and $W^{\prime\prime}(0)<0$ ;

- (3) $W(t)=W(-t)$ .

The normalisation $W^{\prime\prime}(\pm 1)=1$ is responsible for the decay rate $e^{-|t|}$ in Appendix C. Evenness is used in Section 5 to make the boundary correction odd in the normal variable.

Let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold with boundary. We shall often use $\langle\cdot,\cdot,\rangle$ to denote the inner product with respect to the Riemannian metric $\mathrm{g}$ . Throughout this paper we shall consider stable critical points $u:M\to(-1,1)$ of the Allen–Cahn energy

$$ E_{\varepsilon}(u)=\int_{M}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{g}}. $$

Any such critical point is a solution of (1.1). If $S\subset\partial M$ , then a solution $u$ of (1.1) is stable in $M\cup S$ if

$$ \frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\Bigl|_{t=0}E_{\varepsilon}(u+t\psi)=\int_{M}\left(\varepsilon^{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\psi^{2}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{g}}\geq 0 $$

for every $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(M\cup S)$ . Notice that test functions $\psi$ need not vanish on $S$ .

For a solution $u_{\varepsilon}$ of (1.1) and $x\in M$ such that $|\nabla u(x)|\neq 0$ , we define the enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}(u)$ of the level set $\{u=u(x)\}$ at $x$ by

$$ \mathcal{A}(u)=\nabla\!\left(\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|}\right). $$

Notice that $\nabla u(x)/|\nabla u(x)|$ is the unit normal of the hypersurface $\{u=u(x)\}$ at $x$ . We extend $\mathcal{A}(u)$ to the whole of $M$ by setting $|\mathcal{A}(u)|=0$ on the critical set. It is easy to check that if $|\nabla u(x)|\neq 0$ , then at $x$ , we have

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u)|^{2}=\frac{|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}-|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}}{|\nabla u|^{2}}=|\mathrm{I\!I}(u)|^{2}+|\nabla^{T}\log|\nabla u||^{2}, $$

where $\mathrm{I\!I}(u)$ denotes the second fundamental form of the regular hypersurface $\{u=u(x)\}$ at $x$ and $\nabla^{T}$ denotes tangential differentiation along $\{u=u(x)\}$ . Thus $|\mathcal{A}(u)|$ dominates the second fundamental form of the level sets.

Our sign convention for the second fundamental form $\mathrm{I\!I}$ and the mean curvature $H$ of a hypersurface is

$$ \mathrm{I\!I}(X,Y)=-\langle\nabla_{X}\mathbf{n},Y\rangle,\qquad H=\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{I\!I}, $$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the chosen unit normal. With this convention, the linearization of mean curvature in the normal direction $\psi\mathbf{n}$ is $\Delta\psi+(|\mathrm{I\!I}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}(\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}))\psi$ .

#### 2.1. Balls in Euclidean space

Consider Euclidean coordinates $(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},x_{n+1})$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ . We shall adopt the following notation for various types of balls in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ .

- • $\mathbb{B}_{r}(p)$ (resp. $\bar{\mathbb{B}}_{r}(p)$ ) : the open (resp. closed) ball in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ centered at $p$ with radius $r$ .

- • $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(p)$ (resp. $\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{r}(p)$ ) : the open (resp. closed) half-ball $\mathbb{B}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}\geq 0\}$ (resp. $\bar{\mathbb{B}}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}\geq 0\}$ ).

- • $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(p)$ = $\partial\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}=0\}$ , $\partial_{+}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(p)$ = $\partial\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}>0\}$ .

- • $B_{r}(p)$ (resp. $\bar{B}_{r}(p)$ ) : the open (resp. closed) ball in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ centered at $p$ with radius $r$ .

- • $B^{+}_{r}(p)$ (resp. $\bar{B}^{+}_{r}(p)$ ) : the open (resp. closed) half-ball $B_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}\geq 0\}$ (resp. $\bar{B}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}\geq 0\}$ )

- • $\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r}(p)$ = $\partial B^{+}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}=0\}$ , $\partial_{+}B^{+}_{r}(p)$ = $\partial B^{+}_{r}(p)\cap\{x_{1}=0\}$ .

#### 2.2. Constants dependence

If $a\leq Cb$ , for some universal constant $C$ , we will frequently use the notation $a\lesssim b$ , or $a=O(b)$ . If we wish to explicit the dependence of the constant $C$ on certain parameters $\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{j}$ , we will use the symbol $\lesssim_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{j}}$ , or simply $O_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{j}}$ . When we have the two-sided bound $C^{-1}b\leq a\leq Cb$ , we will write $a\sim b$ , or $a\sim_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{j}}$ , if the dependence depends on the parameters ${\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{j}}$ .

Unless explicitly indicated otherwise, all constants are independent of $\varepsilon$ , of the number of layers, and of the layer index. An estimate containing an unspecified derivative order is understood for each fixed order, with the constant allowed to depend on that order and on the corresponding smooth bounds for the fixed geometric data. Finally, every little- $o$ estimate in the paper is uniform in all layer and level parameters occurring in its statement.

## Part I Derivation of the Toda system

### 3. Preliminary setup

In this section, we shall prove some preliminary results about stable solutions of (1.1) satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition. This preliminary analysis will allow us to reduce Theorem 1.1 to the local statement of Theorem 3.3.

Throughout this section, let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth compact $(n+1)$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold with non-empty smooth boundary and let $\varepsilon>0$ . Let $S\subset\partial M$ be a relatively open domain in $\partial M=\overline{M}\setminus M$ , and let $u_{\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}(M\cup S,(-1,1))$ be a stable solution of (1.1) satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $S$ . Suppose $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies (3.1) and $M^{\prime}\Subset M\cup S$ . Fix $b^{\prime}\in(b,1)$ , $\Lambda>0$ and $M^{\prime}\Subset M\cup S$ , and assume

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|\leq\Lambda_{0}\quad\text{on }\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b\}\cap\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\neq 0\}. $$

#### Lemma 3.1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, there are constants $\varepsilon_{\bullet}>0$ and $c>0$ , depending only on $b$ , $\Lambda$ , $W$ , and the fixed geometry near $M^{\prime}$ , such that, whenever $0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{\bullet}$ ,

$$ \varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\geq c\qquad\text{in }\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b\}\cap M^{\prime}. $$

#### Proof.

The argument is similar to [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1]. Let us assume by contradiction that there exist sequences $(u_{\varepsilon_{i}},\varepsilon_{i})$ with $\varepsilon_{i}\rightarrow 0$ , $p_{i}\in\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq 1-b\}\cap M^{\prime}$ so that $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\in C^{\infty}(M\cup S,(-1,1))$ is a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{i}$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $S$ and $\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(p_{i})|\rightarrow 0$ . Let $d_{i}=d_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{i},S)=d_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{i},q_{i})$ , where $q_{i}\in S$ is the nearest point projection of $p_{i}$ to $S$ ; we need to consider two cases:

- (i) either $\liminf_{i\rightarrow\infty}\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}d_{i}=\infty$ ,

- (ii) or $\liminf_{i\rightarrow\infty}\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}d_{i}<\infty$ .

Assume first that $d_{i}/\varepsilon_{i}\to\infty$ . In geodesic normal coordinates centreed at $p_{i}$ , define

$$ E_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}(v)=\exp_{p_{i}}(\varepsilon_{i}v),\qquad\mathrm{g}_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}=\varepsilon_{i}^{-2}E_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}^{*}\mathrm{g},\qquad\widetilde{u}_{i}=u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\circ E_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}. $$

After identifying $T_{p_{i}}M^{\prime}$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by choosing an orthonormal basis, the domain of $E_{p,\varepsilon}$ can be identified with $B_{\varepsilon^{-1}r}(0)$ , where $r=\operatorname{inj}_{p}$ . Then $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=1$ on $(B_{r_{i}}(0),\mathrm{g}_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}})$ , where $r_{i}=(2\varepsilon_{i})^{-1}\min\{d_{i},\operatorname{inj}_{p_{i}}\}$ , $|\tilde{u}_{i}(0)|\leq 1-b$ , $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{i}(0)|\rightarrow 0$ and $\mathrm{g}_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}$ converges to the Euclidean metric in $C^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ . Hence, by elliptic estimates, $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ . Therefore, there exists $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ , a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ , such that up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_{i}\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{2}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ . Since $|\tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|\leq 1-b$ , $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|=0$ , $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is non-constant. As in [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1], by (3.1), we have $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b\}\cap\{|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$ . By the unique continuation principle (for example see [16]) for the linear equation $\Delta\partial_{i}\tilde{u}_{\infty}=W^{\prime}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})\partial_{i}\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ ( $i=1,\dots,n+1$ ) and Lebesgue’s density theorem, the critical set $\{\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}=0\}$ has zero Lebesgue measure. By (2.2) and $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\varepsilon})|\leq\Lambda\varepsilon$ (which follows from (3.1)), we conclude that $\{\tilde{u}_{\infty}=t\}$ is a flat hyperplane for almost every $t\in[-1+b,1-b]$ . This implies that $\tilde{u}_{\infty}=U(x\cdot e)$ , where $U:\mathbb{R}\to[-1,1]$ is a nonconstant stable entire solution of the 1-dimensional Allen–Cahn equation and $e$ is a unit vector. In particular, $U$ must be the 1-dimensional heteroclinic solution $\mathbb{H}$ , which implies that $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}(0)|\neq 0$ . Thus we arrive at a contradiction.

Assume now $\liminf_{i\rightarrow\infty}\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}d_{i}<\infty$ , there exists $d\geq 0$ such that, possibly after passing to a subsequence, $\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}d_{i}=d$ . In boundary Fermi coordinates centreed at $q_{i}$ , define

$$ E_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}(x_{1},x^{\prime})=\exp^{M}_{\exp^{\partial M}_{q_{i}}(\varepsilon_{i}x^{\prime})}\!\left(\varepsilon_{i}x_{1}\nu_{\partial M}\bigl(\exp^{\partial M}_{q_{i}}(\varepsilon_{i}x^{\prime})\bigr)\right),\qquad\mathrm{g}_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}=\varepsilon_{i}^{-2}E_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}^{*}\mathrm{g}. $$

These coordinates map $\{x_{1}=0\}$ exactly to $\partial M$ . Thus $\widetilde{u}_{i}=u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\circ E_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}$ satisfies the homogeneous Neumann condition on the flat boundary, the metrics converge smoothly to the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}$ , and the preimages of $p_{i}$ remain in a fixed compact set. Then there is a fixed $r>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $i$ the normal exponential map of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $B^{\partial M}_{r}(q_{i})\times[0,r)$ . In particular, $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=1$ on $(B^{+}_{r_{i}}(0),\mathrm{g}_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}})$ , where $r_{i}=(2\varepsilon_{i})^{-1}\min\{d(q_{i},\partial M\setminus S),r\}$ , and it satisfies the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r_{i}}(0)$ . Moreover, if $\tilde{p}_{i}=E_{q_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}^{-1}(p_{i})$ , then $|\tilde{u}_{i}(\tilde{p}_{i})|\leq 1-b$ and $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{i}(\tilde{p}_{i})|\rightarrow 0$ . Since $\mathrm{g}_{p_{i},\varepsilon_{i}}$ converges to the Euclidean metric in $C^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ , $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ . Therefore, there exists $\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}$ , a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}$ , such that up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_{i}\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}$ in $C^{2}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ . Moreover, there exists $\tilde{p}_{\infty}$ such that up to a subsequence, $\tilde{p}_{i}\rightarrow\tilde{p}_{\infty}$ ; so $|\tilde{p}_{\infty}|=d$ , $|\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|\leq 1-b$ , $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|=0$ . Hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}$ is non-constant. We define $\tilde{u}_{\infty}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ by

$$ \tilde{u}_{\infty}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n+1})=\begin{cases}\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n+1})&\text{ when }x_{1}\geq 0;\\
\tilde{u}_{\infty}^{*}(-x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n+1})&\text{ when }x_{1}\leq 0.\end{cases} $$

Then $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a stable solution of (1.1) with $\varepsilon=1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ . Since $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ satisfies (3.1), arguing as in [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1], we conclude that $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b\}\cap\{|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$ . Similarly to the previous case, by unique continuation and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is again of the form $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(x)=\mathbb{H}(x\cdot e)$ for some unit vector $e$ . Hence $|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}(\tilde{p}_{\infty})|\neq 0$ . Thus we arrive again at a contradiction. ∎

#### 3.1. Fermi coordinates with respect to the boundary and graphical representation of layers

We shall now discuss the definition and the properties of Fermi coordinates with respect to $S$ following [20, Appendix A]. Let $S^{\prime}\Subset S$ and $p\in S^{\prime}$ . Let $x_{1}=\text{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(-,\partial M)$ , which is smooth in a neighbourhood of $p$ contained in $M^{\prime}$ . Suppose $(x_{2},\dots,x_{n+1})$ is a normal coordinate system on $S$ centred at $p$ , which is obtained by fixing an orthonormal basis of $T_{p}S$ . Then $(x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{n+1})$ is a Fermi coordinate system for $(M,\partial M)$ near $p$ . The Fermi distance function from $p$ is defined by $\bar{r}_{p}(x)=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\dots+x_{n+1}^{2}}$ . The Fermi coordinate ball $\mathcal{B}_{r}(p)$ defined by $\mathcal{B}_{r}(p)\coloneqq\{\bar{r}_{p}<r\}$ can be identified with $B^{+}_{r}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ .

#### Lemma 3.2.

[20, Lemma A.2] There exist constants $r_{1}$ and $\{\mathsf{C}_{m}\}_{m=0}^{\infty}$ depending only on the metric $\mathrm{g}$ and $S^{\prime}$ such that the following holds. Let $\mathrm{g}_{ij}$ , $\bar{\Gamma}_{ij}^{k}$ denote the components of $\mathrm{g}$ and the Christoffel symbols in a Fermi coordinate system centreed at $p$ . Then

$$ \mathrm{g}_{11}=1,\quad\mathrm{g}_{1i}=0,\quad\bar{\Gamma}_{i1}^{1}=\bar{\Gamma}_{11}^{i}=\bar{\Gamma}_{11}^{1}=0\quad\forall i\geq 2 $$

and for all $1\leq i,j\leq n+1$ ,

$$ \left|\mathrm{g}_{ij}(x)-\delta_{ij}\right|\leq C_{0}\bar{r}_{p}(x)\text{ on }\mathcal{B}_{r_{1}}(p),\quad\|\mathrm{g}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\|_{C^{m}(\mathcal{B}_{r_{1}}(p))}\leq\mathsf{C}_{m}\;\forall\;m\geq 0. $$

For the current purpose, let $S^{\prime}=\{|u_{\varepsilon}|<1-b\}\cap S\cap M^{\prime}$ , and let $p\in S^{\prime}$ . By Lemma 3.1, $S^{\prime}\Subset\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\neq 0\}$ . Since $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies the vanishing Neumann boundary condition on $S$ , $\nabla u_{\varepsilon}/\left|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\right|\in T_{p}S$ . Choose an orthonormal basis $\{e_{2},\dots,e_{n+1}\}$ of $T_{p}S$ such that $e_{n+1}=\nabla u_{\varepsilon}/\left|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\right|$ . Let $(x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{n+1})$ be the Fermi coordinate system for $(M,\partial M)$ centred at $p$ so that for $i\geq 2$ , $\partial_{x_{i}}|_{p}=e_{i}$ .

Then, for the function $F(x)=u_{\varepsilon}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},x_{n+1})-t$ , $\partial_{x_{n+1}}F(x)=|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|G(x)$ , where the function $G$ is defined by $G(x)=\mathrm{g}\left(\frac{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}}{\left|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\right|},\partial_{x_{n+1}}\right)$ on $\mathcal{B}_{r_{1}}(p)$ (where $r_{1}$ is as in Lemma 3.2). We note that $G(p)=1$ and its derivative on $\{\left|u_{\varepsilon}\right|<1-b^{\prime}\}\cap\mathcal{B}_{r_{1}}(p)$ is bounded by a constant which depends only on $\Lambda$ and $\mathrm{g}$ .

By the mean value theorem and the implicit function theorem, there exists a constant $r_{2}=r_{2}(\Lambda,\mathrm{g})$ such that in $\mathcal{B}_{r_{2}}(p)$ , for all $t\in(-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime})$ , $\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}$ is a union of graphs $\cup_{\alpha}\{x_{n+1}=\bar{f}^{t}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\}$ . Moreover, $\partial_{1}\bar{f}^{t}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}=0$ along $S$ (since $\partial_{1}u_{\varepsilon}=0$ along $S$ ) and $|\nabla^{2}\bar{f}^{t}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}|\leq|\mathcal{A}|$ is bounded by a constant which depends only on $\Lambda$ and $\mathrm{g}$ by (3.1). All of these estimates are uniform in $t$ and in the graphical component.

#### 3.2. A reduction of curvature estimates

In view of the above discussion in Section 3.1, to prove Theorem 1.1, it is enough to prove the following Theorem 3.3. Indeed, Theorem 3.3 implies that Theorem 1.1 holds on the collar neighbourhood $M^{\prime}\cap\mathcal{N}_{r_{2}/3}(\partial M)$ (where $r_{2}$ is as in Section 3.1). On the other hand, on $M^{\prime}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{r_{2}/4}(\partial M)$ , the proof of Theorem 1.1 follows from [28, 29, 22, 5].

The constants $\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ in (3.7), (3.8), (3.9) and (3.10) are fixed before $\varepsilon_{0}$ is chosen and will be assumed to be sufficiently small.

If, in addition, $\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)$ is totally geodesic and $0<b<b^{\prime}<1$ , then, uniformly for $t\in[-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime}]$ , every corresponding graphical component of $\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}$ satisfies

### 4. Geometric setup and twisted Fermi coordinates

In this section we define suitable coordinates (which we refer to as twisted Fermi coordinates) near the boundary which are adapted to the geometry of the components of the zero level set of the solution $u_{\varepsilon}$ .

Before introducing this coordinate system, following [29], we rescale distances by $\varepsilon^{-1}$ , so that we work with a stable solution of the Allen–Cahn equation with parameter 1 in ball of radius of order $\varepsilon^{-1}$ .

#### 4.1. Basic geometric setup

#### 4.1.1. Properties of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ -rescaled geometry

Let $B_{3}^{+}(0)$ be equipped with a Riemannian metric $\hat{g}$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem 3.3. From now on, as in [28, 29], we work in the rescaled domain $(B^{+}_{3R}(0),g)$ where $R=\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $g$ is the rescaled metric given by

$$ g_{ij}(x)=\hat{g}_{ij}(\varepsilon x). $$

Notice that, by (3.7), the metric $g$ satisfies

$$ \sup_{x\in B^{+}_{3R}(0)}\sum_{\ell=0}^{4}\varepsilon^{-\ell}|\partial^{(\ell)}(g_{ij}-\delta_{ij})(x)|\leq C(n)\eta_{0} $$

for all indices $i,j$ . Therefore, the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma_{ij}^{k}$ of the metric $g$ satisfy

$$ \sup_{x\in B^{+}_{3R}(0)}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3}\varepsilon^{-(\ell+1)}|\partial^{(\ell)}\Gamma_{ij}^{k}(x)|\leq C(n)\eta_{0}, $$

and the components $R_{ijkl}$ of the Riemann tensor of $g$ are of order $\varepsilon^{2}$ :

$$ \sup_{x\in B^{+}_{3R}(0)}\varepsilon^{-2}|R_{ijkl}(x)|\leq C(n)\eta_{0}. $$

Finally, the second fundamental form $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B^{+}_{3R}(0)}$ of the boundary and its derivatives also satisfy similar estimates:

$$ \varepsilon^{-(\ell+1)}|\nabla^{\ell}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B^{+}_{3R}(0)}|\leq C(n)\eta_{0} $$

for $\ell=0,1,2,3$ .

If we define $u(x)=u_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon x)$ , then $u:(B^{+}_{3R}(0),g)\rightarrow(-1,1)$ satisfies the Allen–Cahn equation with parameter $1$ , i.e.

$$ -\Delta u+W^{\prime}(u)=0, $$

with Neumann boundary condition $\partial_{x_{1}}u=0$ on $\partial_{0}B_{3R}^{+}(0)$ . In the rescaled coordinates, by (3.10) we have

$$ |\mathcal{A}|=O(\varepsilon) $$

on $B^{+}_{3R-1}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ . In particular, the estimate holds in a fixed neighbourhood of every component of the zero level set.

Note that in above setup, the following derivative estimates holds (see also [28, Lemma 8.1]).

#### Proposition 4.1 (Derivative estimates for the enhanced second fundamental form).

For every fixed integer $k\geq 0$ ,

$$ |\nabla^{k}\mathcal{A}|=O(\varepsilon) $$

on $B^{+}_{3R-1}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ for all $k\geq 0$ . As a consequence, if $x\in\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ and $\Sigma=\{u=u(x)\}$ , then

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}^{k}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma}|=O(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Sigma\cap B^{+}_{3R-1}(0)\ \ \forall k\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

See Appendix A for the proof. ∎

Let $\Xi$ denote the union of all the connected components of $\{u=0\}\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ which have non-empty intersections with $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\times(-1.5R,1.5R)$ . Then, using the notations of Section 3.2, $\Xi$ can be written as a union of graphs

$$ \Xi=\bigcup_{\alpha}\Sigma_{\alpha},\quad\Sigma_{\alpha}=\{x_{n+1}=f_{\alpha}(x^{\prime}):x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\}, $$

where $f_{\alpha}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0),(-1.6R,1.6R))$ , $f_{\alpha}(x^{\prime})=\varepsilon^{-1}\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\varepsilon x^{\prime})$ , $\partial_{1}f_{\alpha}=0\text{ along }\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)$ ,

$$ \left|\nabla f_{\alpha}\right|\leq\eta_{0},\quad|\nabla^{2}f_{\alpha}|\leq\Lambda_{0}\varepsilon,\quad|\nabla^{k}f_{\alpha}|=O(\varepsilon)\ \ \forall k\geq 2\text{ on }\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0). $$

We fix an index $\alpha$ and set $f=f_{\alpha}$ , $\Sigma=\{x_{n+1}=f(x^{\prime}):x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\}$ . Following [23, Page 28], we discuss the definition and the properties of the twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma$ .

Applying the standard extension operator in $C^{m}$ for every fixed $m$ (see [15, Lemma 6.37]), choose smooth extensions $f^{*}$ and $g^{*}$ to the full balls, equal to $\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ and $\hat{g}$ on the corresponding half-balls, such that, for every fixed $m$ used below,

$$ \displaystyle\|f^{*}\|_{C^{m}(\mathbb{B}_{2}(0))} \displaystyle\leq C(n,m)\|\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{C^{m}(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(0))}, \displaystyle\|\delta_{ij}-g^{*}_{ij}\|_{C^{m}(B_{3}(0))} \displaystyle\leq C(n,m)\|\delta_{ij}-\hat{g}_{ij}\|_{C^{m}(B_{3}^{+}(0))}. $$

Define $\widetilde{f}(x^{\prime})=\varepsilon^{-1}f^{*}(\varepsilon x^{\prime})$ and $\widetilde{g}_{ij}(x)=g^{*}_{ij}(\varepsilon x)$ . These extensions are smooth, agree with the original data on the half-balls, and satisfy the rescaled estimates at every derivative order used below. Then $\tilde{f}=f$ on $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)$ and $\tilde{g}=g$ on $B^{+}_{3R}(0)$ . Notice that $\tilde{g}$ satisfies similar estimates to (4.2), (4.3), and (4.4) (possibly with different dimensional constants) by (4.13).

Subsequently, we will assume that all the metric dependent objects on $B_{3R}(0)$ (e.g. $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ , $\nabla$ etc.) are with respect to $\tilde{g}$ . Notice that $\tilde{g}=g$ on $B^{+}_{3R}(0)$ . We define $\tilde{\Sigma}=\{x_{n+1}=\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}):x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\}$ .

#### 4.1.2. Properties of the normal exponential map and Fermi coordinates

Let $\Omega=\mathbb{B}_{2R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ and $T\Omega$ denote the tangent bundle of $\Omega$ which can be canonically identified with $\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ . Let $(x_{1},\dots,x_{n+1},v_{1},\dots,v_{n+1})$ be the standard coordinates on $T\Omega$ , $\pi_{x}:T\Omega\rightarrow\Omega$ and $\pi_{v}:T\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ the projection maps. Let $\Phi(s,-)$ be the flow of the vector field

$$ X(x,v)=\sum_{k}v_{k}\partial_{x_{k}}\big|_{(x,v)}-\sum_{i,j,k}\Gamma_{ij}^{k}(x)v_{i}v_{j}\partial_{v_{k}}\big|_{(x,v)}, $$

$\Phi_{1}=\pi_{x}\circ\Phi$ , $\Phi_{2}=\pi_{v}\circ\Phi$ . Then $\Phi_{1}(s,x,v)=\exp_{x}(sv)$ and $\Phi_{2}(s,x,v)=\frac{d}{ds}\exp_{x}(sv)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{s}\Phi_{1}^{k}=\Phi_{2}^{k},\quad\text{and}\quad\partial_{s}\Phi_{2}^{k}=-\sum_{ij}\Gamma^{k}_{ij}(\Phi_{1})\Phi_{2}^{i}\Phi_{2}^{j}, $$

for all $k$ . Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of $(x,v)$ for which $|v|\leq\delta R$ and the geodesic $s\mapsto\exp_{x}(sv)$ remains in $\Omega$ for $0\leq s\leq 1$ , where $\delta>0$ is fixed and small, and define $\mathscr{E}:\mathcal{S}\to\Omega$ by $\mathscr{E}(x,v)=\exp_{x}(v)$ . Note that the coefficients $\Gamma_{ij}^{k}$ are computed in the $x_{i}$ coordinates.

#### Lemma 4.2.

For all $(x,v)\in\mathcal{S}$ and indices $i,j$ , there holds

$$ |\partial_{x_{i}}\mathscr{E}^{j}(x,v)-\delta_{ij}|+|\partial_{v_{i}}\mathscr{E}^{j}(x,v)-\delta_{ij}|\lesssim\varepsilon|v|,\quad|D^{m}\mathscr{E}^{i}(x,v)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|v|)\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to [17, Proposition A.1]. Since $\mathscr{E}(x,v)=\Phi_{1}(1,x,v)$ , we are going to restrict $\Phi$ on $[0,1]\times\mathcal{S}$ in this proof. Differentiating (4.14) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{s}\partial_{*}\Phi_{1}^{k}=\partial_{*}\Phi_{2}^{k},\qquad\partial_{s}\partial_{*}\Phi_{2}^{k}=-\sum_{ijl}\partial_{x_{l}}\Gamma^{k}_{ij}(\Phi_{1})\partial_{*}\Phi_{1}^{l}\Phi_{2}^{i}\Phi_{2}^{j}-2\sum_{ij}\Gamma^{k}_{ij}(\Phi_{1})\partial_{*}\Phi_{2}^{i}\Phi_{2}^{j}, $$

where $\partial_{*}$ is any element in $\{\partial_{x_{i}},\partial_{v_{i}}:i=1,\dots,n+1\}$ . We note that $\Phi(0,x,v)=(x,v)$ , $|\Phi_{2}(s,x,v)|=|v|$ and (since the metric $\tilde{g}$ is uniformly close to the Euclidean metric) $\varepsilon|v|=O(1)$ for all $(x,v)\in\mathcal{S}$ . Therefore, using Gronwall’s inequality for vector valued functions [19, Theorem D.2], we conclude that $|\partial_{*}\Phi(s,x,v)|$ is uniformly bounded for $(s,x,v)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{S}$ . Using this, one can deduce from (4.16) that $|\partial_{s}\partial_{*}\Phi_{2}^{k}|\lesssim\varepsilon|v|$ and $|\partial_{*}\Phi_{1}^{k}(1,x,v)-\partial_{*}\Phi_{1}^{k}(0,x,v)-\partial_{*}\Phi_{2}^{k}(0,x,v)|\lesssim\varepsilon|v|.$ This implies the $C^{1}$ estimate for $\mathscr{E}$ .

Differentiating (4.16) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&\partial_{s}\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{1}^{k}=\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{2}^{k},\\
&\partial_{s}\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{2}^{k}=-\sum_{ijl}\partial_{x_{l}}\Gamma^{k}_{ij}(\Phi_{1})\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{1}^{l}\Phi_{2}^{i}\Phi_{2}^{j}-2\sum_{ij}\Gamma^{k}_{ij}(\Phi_{1})\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{2}^{i}\Phi_{2}^{j}+\mathcal{E}\end{split} $$

where $\partial_{\circ}$ is any element in $\{\partial_{x_{i}},\partial_{v_{i}}:i=1,\dots,n+1\}$ and $|\mathcal{E}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|v|).$ Note that $\mathcal{E}$ does not contain any second order derivatives of $\Phi$ . Therefore, using Gronwall’s inequality for vector valued functions [19, Theorem D.2], we obtain that $|\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi(s,x,v)|$ is uniformly bounded for $(s,x,v)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{S}$ . Using this, one can deduce from (4.17) that $|\partial_{s}\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{2}^{k}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|v|)$ , which implies $|\partial_{\circ,*}\Phi_{1}^{k}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|v|)$ . Thus we obtain the $C^{2}$ estimate for $\mathscr{E}$ and the higher order estimates can be proved in a similar way. ∎

Let $\tilde{t}:\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\to\mathbb{R}$ be the signed distance function from $\tilde{\Sigma}$ such that $\partial_{x_{n+1}}\tilde{t}>0$ along $\tilde{\Sigma}$ . By (4.11), if $\eta_{0},\Lambda_{0}$ are sufficiently small

- (i) $\tilde{t}$ is smooth on $\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ ;

- (ii) the nearest point projection map $\tilde{\Pi}:\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\rightarrow\tilde{\Sigma}$ is a well-defined smooth map, whose image is contained in $\tilde{\Sigma}\cap(\mathbb{B}_{1.9R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ .

#### Remark 4.3.

In what follows, we will denote by $\nabla$ the gradient of a scalar map, while $D$ will be used for the gradient of vector valued maps, i.e. the gradient of each component. Furthermore, everything will be computed in the ambient coordinates $(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n+1})$ .

#### Lemma 4.4.

There exists $\tilde{\delta}>0$ , independent of $\varepsilon$ , such that the following holds.

$$ |D\tilde{\Pi}|=O(1),\quad|\nabla^{m}\tilde{t}|+|D^{m}\tilde{\Pi}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tilde{t}|)\quad\text{ on }\{|\tilde{t}|\leq\tilde{\delta}R\}\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}:\tilde{\Sigma}\times(-\tilde{\delta}R,\tilde{\delta}R)\to\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ be defined by $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z})=\exp_{y}(\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))=\mathscr{E}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))$ , where $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit normal along $\tilde{\Sigma}$ satisfying $\langle\mathbf{n},\partial_{x_{n+1}}\rangle>0$ , and $\tilde{\delta}>0$ will be determined later in the proof. We note that if $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in\tilde{\Sigma}$ , then $x_{i}(y)=y_{i}$ if $1\leq i\leq n$ and $x_{n+1}(y)=\tilde{f}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{y_{j}}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^{i}(y,\tilde{z})&=\partial_{x_{j}}\mathscr{E}^{i}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))+\partial_{x_{n+1}}\mathscr{E}^{i}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\partial_{x_{j}}f(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\\
&+\sum_{k}\tilde{z}\partial_{v_{k}}\mathscr{E}^{i}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\partial_{y_{j}}\mathbf{n}^{k}(y),\\
\partial_{\tilde{z}}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^{i}(y,\tilde{z})&=\sum_{k}\partial_{v_{k}}\mathscr{E}^{i}(y,\tilde{z}\mathbf{n}(y))\mathbf{n}^{k}(y).\end{split} $$

Therefore, by Lemma 4.2 and (4.11), we have

$$ |\partial_{y_{j}}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}^{i}(y,\tilde{z})-\delta_{ij}|\lesssim\varepsilon|\tilde{z}|+\eta_{0},\;1\leq i,j\leq n+1, $$

where $\partial_{y_{n+1}}$ stands for $\partial_{\tilde{z}}$ . This implies that if $\delta$ and $\eta_{0}$ are sufficiently small, the Jacobian of $\tilde{\mathscr{E}}$ is greater or equal than $1/2$ . Differentiating (4.19) and using Lemma 4.2, one can show that

$$ |D^{m}\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z})|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tilde{z}|)\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

Since $\tilde{t}(\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z}))=\tilde{z}$ and $\tilde{\Pi}(\tilde{\mathscr{E}}(y,\tilde{z}))=y$ , using inverse function theorem, one can deduce from (4.20) and (4.21) that if $\tilde{\delta}$ and $\eta_{0}$ are sufficiently small,

$$ |D\tilde{\Pi}|=O(1),\quad|\nabla^{m}\tilde{t}|+|D^{m}\tilde{\Pi}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tilde{t}|)\text{ on }\{|\tilde{t}|\leq\tilde{\delta}R\}\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

∎

#### 4.2. Definition and properties of twisted Fermi coordinates

#### 4.2.1. The twisted Fermi vector field and twisted Fermi coordinates

Let $\tilde{F}:\mathbb{B}_{2R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $\tilde{F}(x)=x_{n+1}-\tilde{f}(x^{\prime})$ . We define the following vector fields on $\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{Z}=\nabla\tilde{t};\quad Z_{1}=\frac{\nabla\tilde{F}}{|\nabla\tilde{F}|};\quad Z_{2}^{\prime}=\partial_{x_{1}}-\left\langle\partial_{x_{1}},Z_{1}\right\rangle Z_{1};\quad Z_{2}=\frac{Z_{2}^{\prime}}{\left|Z_{2}^{\prime}\right|};\quad Z=\frac{\tilde{Z}-\langle\tilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle Z_{2}}{1-\langle\tilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle^{2}}. $$

Then, $|Z_{2}^{\prime}|\to 1$ and $|\langle\tilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle|\to 0$ uniformly as $(\eta_{0}+\Lambda_{0})\rightarrow 0$ . Along $\Sigma$ , $\tilde{Z}=Z_{1}$ and is orthogonal to $\Sigma$ . Furthermore, $Z_{2}=\partial_{x_{1}}$ along $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ and is tangential to $\Sigma$ .

These facts imply the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.5.

The vector field $Z$ has the following properties.

- (i) $Z$ is tangential to $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ .

- (ii) $Z=\tilde{Z}$ along $\Sigma$ and is perpendicular to $\Sigma$ .

- (iii) $\langle Z,\tilde{Z}\rangle=1$ .

- (iv) $(Z-\tilde{Z})$ is perpendicular to $\tilde{Z}$ .

- (v) If $Z=\sum_{i}Z^{i}\partial_{x_{i}}$ then $|Z^{i}-\delta_{i,n+1}|\lesssim\eta_{0}+\Lambda_{0}$ .

Combining (4.9), (4.18), (4.11), (4.12), and (4.13) we infer

$$ |\nabla^{m}\tilde{Z}|+|\nabla^{m}Z_{1}|+|\nabla^{m}Z_{2}|+|\nabla^{m}Z|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tilde{t}|)\quad\text{on }\{|\tilde{t}|\leq\tilde{\delta}R\}\;\forall m\geq 1. $$

Let $\Theta(\tau,-)=\Theta_{\tau}$ denote the flow of $Z$ on $\mathbb{B}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ , so $\Theta(0,x)=x$ and

$$ \partial_{\tau}\Theta=Z(\Theta). $$

#### Definition 4.6 (Twisted Fermi coordinates).

Given a coordinate system $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})$ on $\Sigma$ , twisted Fermi coordinates on $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.8R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ with respect to $\Sigma$ are defined by $Y_{\Sigma}(y,z)=\Theta_{z}(y)$ , for $y\in\Sigma$ .

By Lemma 4.5 items (i) and (v), and (4.24), if $p\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ , then

- (i) $\Theta_{\tau}(p)\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.7R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ for all $\tau$ belonging to the domain of $\tau\mapsto\Theta_{\tau}(p)$ ,

- (ii) there exists a unique time $\tau_{p}\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\Theta_{-\tau_{p}}(p)\in\Sigma$ ,

provided $\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ are sufficiently small.

#### Definition 4.7 (Twisted Fermi coordinate time function and projection).

The twisted Fermi coordinate time function $t:\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ and projection map $\Pi:\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\rightarrow\Sigma\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.7R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ are defined by $t(p)=\tau_{p}$ and $\Pi(p)=\Theta(-t(p),p)$ .

From now on, $(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},z)$ will denote twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to this coordinate system on $\Sigma$ .

#### Remark 4.8.

Similar coordinate systems near a boundary point appear in [23, Section 10] and [17, Definition 2.10].

#### Lemma 4.9.

Let $p\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ . Then $\tilde{t}(p)=t(p)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $q=\Pi(p)$ . We consider the function $\gamma(\tau)=\tilde{t}(\Theta(\tau,q))$ . Then $\gamma(0)=0$ and by Lemma 4.5(iv), $\gamma^{\prime}(\tau)=\left\langle\nabla\tilde{t},Z\right\rangle(\Theta(\tau,q))=1$ . Hence, $\tilde{t}(p)=\gamma(\tau_{p})=\tau_{p}=t(p)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.10.

Let us fix $K>0$ . For all $(\tau,x)$ satisfying $|\tau|,|t(x)|\leq K\sqrt{R}$ and for all indices $i,j$ , there holds

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{j}(\tau,x)-\delta_{ij}|\lesssim\varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^{2}+|t(x)|^{2}), \displaystyle|D^{m}_{x}\Theta^{i}(\tau,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(|\tau|+\tau^{2}+t(x)^{2}),\qquad|D^{m}\Theta^{i}(\tau,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|^{2}+|t(x)|^{2})\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma 4.2. Differentiating (4.25) we obtain

$$ \partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{k}=\sum_{p}\partial_{x_{p}}Z^{k}(\Theta)\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{p}. $$

Furthermore, (4.24) implies $|\nabla^{m}Z(\Theta(\tau,x))|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|)$ for all $m\geq 1$ . Therefore, using Gronwall’s inequality for vector valued functions [19, Theorem D.2], we conclude that $|\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{k}|=O(1)$ . Using this estimate, we deduce from (4.28) that

$$ |\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{k}(\tau,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|), $$

hence

$$ |\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{k}(\tau,x)-\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{k}(0,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^{2}+|t(x)|^{2}). $$

This implies the $C^{1}$ estimate for $\Theta$ .

Differentiating (4.28), we obtain

$$ \partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}\Theta^{k}=\sum_{p,q}\partial_{x_{p}x_{q}}Z^{k}(\Theta)\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{p}\partial_{x_{j}}\Theta^{q}+\sum_{p}\partial_{x_{p}}Z^{k}(\Theta)\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}\Theta^{p}. $$

Therefore, using Gronwall’s inequality for vector valued functions [19, Theorem D.2], we conclude that $|\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}\Theta^{k}|=O(1)$ . Using this estimate, we deduce from (4.31) that

$$ |\partial_{\tau}\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}\Theta^{k}(\tau,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|+|t(x)|); $$

hence

$$ |\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}\Theta^{k}(\tau,x)|\lesssim\varepsilon(|\tau|+|\tau|^{2}+|t(x)|^{2}). $$

Combining (4.29) and (4.33), we obtain the $C^{2}$ estimates for $\Theta$ . Higher order estimates can be proved in a similar way. ∎

#### Lemma 4.11.

There exists $0<\delta<\tilde{\delta}$ , independent of $\varepsilon$ , such that the following holds.

$$ |D\Pi|=O(1),\quad|\nabla^{m}t|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|),\quad|D^{m}\Pi|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2})\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

#### Proof.

The estimates for $|\nabla^{m}t|$ follow from Lemma 4.4 and Lemma 4.9. Let $\hat{\Theta}$ denote the restriction of $\Theta$ on $[-\delta\sqrt{R},\delta\sqrt{R}]\times\Sigma$ , where $\delta\in(0,\tilde{\delta})$ is to be determined. We note that if $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in\Sigma$ , then $x_{i}(y)=y_{i}$ if $1\leq i\leq n$ and $x_{n+1}(y)=f(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{y_{i}}\hat{\Theta}^{j}(z,y)=\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{j}(z,y)+\partial_{x_{n+1}}\Theta^{j}(z,y)\partial_{x_{i}}f(y_{1},\dots,y_{n}), \displaystyle\partial_{z}\hat{\Theta}^{j}(z,y)=Z^{j}(\Theta(z,y)). $$

Therefore, by Lemma 4.10, (4.11) and Lemma 4.5(v), as $(\delta+\eta_{0}+\Lambda_{0})\to 0$ we infer

$$ |\partial_{y_{i}}\hat{\Theta}^{j}(z,y)-\delta_{ij}|=o(1),\;1\leq i,j\leq n+1, $$

where $\partial_{y_{n+1}}$ stands for $\partial_{z}$ . This implies if $\delta,\;\eta_{0},\;\Lambda_{0}$ are sufficiently small, the Jacobian of $\hat{\Theta}$ is greater or equal than $1/2$ . Differentiating (4.35) and using Lemma 4.10, one can show that

$$ |D^{m}\hat{\Theta}(z,y)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2})\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

Since $t(\hat{\Theta}(z,y))=z$ and $\Pi(\hat{\Theta}(z,y))=y$ , using inverse function theorem, one can deduce from (4.37) and (4.38) that if $\delta,\;\eta_{0},\;\Lambda_{0}$ are sufficiently small,

$$ |D\Pi|=O(1),\quad|D^{m}\Pi|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2})\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 2. $$

∎

Notice that by definition of twisted Fermi coordinates, if $x\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ , then

$$ \partial_{y_{i}}|_{x}=D\Theta_{t(x)}(\Pi(x))\big(\partial_{y_{i}}|_{\Pi(x)}\big). $$

Moreover, for $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in\Sigma$ , clearly $\partial_{y_{i}}|_{y}=\partial_{x_{i}}|_{y}+\partial_{x_{i}}f(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{y}$ , since $\Sigma$ is the graph of $f$ over $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)$ .

Hence, we obtain

$$ \partial_{y_{i}}|_{(y,z)}=\sum_{j}\partial_{x_{i}}\Theta^{j}(z,y)\partial_{x_{j}}|_{(y,z)}+\sum_{j}\partial_{x_{i}}f(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\partial_{x_{n+1}}\Theta^{j}(z,y)\partial_{x_{j}}|_{(y,z)}. $$

Equation (4.41) has several useful consequences, which we shall record below.

#### Lemma 4.12 (Covariant derivative estimates).

The following estimates hold for $\partial_{y_{i}}$ and its covariant derivatives

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{y_{i}}|=O(1) \displaystyle\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}, \displaystyle|\nabla^{m}\partial_{y_{i}}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2}) \displaystyle\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}\;\forall m\geq 1. $$

#### Proof.

The lemma follows from (4.41) and Lemma 4.10. ∎

#### Lemma 4.13 (Neumann derivative estimate).

The following estimate holds

$$ |\partial_{x_{1}}\varphi(y,z)-\partial_{y_{1}}\varphi(y,z)|\lesssim\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)|\nabla\varphi(y,z)|\text{ on }\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times[-\delta\sqrt{R},\delta\sqrt{R}] $$

for any smooth function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ .

#### Proof.

Notice that along $\partial_{0}\Sigma$ , $\partial_{x_{1}}f=0$ by the setup in 4.1, and $\partial_{x_{1}}=\partial_{y_{1}}$ by the definition of twisted Fermi coordinates. Hence, by (4.41), on $\partial_{0}\{|z|\leq K\sqrt{R}|\}$

$$ \partial_{y_{1}}|_{(y,z)}=\sum_{j}\partial_{x_{1}}\Theta^{j}(z,y)\partial_{x_{j}}|_{(y,z)}. $$

Then (4.44) follows directly from Lemma 4.10. ∎

#### Lemma 4.14.

There exists $\delta>0$ such that the following holds:

$$ d_{\Sigma}\left(\tilde{\Pi}(p),\Pi(p)\right)\lesssim\varepsilon(|t(p)|^{2}+|t(p)|^{3})\text{ on }\{|t|\leq\delta R\}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $q=\Pi(p)$ . We consider the function $G(\tau)=(\tilde{\Pi}_{1}(\Theta(\tau,q)),\dots,\tilde{\Pi}_{n}(\Theta(\tau,q)))$ , where $\tilde{\Pi}_{i}=y_{i}\circ\tilde{\Pi}$ . Then $G(0)=(y_{1}(q),\dots,y_{n}(q))$ ,

$$ \frac{d}{d\tau}\tilde{\Pi}(\Theta(\tau,q))=D\tilde{\Pi}(\Theta(\tau,q))(Z(\Theta(\tau,q))). $$

Note that $\tilde{\Pi}$ is constant along the integral curves of $\tilde{Z}$ . Therefore, by Lemma 4.5(ii), $G^{\prime}(0)=(0,\dots,0)$ . By Lemma 4.4 and (4.24), $\left|G^{\prime\prime}(\tau)\right|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|)$ . Therefore, by Taylor’s theorem,

$$ d_{\Sigma}\left(\tilde{\Pi}(p),\Pi(p)\right)\lesssim|G(t(p))-G(0)|\lesssim\varepsilon(|t(p)|^{2}+|t(p)|^{3}). $$

∎

Since $Z=\tilde{Z}$ along $\Sigma$ , the following lemma follows from (4.24).

#### Lemma 4.15.

There holds

$$ |Z-\tilde{Z}|\lesssim\varepsilon(|z|+z^{2}),\quad|\nabla^{m}(Z-\tilde{Z})|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|)\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta R\}\;\forall m\geq 1. $$

#### Remark 4.16.

By Lemma 4.5 (iv),

$$ \partial_{\tilde{z}}=\partial_{z}-T=\partial_{z}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}T^{i}\partial_{y_{i}}. $$

#### 4.2.2. Boundary behaviour of twisted Fermi coordinates

Finally, we shall carefully look at how these twisted Fermi coordinates behave at the boundary. The decomposition in the following lemma will be crucial in the Inverse Function Theorem argument of Section 5.

#### Lemma 4.17.

Let $J:\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $J=\partial_{x_{1}}t=dz(\nu)$ , $w(y)=\partial_{z}J(y,0)$ and $\tilde{J}(y,z)=J(y,z)-w(y)z$ . Then

$$ |J|=|\partial_{\nu}z|\lesssim\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|+|z|^{2})\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}. $$

Moreover,

$$ |\nabla^{k}w|=O(\varepsilon)\text{ on }\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\;\forall k\geq 0, $$

and

$$ |\nabla^{k}_{y}\tilde{J}|\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{3})z^{2}\text{ on }\{|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}\}\;\forall k\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma 4.9, $\nabla t=\widetilde{Z}$ , and hence $J=\langle\widetilde{Z},\nu\rangle$ . The sheet meets the boundary orthogonally, so $J(y,0)=0$ . Since $\partial_{z}=Z$ and the integral curves of $\widetilde{Z}$ are unit-speed geodesics,

$$ \partial_{z}J=\langle\nabla_{Z-\widetilde{Z}}\widetilde{Z},\nu\rangle+\langle\widetilde{Z},\nabla_{Z}\nu\rangle. $$

With the sign convention of Section 2, $\langle X,\nabla_{Y}\nu\rangle=-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}}(Y,X)$ for vectors tangent to the boundary. At $z=0$ , where $Z=\widetilde{Z}$ , this gives

$$ w(y)=\partial_{z}J(y,0)=-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}}(\widetilde{Z},\widetilde{Z})(y,0). $$

In particular, (4.5) and the tangential derivative bounds for $\widetilde{Z}$ imply (4.49).

Differentiating (4.51) once more in the $Z$ -direction, and using $\nabla_{\widetilde{Z}}\widetilde{Z}=0$ , expresses $\partial_{zz}J$ as a sum of contractions of $\nabla^{3}t$ , $\nabla^{2}t$ , $Z-\widetilde{Z}$ , $\nabla(Z-\widetilde{Z})$ , $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}}$ , and $\nabla\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}}$ . Lemmas 4.11 and 4.15, together with (4.5), therefore give

$$ |\nabla_{y}^{k}\partial_{zz}J(y,z)|\lesssim_{k}\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{3})\qquad(|z|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}) $$

for every fixed $k$ . The same differentiated identity, with one fewer $z$ -derivative, gives $|\nabla_{y}^{k}\partial_{z}J|\lesssim_{k}\varepsilon(1+|z|+|z|^{2})$ . Taylor’s theorem at $z=0$ , using $J(y,0)=0$ and the definition of $w$ , now yields (4.48) and

$$ |\nabla_{y}^{k}(J(y,z)-w(y)z)|\leq|z|^{2}\sup_{|s|\leq|z|}|\nabla_{y}^{k}\partial_{zz}J(y,s)|, $$

which is exactly (4.50). ∎

Let $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ be as in (4.10). $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is parametrized by $y\mapsto(y,f_{\alpha}(y))$ , and twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ are defined as in Section 4.2. We shall identify a point $p=Y_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}(y,z)$ with its twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ , and represent the metric $g$ at $p$ as a matrix

$$ g(y,z)=\left(\begin{array}[]{@{}c|c@{}}\big(g_{ij}(y,z)\big)_{i,j=1}^{n}&\big(g_{iz}(y,z)\big)_{i=1}^{n}\\
\hline\cr\big(g_{zj}(y,z)\big)_{j=1}^{n}&g_{zz}(y,z)\end{array}\right) $$

where $g_{ij}(y,z)\coloneqq\langle\partial_{y_{i}}|_{(y,z)},\partial_{y_{j}}|_{(y,z)}\rangle$ , $g_{iz}(y,z)\coloneqq\langle\partial_{y_{i}}|_{(y,z)},\partial_{z}|_{(y,z)}\rangle$ etc.

for all $1\leq i,j\leq n$ .

Sometimes we shall use the abbreviated notation $g_{\alpha,z},\;\Gamma_{\alpha,z},\;\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z},\;H_{\alpha,z}$ to denote the same quantities, or even $g_{\alpha},\;\Gamma_{\alpha},\;\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha},\;H_{\alpha}$ , when there is no danger of ambiguity. #### 4.4. Commutator estimates

We shall now record some easy commutator estimates, which will be used throughout the rest of the paper.

#### Proposition 4.23.

Let $K>0$ be fixed. For all $\varphi\in C^{3}(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ , we have the following commutator estimate

$$ |\Delta_{\alpha,z}\partial_{y_{i}}\varphi-\partial_{y_{i}}\Delta_{\alpha,z}\varphi|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2})(|\nabla^{2}_{\alpha,z}\varphi|+|\nabla_{\alpha,z}\varphi|) $$

for $z\in(-K|\log\varepsilon|,K|\log\varepsilon|)$ . The constant depends on $n,K,\delta,\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Using the formula in (4.69), we see that

$$ \begin{split}\Delta_{\alpha,z}\partial_{y_{i}}\varphi-\partial_{y_{i}}\Delta_{\alpha,z}\varphi&=-\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}(\partial_{y_{i}}g_{\alpha}^{jk})\partial_{y_{j}}\partial_{y_{k}}\varphi+\sum_{j,k,l=1}^{n}\left((\partial_{y_{i}}g_{\alpha}^{jk})\Gamma_{\alpha,jk}^{l}+g_{\alpha}^{jk}(\partial_{y_{i}}\Gamma_{\alpha,jk}^{l})\right)\partial_{y_{l}}\varphi\end{split} $$

where all terms are evaluated at $(y,z)$ . Then (4.71) follows from (4.56), (4.57), (4.58), and (4.59). ∎

We shall also need some commutator estimates for derivatives along the boundary of the domain.

#### Proposition 4.24.

Let $K>0$ be fixed. For all $\varphi\in C^{3}(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ , we have the following commutator estimates

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{z}\partial_{\nu}\varphi-\partial_{\nu}\partial_{z}\varphi| \displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon{(1+|z|)}|\nabla\varphi|, \displaystyle|\partial_{\nu}\partial_{y_{1}}\varphi-\partial_{y_{1}}\partial_{\nu}\varphi| \displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2})|\nabla\varphi|, \displaystyle|\partial_{\nu}\partial_{y_{i}}\varphi-\partial_{y_{i}}\partial_{\nu}\varphi| \displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon|z|(1+|z|)|\nabla\varphi|\;\text{ for all $2\leq i\leq n$} $$

on $\partial_{0}\{|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}$ . The constants depend on $n,K,\delta,\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Recall that $\nu=\partial_{x_{1}}$ on $\partial_{0}\{|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}$ . Thus, $\partial_{z}\partial_{\nu}\varphi-\partial_{\nu}\partial_{z}\varphi=[Z,\partial_{x_{1}}]\varphi$ . If we write $Z=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}Z^{k}\partial_{x_{k}}$ , then $[Z,\partial_{x_{1}}]=-\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_{1}}Z^{k})\partial_{x_{k}}$ , and (4.73) follows directly from (4.24).

Now, let $L_{i}\coloneqq[\partial_{x_{1}},\partial_{y_{i}}]$ , so that (4.74) and (4.75) amount to estimating $L_{i}$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n$ . Let $L_{i}|_{(y,z)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}L_{i}^{k}(y,z)\partial_{x_{k}}|_{(y,z)}$ . On $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , $\partial_{y_{i}}|_{(y,0)}=\partial_{x_{i}}|_{(y,0)}+\partial_{x_{i}}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)}$ . Therefore,

$$ [\partial_{x_{1}},\partial_{y_{i}}]|_{(y,0)}=\partial_{x_{1}}\partial_{x_{i}}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)}=\partial_{x_{i}}\partial_{x_{1}}f(y)\partial_{x_{n+1}}|_{(y,0)}. $$

If $i=1$ , for $(y,0)\in\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ we have

$$ |L^{k}_{1}(y,0)|\lesssim\Lambda_{0}\varepsilon $$

for all $k=1,\dots,n+1$ by (4.11). On the other hand, if $2\leq i\leq n$ , then by the Neumann condition for $f$ on $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)$ , if $(y,0)\in\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ .

$$ L^{k}_{i}(y,0)=0 $$

for all $k=1,\dots,n+1$ .

We now want to estimate $L_{i}^{k}(y,z)$ by deriving the ODE it satisfies.

Since $\partial_{y_{i}},\partial_{z}$ are coordinate vectors $[Z,\partial_{y_{i}}]=0$ everywhere. Moreover, by direct computation $[Z,L_{i}]=[[Z,\partial_{x_{1}}],\partial_{y_{i}}]$ , i.e.

$$ \begin{split}\partial_{z}L_{i}^{k}=[Z,L_{i}]^{k}+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_{j}}Z^{k})L_{i}^{j}=[[Z,\partial_{x_{1}}],\partial_{y_{i}}]^{k}+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}(\partial_{x_{j}}Z^{k})L_{i}^{j}.\end{split} $$

#### 4.5. Comparison of twisted Fermi distance functions

As in [28, 29], we shall need to compare distances with respect to different sheets. The following proposition in the analogue of [29, Lemma 3.4], which is itself [28, Lemma 8.3]. The only difference in our situation is that we shall use twisted Fermi coordinates as defined in Section 4.2. In particular, given distinct connected components $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , $\Sigma_{\beta}$ of $\Xi$ , $t_{\alpha}$ and $\Pi_{\alpha}$ denote the twisted Fermi coordinate time function and projection map with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , and let $t_{\beta}$ and $\Pi_{\beta}$ denote the twisted Fermi coordinate time function and projection map with respect to $\Sigma_{\beta}$ . Let $d_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}$ , $d_{\Sigma_{\beta}}$ denote the intrinsic distances on the hypersurfaces $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\Sigma_{\beta}$ respectively, and let $d$ denote the ambient distance, so that $d|_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},d|_{\Sigma_{\beta}}$ are the restrictions of the ambient distance to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\Sigma_{\beta}$ respectively.

#### Proposition 4.25.

For any $K>0$ , there is a constant $C(K)$ so that for $\alpha\not=\beta$ , $x\in\mathbb{B}_{2R}^{+}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ with $|t_{\alpha}(x)|,|t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ ,

$$ \displaystyle d_{\Sigma_{\beta}}(\Pi_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\alpha}(x),\Pi_{\beta}(x)) \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2} \displaystyle|t_{\beta}(\Pi_{\alpha}(x))+t_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(x))| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2} \displaystyle|t_{\alpha}(x)-t_{\beta}(x)+t_{\beta}(\Pi_{\alpha}(x))| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2} \displaystyle|t_{\alpha}(x)-t_{\beta}(x)-t_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(x))| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2} \displaystyle\left|1-\langle\nabla t_{\alpha}(x),\nabla t_{\beta}(x)\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2} $$

The proof is a simple modification of [28, Lemma 8.3] (or, more precisely, its Riemannian version in [5, Lemma B.1]), thanks to Lemma 4.9 and Lemma 4.14, which show that, under the current assumptions, the twisted Fermi coordinate time functions $t_{\alpha},t_{\beta}$ coincide with the corresponding Fermi distance functions $\tilde{t}_{\alpha},\tilde{t}_{\beta}$ , and that the twisted Fermi projection maps $\Pi_{\alpha},\Pi_{\beta}$ are comparable to the corresponding Fermi projection maps $\tilde{\Pi}_{\alpha},\tilde{\Pi}_{\beta}$ , up to a small error of order $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{3}$ . ∎

Let us now state a few simple but rather useful consequences of Proposition 4.25. Let $\alpha,\beta,K$ be as in Proposition 4.25, and let $(y,z)$ denote twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Assume $x\in\mathbb{B}_{1.5R}^{+}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ is such that $t_{\alpha},\Pi_{\alpha}$ and $t_{\alpha},\Pi_{\alpha}$ are defined at $x$ , and that $|t_{\alpha}(x)|,|t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ , so that the conclusions of Proposition 4.25 apply.

#### Proposition 4.26.

Let $x$ be as above and assume it has twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Then the following estimates hold:

$$ \displaystyle t_{\beta}(y,z)=t_{\beta}(y,0)+z+o(\varepsilon^{1/3}) \displaystyle|\partial_{z}t_{\beta}-1|\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/3} \displaystyle|\nabla_{\alpha,z}t_{\beta}|\lesssim\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{5}} \displaystyle|\nabla^{2}_{\alpha,z}t_{\beta}|\lesssim\varepsilon $$

The exponents appearing in (4.87), (4.88), and (4.89) are not sharp. Indeed, as it is apparent from the proof, from Proposition 4.25, we can obtain
