&\leq|\langle\nabla t_{\alpha},\nabla t_{\beta}\rangle-1|+|\langle\partial_{z}-\nabla t_{\alpha},\nabla t_{\beta}\rangle|\\
&\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2}+\varepsilon(|t_{\alpha}(x)|+|t_{\alpha}(x)|^{2})\\
&\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/2}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2}+\varepsilon(|\log\varepsilon|+|\log\varepsilon|^{2})\\
&\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/2-\theta}\end{split} $$

for any $\theta\in(0,1/2)$ , by Lemma 4.15 and Proposition 4.25, which implies (4.88).

Similarly,

$$ |\nabla_{\alpha,z}t_{\beta}|\lesssim|\nabla t_{\beta}-\langle\nabla t_{\beta},\nabla t_{\alpha}\rangle\nabla t_{\alpha}|\!=\!\sqrt{1-\langle\nabla t_{\alpha},\nabla t_{\beta}\rangle^{2}}\leq\sqrt{2(1-\langle\nabla t_{\beta},\nabla t_{\alpha}\rangle)}\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/4}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/4} $$

by (4.86). In particular, $|\nabla_{\alpha,z}t_{\beta}|\lesssim\varepsilon^{1/4-\theta}$ for any $\theta\in(0,1/4)$ , thus proving (4.89).

Next, notice that $\nabla_{\alpha,z}^{2}t_{\beta}=\nabla^{2}t_{\beta}+\langle\nabla t_{\beta},\nabla t_{\alpha}\rangle\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}$ . Since $t_{\beta}=\tilde{t}_{\beta}$ , then $\nabla^{2}t_{\beta}$ is precisely the second fundamental form of $\Sigma_{\beta,t_{\beta}}$ . Recall that by (4.11), $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,0}|=O(\varepsilon)$ and $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\beta,0}|=O(\varepsilon)|$ . Since we are assuming $|t_{\alpha}(x)|,|t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ , by (4.60),

$$ |\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,0}|=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,t_{\alpha}(x)}-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,0}|\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{4}, $$

so that $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|=O(\varepsilon)$ , and, similarly, $|\nabla^{2}t_{\beta}|=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\beta,t_{\beta}(x)}|=O(\varepsilon)$ . Hence, by (4.86), (4.90) holds. ∎

As mentioned in the proof of Proposition 4.25, by [29, Lemma 2.2], $d_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},d_{\Sigma_{\beta}}$ are comparable to $d|_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},d|_{\Sigma_{\beta}}$ respectively, up to a universal constant depending on $\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ . By Lemma 4.11, $\Pi_{\alpha}|_{\Sigma_{\beta}}$ and $\Pi_{\beta}|_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}$ are uniformly bi-Lipschitz in the regions where $|t_{\alpha}|,|t_{\beta}|\leq\delta\sqrt{R}$ .

The following lemma is an easy consequence of the results of this section.

#### Lemma 4.28.

Let $K>0$ be fixed. Let $(y,z)$ be twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , and let $\Pi_{\beta}$ denote the twisted Fermi coordinate projection map with respect to $\Sigma_{\beta}$ . Then,

$$ |D\Pi_{\beta}(\partial_{y_{i}})|=O(1) $$

for $i=1,\dots,n$ , and

$$ |D\Pi_{\beta}(\partial_{z})|\lesssim\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{5}} $$

uniformly in the region where $|t_{\alpha}|,|t_{\beta}|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ .

#### Proof.

Equation (4.94) follows from Lemma 4.11. For (4.95), write $Z_{\gamma}$ and $\widetilde{Z}_{\gamma}=\nabla t_{\gamma}$ for the twisted and ordinary Fermi fields associated with $\Sigma_{\gamma}$ . The projection $\Pi_{\beta}$ is constant along the flow of $Z_{\beta}$ , and hence $D\Pi_{\beta}(Z_{\beta})=0$ . Since $\partial_{z}=Z_{\alpha}$ in the $\alpha$ -coordinates,

$$ D\Pi_{\beta}(\partial_{z})=D\Pi_{\beta}(Z_{\alpha}-Z_{\beta}). $$

Moreover,

$$ Z_{\alpha}-Z_{\beta}=(\widetilde{Z}_{\alpha}-\widetilde{Z}_{\beta})+(Z_{\alpha}-\widetilde{Z}_{\alpha})-(Z_{\beta}-\widetilde{Z}_{\beta}). $$

The first term is $O(\varepsilon^{1/4}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/4})$ by (4.86), while the last two are $O(\varepsilon(|\log\varepsilon|+|\log\varepsilon|^{2}))$ by Lemma 4.15. Combining these estimates with the uniform bound for $D\Pi_{\beta}$ gives (4.95). ∎

#### 4.6. Comparison of boundary derivatives

Finally, let us consider how twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to different sheets $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , $\Sigma_{\beta}$ behave along the boundary.

Let $K>0$ be fixed, and let $x\in\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ be such that $|t_{\alpha}(x)|,|t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ . Let $(y,z)$ denote twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ .

Recall from Lemma 4.17, $J_{\alpha}:\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}\times(-2R,2R)\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $J_{\alpha}=\partial_{x_{1}}t_{\alpha}$ . Similarly, one can define $J_{\beta}$ by $J_{\beta}=\partial_{x_{1}}t_{\beta}$ . Now, for $\beta\neq\alpha$ , let $\mathsf{J}_{\alpha\beta}$ denote the restriction of $\partial_{y_{1}}t_{\beta}$ to $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R)$ . We have the following estimate.

#### Lemma 4.29.

There holds

$$ |\nabla^{m}\mathsf{J}_{\alpha\beta}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{3}+|t_{\beta}|+t_{\beta}^{2})\;\text{ on }\partial_{0}\{x:|t_{\alpha}(x)|,|t_{\beta}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}\quad\forall m\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

We note that

$$ \mathsf{J}_{\alpha\beta}=\langle\nabla t_{\beta},\partial_{y_{1}}-\partial_{x_{1}}\rangle+J_{\beta} $$

Since $\partial_{x_{1}}=\partial_{y_{1}}$ along $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , it follows from Lemma 4.12 that

$$ |\nabla^{m}(\partial_{x_{1}}-\partial_{y_{1}})|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|z|^{3})\;\text{ on }\partial_{0}\{|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|\}\quad\forall m\geq 0. $$

Using Lemma 4.17 in the form $J_{\beta}=w_{\beta}t_{\beta}+\widetilde{J}_{\beta}$ , the apparently cubic part of the crude bound is absorbed by $\varepsilon^{2}|t_{\beta}|^{2}(1+|t_{\beta}|^{3})\leq C_{K}\varepsilon$ in the logarithmic strip. Together with the preceding estimate and Lemma 4.11, this gives the stated bound for $\mathsf{J}_{\alpha\beta}$ . ∎

#### 4.7. Separation of layers

Analogously to [29, Section 3.2], given a point $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ , we let

$$ D_{\alpha}(y)\coloneqq\min_{\beta\neq\alpha}|t_{\beta}(y)|. $$

Then, for $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ , define the set

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\lambda}_{\alpha}\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{1.6R}(0)\times(-2R,2R):|t_{\alpha}(x)|<\min\{|t_{\alpha-1}(x)|+\lambda,|t_{\alpha+1}(x)|+\lambda\}\right\}. $$

The following simple lemma will be used throughout the rest of the paper.

#### Lemma 4.30 (c.f. [29, Lem 3.6]).

For any $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\sigma>0$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\beta\not=\alpha}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(y)|}\lesssim_{K,\sigma}e^{-\sigma D_{\alpha}(y)}, $$

uniformly with respect to $y$ and $\alpha$ . For $x\in\mathcal{M}^{4}_{\alpha}$ with $|t_{\alpha}(x)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\beta\not=\alpha}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(x)|}\lesssim_{K,\sigma}e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha+1}(x)|}+e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha-1}(x)|} $$

In order to prove Lemma 4.30, we need the following two preliminary results.

#### Lemma 4.31.

Let $\varepsilon_{i}>0$ be a sequence which converges to $0$ , $R_{i}=\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}$ , $u_{i}(x):=u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(\varepsilon_{i}x)$ , $x_{i}\in\{u_{i}=0\}\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{R_{i}}(0)\times(-R_{i},R_{i}))$ , $\Sigma_{x_{i}}$ be the connected component of $\{u_{i}=0\}$ in $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{R_{i}}(0)\times(-R_{i},R_{i})$ , which contains $x_{i}$ . Suppose in twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{x_{i}}$ , $x_{i}=(y_{i},0)$ , $\tilde{u}_{i}(y,z):=u_{i}(y_{i}+y,z)$ and $u_{i}(y,z)$ has the same sign as $z$ . Then, up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_{i}(y,z)$ converges to $\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1]. Suppose in twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{x_{i}}$ , $x_{i}=(y_{i,1},\dots,y_{i,n},0)$ . When $\liminf_{i\rightarrow\infty}y_{i,1}=\infty$ , $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is a stable solution of (4.6) on $B_{y_{i,1}}(0)$ , $\tilde{u}_{i}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)=0$ and $\partial_{z}\tilde{u}_{i}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)\geq 0$ . By the elliptic estimates, $\tilde{u}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{4}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ . Therefore, there exists $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ , a stable solution of (4.6) on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ , such that up to a subsequence, $\tilde{u}_{i}\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ , $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)=0$ and $\partial_{z}\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)\geq 0$ . As explained in [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1], since $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies (3.1), there holds $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b^{\prime}\}\cap\{|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$ . By the unique continuation principle, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a lift of $\mathbb{H}$ ; hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},z)=\mathbb{H}(z)$ .

If $\liminf_{i\rightarrow\infty}y_{i,1}<\infty$ , then, possibly after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that $y_{i,1}$ is uniformly bounded. Let $x^{\prime}_{i}=(y^{\prime}_{i},0)=(0,y_{i,2},\dots,y_{i,n},0)$ (which is a point in $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{R_{i}}(0)\times(-R_{i},R_{i})$ ). We define $\hat{u}_{i}(y,z)=u_{i}(y^{\prime}_{i}+y,z)$ . Then $\hat{u}_{i}$ is a stable solution of (4.6) on $B^{+}_{R_{i}}(0)$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial_{0}B^{+}_{R_{i}}(0)$ , $\hat{u}_{i}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)=0$ and $\partial_{z}\hat{u}_{i}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)\geq 0$ . $\hat{u}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{4}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ . Hence there exists $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ , a stable solution of (4.6) on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}$ satisfying the vanishing Neumann boundary condition along $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}$ , such that up to a subsequence, $\hat{u}_{i}\rightarrow\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ , $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)=0$ and $\partial_{z}\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},0)\geq 0$ . We extend $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by even reflection (as in (3.3)). Then $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a stable solution of (4.6). Since $u_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies (3.1), arguing as in [29, Proof of Lemma 2.1], we conclude that $|\mathcal{A}(\tilde{u}_{\infty})|=0$ on $\{|\tilde{u}_{\infty}|<1-b^{\prime}\}\cap\{|\nabla\tilde{u}_{\infty}|\neq 0\}$ . By the unique continuation principle, this implies $\tilde{u}_{\infty}$ is a lift of $\mathbb{H}$ ; hence $\tilde{u}_{\infty}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},z)=\mathbb{H}(z)$ . Thus $\hat{u}_{i}(y,z)\rightarrow\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+})$ . Since $y_{i,1}$ is uniformly bounded, this implies $\tilde{u}_{i}(y,z)\rightarrow\mathbb{H}(z)$ in $C^{3}_{\text{loc}}$ . ∎

The next lemma then follows directly. The proof is the same as [29, proof of eq. (2.1)].

#### Lemma 4.32.

As $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , $\inf\limits_{\alpha}\inf\{D_{\alpha}(y):y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{R}(0)\times(-R,R))\}\rightarrow+\infty$ .

We can finally give the proof of Lemma 4.30.

#### Proof of Lemma 4.30.

The proof of (4.101) is identical to the proof of [29, Lemma 3.6], with Lemma 4.32 replacing [29, Lemma 2.2], and Proposition 4.25 replacing [29, Lemma 3.4]. Then, (4.102) follows directly from (4.101). ∎

### 5. An optimal approximate solution

In this section, we aim to find the optimal approximate solution of $u$ by modifying the sign alternating heteroclinic approximation $\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)$ in (5.7) to vanishing Neumann boundary adapted sign alternating approximation $g(y,z;h)$ defined in (5.24), and proving the existence of optimal layer shift $h$ in Proposition 5.7.

#### 5.1. Optimal approximate solution ansatz

We fix a smooth even cut-off function $\zeta\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R})$ with $\zeta=1$ on $(-1,1)$ , $0\leq\zeta\leq 1$ , $\spt\zeta\subset(-2,2)$ , and $|\zeta^{\prime}|+|\zeta^{\prime\prime}|\leq 16$ . Define

$$ \zeta_{\varepsilon}(t)\coloneqq\zeta\left(\frac{t}{4|\log\varepsilon|}\right) $$

and, similarly, $\zeta^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}(t)\coloneqq\zeta^{\prime}((4|\log\varepsilon|)^{-1}t)$ , $\zeta^{\prime\prime}_{\varepsilon}(t)\coloneqq\zeta^{\prime\prime}((4|\log\varepsilon|)^{-1}t)$ . Then, let

$$ \overline{\mathbb{H}}(t)=\zeta_{\varepsilon}(t)\mathbb{H}(t)+[1-\zeta_{\varepsilon}(t)]\textrm{sgn}(t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}. $$

Then $\overline{\mathbb{H}}=1$ on $(8|\log\varepsilon|,\infty)$ and $\overline{\mathbb{H}}=-1$ on $(-\infty,-8|\log\varepsilon|)$ . Notice that

$$ \overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime\prime}=W^{\prime}(\overline{\mathbb{H}})+\bar{\xi}_{1},\quad\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime\prime\prime}=W^{\prime\prime}(\overline{\mathbb{H}})\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}+\bar{\xi}^{\prime}_{1}, $$

where $\textrm{spt}(\bar{\xi}_{1})\subset(4|\log\varepsilon|,8|\log\varepsilon|)\cup(-8|\log\varepsilon|,-4|\log\varepsilon|)$ and

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{m}|\bar{\xi}^{(k)}_{1}(t)|\lesssim_{m}e^{-\frac{1}{4}|t|}\varepsilon^{3} $$

Recall the definition of $\sigma_{0}$ in Appendix C, and notice that by (5.4) we have

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(t)^{2}dt=\sigma_{0}+O(\varepsilon^{3}). $$

We define the approximate solution $\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)\in C^{3}(M)$ in the following way. First, recall from Section 4.1 the union $\Xi$ of all the connected components of $\{u=0\}\cap(\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\times(-2R,2R))$ which have non-empty intersections with $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\times(-1.5R,1.5R)$ can be written as a union graphical sheets

$$ \Xi=\bigcup_{\alpha}\Sigma_{\alpha}, $$

as in (4.10). Let $t_{\alpha}$ denote the twisted Fermi coordinate time function with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ as in Definition 4.7, and consider the sets $\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}^{\lambda}$ as defined in (4.100). Without loss of generality, we can assume that near $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , $u$ has the same sign as $(-1)^{\alpha}t_{\alpha}$ . Given a vector of functions $h=(h_{\alpha})$ , where $h_{\alpha}:\Sigma_{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}$ , in each $\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\alpha}$ (which is a neighbourhood of $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ ), let $\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)$ be defined by

$$ \mathbb{H}(y,z;h)=\sum_{\beta}\left(\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,z;h_{\beta})+\textrm{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)(-1)^{\beta}\right), $$

where $(y,z)\in\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\alpha}$ denotes the twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and

$$ \mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,z;h_{\beta})=\overline{\mathbb{H}}\left((-1)^{\beta}(t_{\beta}(y,z)-h_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z)))\right). $$

In particular $\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})=\overline{\mathbb{H}}((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y)))$ .

We shall use the following notation about for derivatives of $\mathbb{H}_{\beta}$ :

$$ \mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\beta})=\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{(k)}\left((-1)^{\beta}(t_{\beta}(y,z)-h_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z)))\right),\ \;k\geq 1. $$

To derive the desired curvature estimates, we need to modify the approximate solution $\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)$ so that the corrected approximate solution satisfies good estimates on its Neumann derivative along the boundary of the domain.

By Proposition F.3, we can define a function $\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}\in C^{\infty}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R})$ by solving the following mixed boundary value problem (as the boundary datum is odd in $\tau$ ):

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\Delta_{\alpha,0}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)+\partial_{\tau\tau}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(\tau))\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)=0&\text{ on }\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\partial_{y_{1}}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)+w_{\alpha}(y)\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(\tau)\tau=0&\text{ along }\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}=0&\text{ along }\partial_{+}\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(\tau)d\tau=0,\end{cases} $$

where $w_{\alpha}$ is as in Lemma 4.17.

Since, by Lemma F.3, the solution to this problem is unique, it must satisfy the following condition

$$ -\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,-z)=\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z), $$

i.e. $\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}$ is odd in the $z$ variable. Also, by (F.4) in Lemma F.3, and, for every $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and every fixed non-negative integer $m$ ,

$$ \sum_{\ell=0}^{m}|\nabla^{\ell}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,\tau)|\leq C_{m,\sigma}\varepsilon e^{-\sigma|\tau|}. $$

The constants are uniform in $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon$ .

As we did in the case of the one-dimensional heteroclinic solution, we need to evenly cut off the correction function $\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}$ in order for it to have compact support. Therefore, let

$$ \overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\zeta_{\varepsilon}(z)\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z) $$

for $z\in\mathbb{R}$ . Since the cut-off function $\zeta$ was assumed to be even, it is easy to see that $\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}$ is an odd function in the $z$ -variable.

Notice that $\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\Delta_{\alpha,0}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)+\partial_{zz}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)-W^{\prime\prime}(\overline{\mathbb{H}}(z))\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\bar{\xi}_{2,\alpha}(y,z),&\text{ on }\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\partial_{y_{1}}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)+w_{\alpha}(y)\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)z=\delta_{\alpha}(y,z)&\text{ along }\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}=0&\text{ along }\partial_{+}\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\mathbb{R};\\
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)dz=0,\end{cases} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\xi}_{2,\alpha}(y,z)={} \displaystyle\frac{1}{2|\log\varepsilon|}\zeta_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(z)\partial_{z}\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)+\frac{1}{16|\log\varepsilon|^{2}}\zeta_{\varepsilon}^{\prime\prime}(z)\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z) \displaystyle+\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(z))-W^{\prime\prime}(\overline{\mathbb{H}}(z))\bigr)\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z), $$

and

$$ \delta_{\alpha}(y,z)=(1-\zeta_{\varepsilon}(z))w_{\alpha}(y)\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)z. $$

Notice that the last property in (5.14) is a consequence of oddness in the $z$ -variable. By definition of the cutoff function, $\bar{\xi}_{2}$ is supported in $\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\left((4|\log\varepsilon|,8|\log\varepsilon|)\cup(-8|\log\varepsilon|,-4|\log\varepsilon|)\right)$ . Similarly, $\delta_{\alpha}$ is supported in $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\times\left((4|\log\varepsilon|,8|\log\varepsilon|)\cup(-8|\log\varepsilon|,-4|\log\varepsilon|)\right)$ . Moreover, by (5.12)

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{m}|\nabla^{k}\bar{\xi}_{2,\alpha}(y,z)|+|\nabla^{k}\delta_{\alpha}(y,z)|\lesssim_{m}e^{-\frac{1}{4}|z|}\varepsilon^{3}. $$

Given $h_{\alpha}:\Sigma_{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}$ , we define

$$ \mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\coloneqq\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))), $$

and, given a vector of functions $h=(h_{\alpha})$ , where $h_{\alpha}:\Sigma_{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}$ , we define

$$ \mathbb{G}(-;h):=\sum\limits_{\beta}\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(-;h_{\beta}), $$

where $\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(-;h_{\beta})$ is defined analogously to (5.8). For simplicity, we will use the following notation

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\alpha}) \displaystyle\coloneqq(\partial^{(k)}_{z}\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha})(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))), \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}(y,z;h_{\alpha}) \displaystyle\coloneqq(\partial_{y_{i}}\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha})(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))), \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,ij}(y,z;h_{\alpha}) \displaystyle\coloneqq(\partial_{y_{i}y_{j}}\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha})(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))), $$

for $1\leq i,j\leq n$ . When $k=1$ , we shall write $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ instead of $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(1)}$ .

These can also be combined, as in $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,ij}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})=(\partial_{y_{i}y_{j}z}\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha})(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y)))$ etc. Similarly, let $\xi_{2,\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\coloneqq\bar{\xi}_{2,\alpha}(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y)))$ , $\xi^{\prime}_{2,\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\coloneqq(\partial_{z}\bar{\xi}_{2,\alpha})(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y)))$ etc. Finally, let $\delta^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z)\coloneqq(\partial_{z}\delta_{\alpha})(y,z)$ , $\delta_{\alpha,i}(y,z)\coloneqq(\partial_{y_{i}}\delta_{\alpha})(y,z)$ , etc.

For $k\geq 0$ , we define

$$ g_{\beta}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\beta})=\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\beta})+\mathbb{G}_{\beta}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\beta}) $$

and

$$ g(y,z;h)=\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)+\mathbb{G}(y,z;h). $$

Clearly, an easy computation gives the following.

#### Lemma 5.1.

We have

$$ \displaystyle(\Delta_{\alpha,0}+\partial_{z}^{2}-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}))\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}={} \displaystyle|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}|^{2}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(2)}-(-1)^{\alpha}(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha})\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(1)} \displaystyle-2(-1)^{\alpha}\sum_{i,j}g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)\mathbb{G}^{\prime}_{\alpha,i}\,\partial_{y_{j}}h_{\alpha}+\xi_{2,\alpha}, $$

$$ \displaystyle(\Delta_{\alpha,0}+\partial_{z}^{2}-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}))\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(1)}={} \displaystyle|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}|^{2}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(3)}-(-1)^{\alpha}(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha})\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(2)} \displaystyle-2(-1)^{\alpha}\sum_{i,j}g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)\mathbb{G}^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha,i}\,\partial_{y_{j}}h_{\alpha}+W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{(1)}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}+\xi^{\prime}_{2,\alpha}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{y_{1}}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)+(-1)^{\alpha}w_{\alpha}(y)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)z \displaystyle=\delta_{\alpha} \displaystyle\partial_{y_{1}y_{i}}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)+(-1)^{\alpha}\partial_{y_{i}}w_{\alpha}(y)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)z \displaystyle=\delta_{\alpha,i}\quad(2\leq i\leq n). $$

Finally, we shall need some elementary estimates, which we record below in Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.3. The proofs, which follow more or less directly from the results of Section 4.5 and the properties of the heteroclinic solution $\mathbb{H}$ , are in Appendix D.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $K>0$ be fixed, let $\beta\neq\alpha$ satisfy $|t_{\beta}(y,0)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ , and let $\sigma,\varsigma\geq 0$ with $\sigma+\varsigma>0$ . For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-K|\log\varepsilon|}^{K|\log\varepsilon|}|z|^{k}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(y,z)|-\varsigma|z|}\,dz \displaystyle\lesssim(1+|t_{\beta}(y,0)|)^{k+1}e^{-\min\{\sigma,\varsigma\}|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}, \displaystyle\int_{-K|\log\varepsilon|}^{K|\log\varepsilon|}|t_{\beta}(y,z)|^{k}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(y,z)|-\varsigma|z|}\,dz \displaystyle\lesssim(1+|t_{\beta}(y,0)|)^{k+1}e^{-\min\{\sigma,\varsigma\}|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}. $$

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $K>0$ be fixed. If $\beta\neq\alpha$ and $|t_{\beta}(y,0)|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ , then

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\overline{\mathbb{H}}(t_{\beta}(y,z))+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)\right||\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)|\,dz\lesssim(1+|t_{\beta}(y,0)|)e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}. $$

Consequently, for every $\sigma\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\overline{\mathbb{H}}(t_{\beta}(y,z))+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)\right||\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)|\,dz\lesssim_{\sigma}e^{-\sigma|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}. $$

#### 5.2. Notation for Proposition 5.7

We are now going to introduce some notation which will be used in the statement and the proof of Proposition 5.7.

#### 5.2.1. Coordinate balls

Let us fix an index $\alpha$ . Recall that $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is the graph of a smooth function $f_{\alpha}:\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\to(-1.6R,1.6R)$ which satisfies (4.11). Therefore,

$$ \Sigma_{\alpha}=\{(y,f_{\alpha}(y)):y\in\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\}\ \text{ and }\ \partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}=\{(y,f_{\alpha}(y)):y\in\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{2R}(0)\}. $$

Let us now define the following coordinate balls.

#### Definition 5.4.

For $\bar{x}=(\bar{y},f_{\alpha}(\bar{y}))\in\Sigma_{\alpha}$ set

$$ B_{r}^{\alpha}(\bar{x})=\{(y,f_{\alpha}(y)):y\in\mathbb{B}_{2R}^{+}(0),\ |y-\bar{y}|<r\}. $$

For $\bar{x}\in\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ set

$$ B_{r}^{0,\alpha}(\bar{x})=\{(y,f_{\alpha}(y)):y\in\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}_{2R}^{+}(0),\ |y-\bar{y}|<r\}. $$

Their relative closures are $\bar{B}_{r}^{\alpha}(\bar{x})$ and $\bar{B}_{r}^{0,\alpha}(\bar{x})$ . The notation with centre $\bar{y}$ has the same meaning under the graph parametrization.

#### Remark 5.5.

Notice that, by (4.2) and (4.11), it is easy to see that for all small enough $\eta_{0}$ (independent of $\varepsilon$ ), the coordinate balls $B^{\alpha}_{r}(\cdot)$ , $B^{0,\alpha}_{r}(\cdot)$ are uniformly comparable to the (intrinsic) geodesic balls in $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ respectively. In particular, it is easy to check that there are constants $c_{0}(n),c_{1}(n)$ such that for all sufficiently small $\eta_{0}$ ,

$$ B^{\alpha}_{(1-c_{1}(n)\eta_{0})r}(x)\subset B^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}_{r}(x)\subset B^{\alpha}_{(1+c_{1}(n)\eta_{0})r}(x)\ \text{ for all }x\in\Sigma_{\alpha}, $$

and

$$ B^{0,\alpha}_{(1-c_{0}(n)\eta_{0})r}(x)\subset B^{\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}}_{r}(x)\subset B^{0,\alpha}_{(1+c_{0}(n)\eta_{0})r}(x)\ \text{ for all }x\in\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}, $$

where $B^{\Sigma_{\alpha}}_{r}(x)$ (resp. $B^{\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}}_{r}(x)$ ) denotes the open geodesic ball of radius $r$ centred at $x$ in $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ ).

#### 5.2.2. Hölder seminorms on coordinate balls

Let $k\geq 0$ , $\theta\in(0,1]$ , and let $\varphi\in C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha})$ (resp. $C^{k,\theta}(\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha})$ ). Let $\bar{x}=(\bar{y},f(\bar{y}))\in\Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ ), and let $x=(y,f(y))$ denote another point in $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ ).

Let $j\leq k$ , and a multi-index $I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{j})$ (where each $i_{l}\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ , resp. $i_{l}\in\{2,\dots,n\}$ ) with $|I|=j$ . Define $\varphi_{I}=\partial_{y_{i_{1}}\dots y_{i_{j}}}\varphi$ , and the following quantities:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&|\varphi|_{0}(\bar{x})=|\varphi(\bar{x})|,\\
&|\varphi|_{0,\theta}(\bar{x})=\sup\left\{\frac{|\varphi(x)-\varphi(\bar{x})|}{|y-\bar{y}|^{\theta}}:x\in\bar{B}_{1}^{\alpha}(\bar{x}),\ x\neq\bar{x}\right\}\quad\text{(respectively, $\bar{B}_{1}^{0,\alpha}(\bar{x})$)},\\
&|\varphi|_{j}(\bar{x})=\max_{|I|=j}|\varphi_{I}(\bar{x})|,\qquad|\varphi|_{j,\theta}(\bar{x})=\max_{|I|=j}|\varphi_{I}|_{0,\theta}(\bar{x}),\\
&|\varphi|^{\prime}_{j}(\bar{x})=\sup\left\{|\varphi|_{j}(x):x\in\bar{B}_{1}^{\alpha}(\bar{x})\right\}\quad\text{(respectively, $\bar{B}_{1}^{0,\alpha}(\bar{x})$)}.\end{split} $$

We note the following elementary inequalities

$$ |\psi^{-1}|_{0,\theta}\leq|\psi|_{0,\theta}|\psi^{-2}|^{\prime}_{0},\text{ if }\psi>0;\quad|\psi|_{0,\theta}\leq|\psi|^{\prime}_{1};\quad|\varphi\psi|_{0,\theta}\leq|\varphi|_{0}|\psi|_{0,\theta}+|\varphi|_{0,\theta}|\psi|^{\prime}_{0}. $$

and analogous higher order versions.

#### Remark 5.6.

Much like in Remark 5.5, notice that, again by by (4.2) and (4.11), up to a harmless dimensional constant, for all small enough $\eta_{0}$ (independent of $\varepsilon$ ) and all $S\subset\Sigma_{\alpha}$ (resp. $S\subset\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ ), $\sup_{x\in S}|\varphi|_{0,\theta}(x)$ is uniformly comparable to the Hölder seminorm $[\varphi]_{\theta,S}$ defined using the intrinsic distance on $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Similarly for $\sup_{x\in S}|\varphi|_{j,\theta}(x)$ and $[\nabla^{j}\varphi]_{\theta,S}$ .

Therefore, after taking $\eta_{0}$ sufficiently small (independent of $\varepsilon$ ), we can use appropriate suprema of the quantities in (5.36) to define the Hölder seminorms.

#### 5.2.3. The restriction map

For $R/2\leq r\leq R$ , $C^{+}_{r}(0):=\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{r}(0)\times[-r,r]$ . Let

$$ \mathscr{R}:C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))\to C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)) $$

denote the restriction map. By [15, Lemma 6.37], there exists $\mathscr{R}^{-1}$ , which is a continuous right inverse of $\mathscr{R}$ . Moreover if $\mathscr{R}^{-1}(\varphi)=\tilde{\varphi}$ , then $\tilde{\varphi}$ can be described more concretely as follows. Since $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is the graph of $f_{\alpha}$ over $\mathbb{B}_{2R}^{+}(0)$ , $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{r}(0)$ (with $r\leq R$ ) can be identified with $\mathbb{B}_{r}^{+}(0)$ using the map $(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\mapsto(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},f_{\alpha}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n}))$ . If we make this identification and use the polar coordinate $(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)$ on $\bar{\mathbb{B}}_{R}^{+}(0)$ (where $\mathfrak{r}$ denotes the radial coordinate), then $\tilde{\varphi}(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)=\varphi(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)$ , if $\mathfrak{r}\leq r_{0}=9R/10$ and

$$ \tilde{\varphi}(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}c_{i}\varphi\left(r_{0}-\frac{\mathfrak{r}-r_{0}}{i+1},\upsilon\right),\text{ if }\mathfrak{r}\geq r_{0}, $$

where the constants $c_{i}$ are chosen in such a way that $\tilde{\varphi}$ is a $C^{k,\theta}$ function. Further, $\bar{\mathscr{R}}:C^{0}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))\to C^{0}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$ is defined by $\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\varphi)=\bar{\varphi}$ , where $\bar{\varphi}(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)=\varphi(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)$ , if $\mathfrak{r}\leq r_{0}=9R/10$ and

$$ \bar{\varphi}(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)=\frac{1}{2}\varphi(\mathfrak{r},\upsilon)+\frac{1}{2(k+1)}\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\varphi\left(r_{0}-\frac{\mathfrak{r}-r_{0}}{i+1},\upsilon\right),\text{ if }\mathfrak{r}\geq r_{0}. $$

#### 5.3. Existence and estimates of optimal layer shift with orthogonality condition

In order to state Proposition 5.7, let us define

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}=\{\beta:\beta\neq\alpha,\;|t_{\beta}(y,0)|<17|\log\varepsilon|\},\\
&v_{\alpha}(y,z)=u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;0),\\
&\omega_{\alpha}^{(j)}(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Big(\sum_{i=0}^{j}|v_{\alpha}|^{\prime}_{i}+|v_{\alpha}|_{i,\theta}\Big)(y,z)(1+|z|^{3})e^{-|z|}dz,\\
&\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(j)}(y)=\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}(y)+\max_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}\sup\{\omega^{(j)}_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y^{\prime},z)):y^{\prime}\in\bar{B}^{\alpha}_{1}(y),|z|<9|\log\varepsilon|\},\\
&\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}(y)=|e^{-D_{\alpha}}|^{\prime}_{0}(y),\\
&\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}(y)=\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}(y)+\max_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}\sup\{\mathrm{a}_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y^{\prime},z)):y^{\prime}\in\bar{B}^{\alpha}_{1}(y),|z|<9|\log\varepsilon|\}.\end{split} $$

#### Proposition 5.7 (Optimal layer shift).

There exists $h_{\alpha}\in C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$ such that for each index $\alpha$ and $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)$ , for $\phi(y,z;h)=u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)$ there holds

$$ \int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\phi(y,z;h)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz=0, $$

where $(y,z)$ are twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Moreover, the following estimates hold uniformly with respect to the index $\alpha$ . As $\varepsilon\to 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|h_{\alpha}|_{j}+|h_{\alpha}|_{j,\theta}\lesssim\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9},\;0\leq j\leq k,\text{ on }\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0), \displaystyle|\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}|_{(j-1)}+|\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}|_{(j-1),\theta}\lesssim(\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9})(\varepsilon+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(j)}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}),\;1\leq j\leq k,\text{ on }\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0), $$

#### Remark 5.8.

In later application, we will fix $k=3$ and $j=2$ in Proposition 5.7, so that $h_{\alpha}=o(1)\in C^{3,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$ . In this case, for ease of notation, we write (compare with (5.41))

$$ \mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}=\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(2)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\omega_{\alpha}=\omega_{\alpha}^{(2)}. $$

In particular, we can simplify the estimate (5.43) satisfied by $h_{\alpha}$ in Proposition 5.7 to

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2}|h_{\alpha}|_{i}+|h_{\alpha}|_{2,\theta}\lesssim\varepsilon+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}\text{ on }\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0), \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{1}|\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}|_{i}+|\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}|_{1,\theta}\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{2}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{1.8}\text{ on }\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0). $$

#### Proof of Proposition 5.7.

To this end, we shall modify the proof in [29, Proof of Proposition 4.1] as follows. For each $k$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $\alpha$ , we define new norms $\|\cdot\|_{*}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\star}$ on $C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0))$ and $C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0))$ . We introduce $\|\mathfrak{h}\|_{*}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}[\mathfrak{h}]_{*;j}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}[\mathfrak{h}]^{\prime}_{*;j}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle[\mathfrak{h}]_{*;j}=\Lambda^{-1}\sup_{\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)}\frac{|\mathfrak{h}|_{j}+|\mathfrak{h}|_{j,\theta}}{\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9}}, \displaystyle[\mathfrak{h}]^{\prime}_{*;j}=\Lambda^{-2}\sup_{\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)}\frac{|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1)}+|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1),\theta}}{(\varepsilon+\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\mathrm{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9})(\varepsilon+\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(j)}+\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}^{0.9})}, $$

$\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}$ denotes the restriction of $\partial_{y_{1}}\mathfrak{h}$ on $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , $\Lambda>1$ is a constant, which will be specified later. Let us denote $\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\omega^{(j)}_{\alpha})$ , $\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathrm{a}_{\alpha})$ , $\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha})$ , and $\bar{\mathscr{R}}(\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha})$ by $\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha}$ , $\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha}$ , $\bar{\mathfrak{w}}_{\alpha}$ , and $\bar{\mathfrak{a}}_{\alpha}$ , where restriction map $\bar{\mathscr{R}}$ is defined in (5.38). $\|\mathfrak{h}\|_{\star}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}[\mathfrak{h}]_{\star;j}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}[\mathfrak{h}]^{\prime}_{\star;j}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle[\mathfrak{h}]_{\star;j}=\Lambda^{-1}\sup_{\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0)}\frac{|\mathfrak{h}|_{j}+|\mathfrak{h}|_{j,\theta}}{\varepsilon+\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9}}, \displaystyle[\mathfrak{h}]^{\prime}_{\star;j}=\Lambda^{-2}\sup_{\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0)}\frac{|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1)}+|\mathfrak{h}_{\nu}|_{(j-1),\theta}}{(\varepsilon+\bar{\omega}^{(j)}_{\alpha}+\bar{\mathrm{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9})(\varepsilon+\bar{\mathfrak{w}}_{\alpha}^{(j)}+\bar{\mathfrak{a}}_{\alpha}^{0.9})}. $$

Following [29, Proof of Proposition 4.1], we define

$$ \mathcal{X}_{\alpha}=(C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{R}(0)),\|\cdot\|_{\star}),\quad\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}=(C^{k,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap C^{+}_{9R/10}(0)),\|\cdot\|_{*}), $$

$\mathcal{X}=\bigoplus_{\alpha}\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}$ , $\mathcal{Y}=\bigoplus_{\alpha}\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ . The norm on $\mathcal{X}$ is defined by $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\sup_{\alpha}\|\mathbf{x_{\alpha}}\|_{\star},$ where $\mathbf{x_{\alpha}}$ is the $\mathcal{X}_{\alpha}$ component of $\mathbf{x}$ . The norm on $\mathcal{Y}$ is defined in a similar way.

Recall the definition of $g_{\beta}(y,z;h_{\beta})$ and $g(y,z;h)$ from (5.23) and (5.24). Then we define $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ by

$$ \displaystyle F_{\alpha}(h)(y) \displaystyle=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y,z)-g(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz \displaystyle=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}[u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz, $$

where $F_{\alpha}(h)$ denotes the $\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ component of $F(h)$ and $(y,z)$ denotes the twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . We restrict $F$ on the closed unit ball in $\mathcal{X}$ . We note that, for $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and $\mathsf{y}\in\bar{B}_{1}^{\alpha}(y)$ , $(g_{\beta}(\mathsf{y},z;h_{\beta})+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)(-1)^{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(\mathsf{y},z;h_{\alpha})\neq 0$ , $\beta\neq\alpha$ , implies $|z|<9|\log\varepsilon|$ and $\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}$ ; hence

$$ F_{\alpha}(h)(\mathtt{y})=\int^{\infty}_{-\infty}\big[u(\mathtt{y},z)-g_{\alpha}(\mathtt{y},z;h_{\alpha})-\sum_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}(g_{\beta}(\mathtt{y},z;h_{\beta})+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)(-1)^{\beta})\big]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(\mathtt{y},z;h_{\alpha})dz. $$

Notice that $F$ is a $C^{1}$ map, and its derivative $(DF_{\alpha}(h)\xi)(y)$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{\alpha}\xi_{\alpha}(y)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})^{2}+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\right]dz \displaystyle-(-1)^{\alpha}\xi_{\alpha}(y)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)-\mathbb{G}(y,z;h)\big]\mathbb{H}^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz \displaystyle+\sum_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}(-1)^{\beta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\xi_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z))\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz \displaystyle+\sum_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}(-1)^{\beta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\xi_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z))\mathbb{G}^{\prime}_{\beta}(y,z;h_{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;h_{\alpha})dz. $$

Thus, there exist continuous linear maps $D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(h):\mathcal{X}_{\beta}\to\mathcal{Y}_{\alpha}$ such that

$$ DF_{\alpha}(h)\xi=D_{\alpha}F_{\alpha}(h)\xi_{\alpha}+\sum_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(h)\xi_{\beta}. $$

Let $\mathsf{T}=DF(0)$ , $\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}=D_{\alpha}F_{\alpha}(0)$ , $\mathsf{T}_{\beta\alpha}=D_{\beta}F_{\alpha}(0)$ for $\beta\not=\alpha$ . Then, $(\mathsf{T}_{\alpha\alpha}\xi_{\alpha})(y)=\vartheta_{\alpha}(y)\xi_{\alpha}(y)$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\vartheta_{\alpha}(y)= \displaystyle(-1)^{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)^{2}+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(y,z;0)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)\right]dz \displaystyle-(-1)^{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)-\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)\big]\mathbb{H}^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)dz \displaystyle+(-1)^{\alpha}\sum_{\beta\in\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big[\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,z;0)+\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(y,z;0)\big]\mathbb{H}^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)dz. $$

#### Claim 5.9.

We have the following properties.

- (i) There exists $DF(0)^{-1}$ , which is a right inverse of $DF(0)$ , such that the operator norm of $DF(0)^{-1}$ satisfies $\|DF(0)^{-1}\|\leq C(\sigma_{0})$ , where $\sigma_{0}$ is the energy of the one-dimensional solution, as in (C.3).

- (ii) $h\mapsto DF(h)$ is Lipschitz continuous at $h=0$ and its Lipschitz constant at $0$ is $\Lambda c_{\varepsilon}$ , where $c_{\varepsilon}=o(1)$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .

- (iii) $\|F(0)\|_{\mathcal{Y}}\leq C\Lambda^{-1}$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .

First, let us assume Claim 5.9 and let us finish the proof of Proposition 5.7. We will show the existence of $h\in\mathcal{X}$ satisfying (5.42) and estimates (5.43) by the contraction mapping principle, as in [4, Theorem 1.2.4].

Note that it is enough to show that there exists $h\in\mathcal{X}$ such that $\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1$ and $F(h)=0$ . Let $\mathsf{R}:\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_{1}(0)}\to\mathcal{Y}$ be defined by $\mathsf{R}(h)=F(h)-DF(0)h$ . $F(h)=0$ if and only if $DF(0)h=-\mathsf{R}(h)$ . Let $\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h):=-DF(0)^{-1}\mathsf{R}(h)$ . If $h$ is a fixed point of $\bar{\mathsf{R}}$ , then $F(h)=0$ .

We note that

$$ \mathsf{R}(h)-\mathsf{R}(\tilde{h})=\int_{0}^{1}\left(DF(\gamma(t))-DF(0)\right)(h-\tilde{h})dt,\;\text{ where }\gamma(t)=th+(1-t)\tilde{h}. $$

Hence, denoting the Lipschitz constant of $DF$ at $0$ by $\Lambda c_{\varepsilon}$ ( $c_{\varepsilon}=o(1)$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ ) and using (i) and (ii) of Claim 5.9,

$$ \|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h)-\bar{\mathsf{R}}(\tilde{h})\|\leq C(\sigma_{0})\Lambda c_{\varepsilon}\|h-\tilde{h}\|, $$

which implies

$$ \|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(h)\|\leq C(\sigma_{0})\Lambda c_{\varepsilon}\|h\|+\|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(0)\|. $$

By (i) and (iii) of Claim 5.9, we can fix $\Lambda$ sufficiently large so that

$$ \|\bar{\mathsf{R}}(0)\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1/2. $$

Then, (5.61) and (5.62) imply that if $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, $\bar{\mathsf{R}}:\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_{1}(0)}\to\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_{1}(0)}$ is a contraction. Hence, $\bar{\mathsf{R}}$ has a fixed point $h$ in $\overline{B^{\mathcal{X}}_{1}(0)}$ satisfying estimates (5.43) and $F(h)=0$ . This finishes the proof of Proposition 5.7.

Let us now prove Claim 5.9.

Hence (5.79), (5.12), (5.37), and Lemmas 5.2, 4.30 imply

Let us now use (a) and (b) to construct the desired right inverse of $DF(0)$ . Given $\eta\in\mathcal{Y}$ , as in [29, page 17] we define $S_{\eta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}$ by

From now on, let $h=(h_{\alpha})$ be the optimal layer shift function given by Proposition 5.7. We shall use the following notation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{(k)}(y,z) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\alpha}),\qquad \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha}), \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}(y,z) \displaystyle=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\qquad \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}(y,z)=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}(y,z;h_{\alpha}) \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,ij}^{(k)}(y,z) \displaystyle=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,ij}^{(k)}(y,z;h_{\alpha})\qquad \displaystyle\partial\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}=(\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,1},\dots,\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,n},\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\mathbb{H}_{*}(y,z) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}(y,z;h)\qquad \displaystyle\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,z)=\mathbb{G}(y,z;h) \displaystyle g_{*}(y,z) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}_{*}(y,z)+\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,z) $$

Finally, we denote by

$$ \phi=u-g_{*}=u-(\mathbb{H}_{*}+\mathbb{G}_{*}) $$

the difference between the real solution and the approximate one.

#### Corollary 5.10.

Let $K>0$ . For any polynomial $p(z)$ in $|z|$ , $k\geq 0$ and $\sigma\in(0,1)$ , we have

$$ \|p(z)e^{\sigma|z|}{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)\|_{C^{2,\theta}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\times(-2R,2R))}\lesssim_{k,p,\sigma}\varepsilon $$

and

$$ \|\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,z)\|_{C^{2,\theta}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\times(-2R,2R))}\lesssim\varepsilon $$

as well as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&\|{\mathbb{G}}(y,z;h)-{\mathbb{G}}(y,z;0)\|_{C^{2,\theta}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\times(-2R,2R))}\\
&\qquad\lesssim\varepsilon\|e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha+1}(y,z)|}+e^{-\sigma|t_{\alpha-1}(y,z)|}\|_{C^{0}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\times(-2R,2R))}+\varepsilon\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Sigma_{\alpha})}.\end{split} $$

#### Proof.

Note first that since the pointwise estimates in (5.12) for $\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)$ are valid for every $\sigma\in(0,1)$ , then the same holds for $\bar{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,z)$ (it is useful to note here that derivatives of the cut-off $\zeta_{\varepsilon}$ are supported in the annulus $(-8|\log\varepsilon|,-4|\log\varepsilon|)\cup(4|\log\varepsilon|,8|\log\varepsilon|)$ ). In particular, the size of the interval in the $z$ -direction does not affect the estimates.

To prove (5.115), fix $\sigma>0$ , and choose $\sigma^{\prime}\in(0,1)$ in (5.12) satisfying $\sigma^{\prime}>\sigma$ , so that the term $p(z)e^{\sigma|z|}$ can be absorbed by $e^{-\sigma^{\prime}|z|}$ , leaving only the bound $\varepsilon.$ The bound in (5.116) follows from (5.12). Lastly, (5.117) follows by expressing everything in twisted Fermi coordinates $(y,z)$ with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and combining (4.102) with the higher order version of the estimate (5.12). ∎

To better estimate the terms $\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}$ from Proposition 5.7 we need to introduce the following quantity (cf. [29, Subsection 3.2])

$$ A(r;x):=\max_{\alpha}\max_{y\in\overline{\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r}(x)}}e^{-D_{\alpha}(y)}, $$

where the setup is an in Section 4, while $D_{\alpha}(\cdot)$ has been defined in (4.99).

#### Lemma 5.11.

For $\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}$ defined in (5.44) and (5.41), we have the following estimate

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}(y) \displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon+\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{2}^{\alpha}(y)\times[-25|\log\varepsilon|,25|\log\varepsilon|])}+A(40|\log\varepsilon|;(y,0))^{3/4} \displaystyle+\sup_{\beta:|t_{\beta}(y,0)|<17|\log\varepsilon|}\|h_{\beta}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{3}^{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0)))} \displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}(y) \displaystyle\lesssim A(40|\log\varepsilon|;(y,0)) $$

#### Proof.

In order to prove the lemma, we start by establishing the following pointwise estimate

$$ \displaystyle|\omega_{\alpha}(y)|\lesssim\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{2}(y)\times[-10|\log\varepsilon|,10|\log\varepsilon|])}+\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{2}(y))}+\max_{B^{\alpha}_{2}(y)}e^{-\frac{3}{4}D_{\alpha}(y)}+\varepsilon, $$

where we recall from (5.41) the definition of $\omega_{\alpha}(y)=\omega_{\alpha}^{(2)}(y)$ . To do so, we expand $v_{\alpha}$ as follows

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}v_{\alpha}(y,z)&=\phi(y,z)+\bigl(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})-\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;0)\bigr)+\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,z)\\
&\quad+\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}\left(\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,z;h_{\beta})+\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)(-1)^{\beta}\right).\end{split} $$

where the second equality follows from the definition of $\phi$ in (5.114). To infer the desired bound, we need to estimate the terms $|v_{\alpha}|_{0}$ , $|v_{\alpha}|_{1}$ , $|v_{\alpha}|_{2}$ , and $|v_{\alpha}|_{2,\theta}$ multiplied by $(1+|z|^{3})e^{-|z|}$ . The first order term $|v_{\alpha}|_{0}$ can be dealt with by appealing to Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.3 directly. In particular, the first term on the right-hand side of (5.120) arises from estimating the first term on the right-hand side of (5.121). Similarly, by Lemma 4.30, Remark 5.8, the estimates of $\mathbb{G}_{*}$ in Corollary 5.10 the second, third, and fourth terms in (5.120) come from (in order of appearance) from estimating the second, third, and fourth terms of (5.121). Note that we used the estimate $h_{\alpha}=o(1)$ from Proposition 5.7, see Remark 5.8.

The higher order estimates on $v_{\alpha}$ can be estimated in a similar fashion, after differentiating the above expression for $v_{\alpha}$ . Hence we obtain (5.120).

To conclude, recall the definition of $\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}(y)$ and $\mathtt{I}_{\alpha,y}$ in (5.41). Combining them with (5.120), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}(y)=\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha}^{(2)}(y)\lesssim \displaystyle\;\varepsilon+\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{2}(y)\times[-25|\log\varepsilon|,25|\log\varepsilon|])} \displaystyle+\sup_{\beta:|t_{\beta}(y,0)|<17|\log\varepsilon|}\left(\|h_{\beta}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\beta}_{2}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0)))}+\max_{B^{\beta}_{2}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0))}e^{-\frac{3}{4}D_{\beta}}\right). $$

Using this, the definition of $\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}(y)$ and the definition of $A(r;x)$ in (5.118), we obtain the two estimates in (5.119). ∎

#### 5.4. Controlling $h$ by $\phi$

In order to derive the Toda system, we prove the following estimates on $h_{\alpha}$ . Compare them with the ones in Remark 5.8. In later sections, we will further improve on these.

#### Lemma 5.12 (First improved estimates).

For each $\alpha$ and for $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B^{+}_{\frac{7}{8}R-2}(0)$ , we have

$$ \|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}\leq C\|\phi(\cdot,0)\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y,0))}+C\max_{B^{\alpha}_{1}(y)}e^{-D_{\alpha}}+C\varepsilon^{2} $$

and

$$ \begin{split}\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}\leq&\;C\varepsilon^{2}+C\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\phi(\cdot,0)\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y,0))}+C\varepsilon^{1/6}\max_{B^{\alpha}_{1}(y)}e^{-D_{\alpha}}\\
&+C\left(\max_{\beta:|t_{\beta}(y,0)|\leq 9|\log\varepsilon|}\|\nabla_{\beta,0}h_{\beta}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{\beta}_{2}(\Pi^{\beta}(y,0)))}\right)\max_{B^{\alpha}_{1}(y)}e^{-D_{\alpha}}.\end{split} $$

If, in addition, $y\in\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , then

$$ \|\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{0,\alpha}_{1}(y))}\leq C\|\phi\|^{2}_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{4}(y,0)\times[-50|\log\varepsilon|,50|\log\varepsilon|])}+CA(50|\log\varepsilon|;(y,0))^{3/2}+C\varepsilon^{2} $$

where the constants $C$ in the above estimates are uniform in $\alpha$ and $y$ .

In twisted Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ we have $\phi(y,0)=-\mathbb{H}_{*}(y,0)-\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,0)$ . Since $\|h_{\beta}\|_{C^{2,\theta}}=o(1)$ , arguing as in [29, Lemma 4.6], we obtain

$$ \|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}\lesssim\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y,0))}+\max_{B^{\alpha}_{1}(y)}e^{-D_{\alpha}(\cdot)}+\|\mathbb{G}_{*}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}. $$

$$ \|\mathbb{G}_{*}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}\lesssim\varepsilon\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\alpha}_{1}(y))}+\varepsilon\max_{B^{\alpha}_{1}(y)}e^{-\sigma D_{\alpha}}\qquad\text{where $\sigma\in(1/2,1)$}. $$

The two inequalities above, together with Cauchy’s inequality, imply the desired bound (5.124). Differentiating the expression $\phi(y,0)=-\mathbb{H}_{*}(y,0)-\mathbb{G}_{*}(y,0)$ , appealing to Proposition 4.26 to handle the terms $\nabla_{\alpha,0}t_{\beta}$ and to Lemma 4.11 to have uniform boundedness of $|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\Pi_{\beta}|$ , and arguing in a similar fashion, we obtain (5.125) as well. Second derivatives $\nabla_{\alpha,0}^{2}h_{\alpha}$ are handled in the exact same way, while for the Hölder terms we need to use the bound $|\nabla_{\alpha,0}^{2}t_{\beta}|\lesssim\varepsilon$ .

To obtain (5.126), recall the estimate on the Neumann derivative of $h_{\alpha}$ from Remark 5.8. This, together with the estimates for $\mathfrak{w}_{\alpha},\mathfrak{a}_{\alpha}$ in (5.119) of Lemma 5.11, and the improved estimates on $h_{\alpha}$ just shown in (5.124), give (5.126). ∎

#### Remark 5.13.

Compared with [29, (4.13) in Lemma 4.6], the influence of the error term of order $C\varepsilon^{2}$ in (5.124) on our final curvature estimates is negligible.
