## Part II Stability of Toda system implies curvature estimates

### 9. Stability inequality for Toda system

We transfer the stability inequality for $u$ to the Toda system governing the sheet distances. As in Section 8 of [29], the test function associated with $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is the product of a function on $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and the full translation derivative

$$ g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime} $$

introduced in Section 5. Since $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ depends also on its first argument, horizontal derivatives of $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ occur in the equation for $g_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ . We therefore combine the horizontal and normal parts of the diagonal energy by the divergence theorem before estimating either part. The interaction integrals and the ordered cross terms are then treated as in Sections 8.3–8.4 of [29], with the additional terms produced by the twisted Fermi coordinates and by the boundary.

Fix

$$ x\in B^{+}_{5R/6}(0),\qquad 0<r\leq R/80,\qquad 1<\tau<2. $$

All functions on a sheet are smooth up to $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , compactly supported in $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}^{+}(x)$ , and extended by zero outside that support. They need not vanish on $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Unless another measure is displayed, an integral over $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is taken with respect to $dA_{\alpha,0}$ .

#### Proposition 9.1 (Stability inequality).

Let $\eta_{\alpha}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r}^{+}(x))$ . For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ , there is a nonnegative quadratic form $Q$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}+Q(\eta)\geq{} \displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\frac{2A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}}{\tau\sigma_{0}}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|}\bigl[\eta_{\alpha}(y)+\eta_{\alpha-1}(\Pi_{\alpha-1}(y,0))\bigr]^{2}. $$

Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq Q(\eta)\leq{} \displaystyle C(N,\tau)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{1/4}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{1/2}\Bigr)\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2} \displaystyle+C(N,\tau)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\Bigr)\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}, $$

where $N$ is the number of non-vanishing $\eta_{\alpha}$ .

#### 9.1. The diagonal terms

Set

$$ \varphi=\sum_{\alpha}\varphi_{\alpha},\qquad\varphi_{\alpha}=\eta_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime},\qquad g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}, $$

so that each $\varphi_{\alpha}$ is supported in $B^{+}_{r+20|\log\varepsilon|}(x)$ . Here $h_{\alpha}$ and $\eta_{\alpha}$ are extended constantly along the $\alpha$ -fibres. Every quantity carrying an index $\beta$ is first calculated in the twisted Fermi coordinates of $\Sigma_{\beta}$ and then evaluated at the ambient point through $(\Pi_{\beta},t_{\beta})$ .

For $k\geq 0$ we retain the conventions of Section 5:

$$ \mathbb{H}^{(k)}_{\alpha}=\mathbb{H}^{(k)}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\bar{\mathbb{H}}^{(k)}((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y)))\quad\mathbb{G}^{(k)}_{\alpha}=\mathbb{G}^{(k)}_{\alpha}(y,z)=\bar{\mathbb{G}}^{(k)}((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))) $$

The cut-offs introduced in Section 5 imply that all differentiated one-dimensional factors vanish at the endpoints of every $z$ -integration below. Thus integrations by parts in $z$ have no endpoint terms.

For every fixed $k$ , every fixed polynomial factor, and every $0<\sigma<1$ ,

$$ |\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{(k)}|\leq C_{k}e^{-|z-h_{\alpha}|}\ \ (k\geq 1),\quad|\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}|+|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}|\leq C_{k,\sigma}\varepsilon e^{-\sigma|z-h_{\alpha}|}\ \ (k\geq 0). $$

Taking $\sigma=31/32$ and decreasing $\varepsilon_{0}$ gives, on the support of the differentiated factors,

$$ |\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}|+|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{(k)}|\leq C_{k}\varepsilon^{3/4}e^{-|z-h_{\alpha}|}. $$

for $k\geq 0$ . Indeed, $|z-h_{\alpha}|\leq 8|\log\varepsilon|+1$ there and $\varepsilon e^{|z-h_{\alpha}|/32}\leq C\varepsilon^{3/4}$ . Consequently, for every fixed $m\geq 0$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}\,dz=\sigma_{0}+O(\varepsilon),\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|z|)^{m}\bigl(|g_{\alpha}^{\prime}|^{2}+|\partial_{z}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}|^{2}+|\partial_{zz}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}|^{2}\bigr)\,dz\leq C_{m}. $$

Proposition 7.1, applied on the enlarged domains used below, gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}}+\max_{\alpha}\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}}+\max_{\alpha}\|H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr), $$

where each norm is taken on the corresponding portion of the enlarged ball. The improved horizontal estimates proved in the preceding section yield

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\alpha,i}\|\phi_{y_{i}}\|_{C^{1,\theta}}+ \displaystyle\max_{\alpha}\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}} \displaystyle\leq C\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr). $$

Throughout the remainder of this section, the two scalar functions produced by differentiating the equations for $\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ are denoted by

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h). $$

#### Lemma 9.2.

We have the following

$$ \mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime\prime}=-\Delta_{\alpha,0}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h), $$

$$ \mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime\prime}=-\Delta_{\alpha,0}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}+\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h)={} \displaystyle|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}|^{2}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime\prime}-(-1)^{\alpha}(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}+\bar{\xi}_{1}^{\prime}\bigl((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\bigr), \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h)={} \displaystyle|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}|^{2}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime\prime}-(-1)^{\alpha}(\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha})\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime} \displaystyle-2(-1)^{\alpha}\sum_{i,j}g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}^{\prime\prime}\,\partial_{y_{j}}h_{\alpha}+\xi_{2,\alpha}^{\prime}. $$

Hence

$$ (\Delta_{\alpha,0}+\partial_{zz}-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}))g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}+\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h)+\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h). $$

If $\Delta$ is the ambient Laplacian, then

$$ \displaystyle(-\Delta+W^{\prime\prime}(u))g^{\prime}_{\alpha} \displaystyle=\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)g^{\prime}_{\alpha}-W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}^{\prime}_{\alpha}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha} \displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h)-\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h)-(\Delta_{\alpha,z}-\Delta_{\alpha,0})g^{\prime}_{\alpha}+H_{\alpha}\partial_{z}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}-\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix an arbitrary base point and choose geodesic coordinates for $g_{\alpha,0}$ at that point. There the Christoffel symbols vanish, so differentiating the equations defining $\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ and applying the chain rule to $z-h_{\alpha}(y)$ gives

$$ \partial_{y_{i}}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}^{\prime}-(-1)^{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}h_{\alpha,i}, $$

$$ \partial_{y_{i}y_{j}}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,ij}^{\prime}-(-1)^{\alpha}\bigl(\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}^{\prime\prime}h_{\alpha,j}+\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,j}^{\prime\prime}h_{\alpha,i}+g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}h_{\alpha,ij}\bigr)+g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime\prime}h_{\alpha,i}h_{\alpha,j}. $$

Contracting the second identity with $g_{\alpha}^{ij}(y,0)$ proves (9.9)-(9.11); adding (9.9) and (9.10) proves (9.12). This is the analogue of differentiating [29, (4.1), p. 15] and applying the resulting identity as in [29, Section 8.2, p. 34]; unlike in that Euclidean calculation, the first-argument derivatives of $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ and the term $\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ must also be retained. ∎

Recall that by the definition of twisted Fermi coordinates and the geometric approximation identities of Section 4, in twisted Fermi coordinate with respect to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , we have

$$ |\nabla f|^{2}=|\nabla_{\alpha,z}f|^{2}+\bigl(\partial_{z}f-\sum_{i}T^{i}\partial_{y_{i}}f\bigr)^{2},\qquad d\operatorname{vol}_{g}=\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)\,dy\,dz, $$

and

$$ \begin{split}\Delta f={}&\Delta_{\alpha,z}f+\partial_{zz}f-H_{\alpha}(y,z)\partial_{z}f+\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}f,\\
\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}f={}&\lambda_{\alpha}^{-1}\partial_{y_{i}}\bigl(\lambda_{\alpha}T_{\alpha}^{i}T_{\alpha}^{j}\partial_{y_{j}}f\bigr)-T_{\alpha}^{i}\partial_{y_{i}z}f-\lambda_{\alpha}^{-1}\partial_{z}\bigl(\lambda_{\alpha}T_{\alpha}^{j}\partial_{y_{j}}f\bigr).\end{split} $$

Moreover,

$$ \partial_{z}\lambda_{\alpha}=\bigl(-H_{\alpha}(y,z)+\operatorname{div}_{\alpha,z}T\bigr)\lambda_{\alpha}, $$

and, for a fixed integer $m$ ,

$$ \bigl|\partial_{z}\bigl(H_{\alpha}(y,z)\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)\bigr)\bigr|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{m})\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0). $$

Finally,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,d\sigma_{\alpha,0}\leq{} \displaystyle C\left(\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}\right)^{1/2}+C\varepsilon\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

To prove this, integrate $\operatorname{div}_{\alpha,0}(\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\partial_{y_{1}})$ over $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , and use $|\mathrm{div}_{\alpha,0}\partial_{y_{1}}|\leq C\varepsilon$ .

#### Lemma 9.3 (Flux through the boundary).

For every $\delta>0$ , the sum of the absolute values of all diagonal and cross boundary integrals

$$ \int_{\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\partial_{\nu}g_{\beta}^{\prime}\,d\sigma_{g} $$

that arise from (9.3) is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\delta\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0} \displaystyle\quad+C(N,\delta)\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr)\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

#### Proof.

The following identity holds on $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ .

$$ \partial_{\nu}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}=\sum_{i}(\partial_{\nu}y_{i})\bigl(\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}^{\prime}-(-1)^{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\partial_{y_{i}}h_{\alpha}\bigr)+(-1)^{\alpha}J_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}. $$

Differentiating the boundary equation for $\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}$ gives

$$ \mathbb{G}_{\alpha,1}^{\prime}=-w_{\alpha}\bigl(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\bigr)+\delta_{\alpha}^{\prime}\bigl(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\bigr). $$

Using $J_{\alpha}=w_{\alpha}z+(J_{\alpha}-w_{\alpha}z)$ in (9.19), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\nu}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}={} \displaystyle-w_{\alpha}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+(-1)^{\alpha}\bigl(w_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}+J_{\alpha}-w_{\alpha}z\bigr)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}+(-1)^{\alpha}J_{\alpha}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime} \displaystyle-(-1)^{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\partial_{\nu}h_{\alpha}+\sum_{i}(\partial_{\nu}y_{i}-\delta_{1i})\mathbb{G}_{\alpha,i}^{\prime}+\delta_{\alpha}^{\prime}\bigl(y,(-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\bigr). $$

The first term is $O(\varepsilon)$ . Moreover,

$$ \partial_{\nu}h_{\alpha}=\partial_{y_{1}}h_{\alpha}+\sum_{i}(\partial_{\nu}y_{i}-\delta_{1i})\partial_{y_{i}}h_{\alpha},\qquad|\partial_{\nu}y_{i}-\delta_{1i}|\leq C\varepsilon(1+|z|^{3}). $$

Equations (9.5), (9.8), and (9.20) show that the $z$ -integral of each boundary product is bounded by

$$ C\bigl(\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr) $$

times the corresponding squared boundary test functions. For a cross product, use $2|\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}|\leq\eta_{\alpha}^{2}+\eta_{\beta}^{2}$ . The boundary area measure is uniformly comparable to $d\sigma_{\alpha,0}\,dz$ .

Apply (9.17) and Young’s inequality, choosing the coefficient of $|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}$ to be $\delta$ . Since $0\leq A(\cdot;\cdot)\leq 1$ ,

$$ (\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{2}+A^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}A)^{2}+\varepsilon(\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{2}+A^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}A)\leq C(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A). $$

Here every $A$ in the numerical inequality is evaluated at $r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ and $x$ . This proves (9.18). ∎

#### Lemma 9.4 (Combined diagonal contribution).

For every $\delta>0$ , the difference between

$$ \int_{B^{+}_{r+20|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\bigl(|\nabla\varphi_{\alpha}|^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\varphi_{\alpha}^{2}\bigr)\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{0}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0} \displaystyle\quad+\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Bigl[\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}-W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\Bigr]\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)\,dz\,dy $$

is bounded in absolute value by

$$ \displaystyle(C\varepsilon^{1/4}+\delta)\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0} \displaystyle\quad+C(\delta)\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr)\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

#### Proof.

Green’s identity, with $\nu$ the inward normal to the boundary, gives

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\bigl(|\nabla(\eta_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime})|^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\eta_{\alpha}^{2}(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}\bigr)\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}={} \displaystyle\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}|\nabla\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g} \displaystyle+\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}(-\Delta+W^{\prime\prime}(u))g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g} \displaystyle-\int_{\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\partial_{\nu}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\,d\sigma_{g}. $$

Since $\eta_{\alpha}$ is constant along the coordinate fibres, (9.14), (9.6), and the coefficient estimates give

$$ \int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}|\nabla\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}=\sigma_{0}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}+O(\varepsilon)\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

The terms containing the tangential component $T$ obey the same bound.

Substitution of (9.13) in the second line of (9.23) leaves the two terms in (9.21) and the four integrals

$$ \displaystyle-\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\bigl(E_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H},h)+E_{\alpha}(\mathbb{G},h)\bigr)\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}, \displaystyle-\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}(\Delta_{\alpha,z}-\Delta_{\alpha,0})g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}, \displaystyle\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}H_{\alpha}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\partial_{z}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g},\qquad-\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}. $$

The first, second and fourth lines are estimated by (9.5)-(9.8) and the geometric coefficient bounds. In the third line, integrate in $z$ before estimating:

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}H_{\alpha}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\partial_{z}g^{\prime}_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}\,dz=-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g^{\prime}_{\alpha})^{2}\partial_{z}(H_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha})\,dz=O(\varepsilon^{2})\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0), $$

where (9.16) is used. Finally apply Lemma 9.3 to the last line of (9.23). This proves the lemma. ∎

#### 9.2. Interaction estimates

#### Lemma 9.5 (Overlap and projection estimates).

For $\beta\neq\alpha$ and every fixed nonnegative integer $m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|z|+|t_{\beta}(y,z)|)^{m}e^{-|z|-|t_{\beta}(y,z)|}\,dz \displaystyle\hskip 71.13188pt\leq C_{m}(1+|t_{\beta}(y,0)|)^{m+1}e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}. $$

The sum of the right-hand side over $\beta\neq\alpha$ is bounded by $C_{m}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{11/12}$ , while the sum over $|\beta-\alpha|\geq 2$ is bounded by

$$ C_{m}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{3/2}+C_{m}\varepsilon^{2}. $$

For $\beta=\alpha\pm 1$ and $|t_{\beta}(y,0)|\leq 100|\log\varepsilon|$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|t_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0),0)+t_{\beta}(y,0)| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{1/3}, \displaystyle(\Pi_{\beta}|_{\Sigma_{\alpha}})^{*}dA_{\beta,0} \displaystyle=(1+O(\varepsilon^{1/3}))dA_{\alpha,0}, \displaystyle|\Pi_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0),0)-y| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{1/3}. $$

#### Proof.

The signed-distance comparison of Proposition 4.25 gives

$$ |t_{\beta}(y,z)-t_{\beta}(y,0)-z|\leq C\varepsilon^{1/2}|z|(1+|z|). $$

The two estimates of Lemma 5.2, applied with $\sigma=\varsigma=1$ , therefore give (9.25). Exponential separation of the ordered sheets and $(1+s)^{m}e^{-s/12}\leq C_{m}$ give the two asserted sums.

The first and third lines of (9.26) follow from the signed-distance and projection comparison in Proposition 4.25. Differentiating

$$ Y_{\Sigma_{\beta}}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0),t_{\beta}(y,0))=y $$

along $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ gives the area-form comparison. Indeed, the derivative of the normal flow changes the base metric by $O(\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|^{2}))$ , whereas the tangential component of $\nabla t_{\beta}$ along $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ is bounded by $C\varepsilon^{1/4}|\log\varepsilon|^{3/4}$ . The pulled-back metric therefore changes by $O(\varepsilon^{1/3})$ for small $\varepsilon$ . If the separation exceeds $100|\log\varepsilon|$ , the exponential factor is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ , and the coarse bounded-Jacobian estimates suffice. ∎

By the one-dimensional computation used in Section 8.3 of [29], we have the following lemma.

#### Lemma 9.6 (Adjacent one-dimensional interaction).

For $\beta=\alpha\pm 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\bigr)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}\,dz \displaystyle\quad=-2A_{(-1)^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}+O\Bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\Bigr). $$

The sum of the absolute values of the same integrals over $|\beta-\alpha|\geq 2$ is bounded by $C(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{3/2})$ .

#### Lemma 9.7 (Corrected diagonal interaction).

We have

$$ \displaystyle\Bigl|\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl[\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}-W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\bigr]\lambda_{\alpha}\,dz\,dy \displaystyle\quad+2\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\bigl[A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|}+A_{(-1)^{\alpha}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)|}\bigr]dA_{\alpha,0}\Bigr| \displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt\leq C\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr)\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

#### Proof.

A direct Taylor estimate of the term linear in $\phi$ gives only an $O(A)$ bound. To recover the required error, we first remove $\mathbb{G}_{*}$ from the nonlinear argument and use the equation for $\phi$ .

The identity

$$ \Delta(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})=W^{\prime}(u)-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-\sum_{\beta}W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\mathbb{G}_{\beta}-\sum_{\beta}\bigl(\Delta\mathbb{G}_{\beta}-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\mathbb{G}_{\beta}\bigr) $$

combined with the equation for $\phi=u-\mathbb{H}_{*}-\mathbb{G}_{*}$ gives (recall the notation introduced in (6.2))

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{zz}-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})+\sum_{\beta}W^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})={} \displaystyle\Delta(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*}) \displaystyle-\Delta_{\alpha,z}\phi+H_{\alpha}(y,z)\phi_{z}-\mathscr{E}_{\alpha}\phi \displaystyle+\sum_{\beta}\Bigl[(-1)^{\beta}\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}\mathcal{R}_{\beta,1}-\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\mathcal{R}_{\beta,2}-\mathscr{E}_{\beta}\mathbb{H}_{\beta}\Bigr] \displaystyle-\sum_{\beta}\bar{\xi}_{1}\bigl((-1)^{\beta}(t_{\beta}-h_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\beta})\bigr). $$

Multiply (9.29) by $\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}$ and integrate in $z$ . The horizontal derivatives of $\phi$ are controlled by (9.8). For the term involving the $\alpha$ -sheet, use $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\,dz=0$ and subtract $H_{\alpha}(y,0)+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}(y)$ from $\mathcal{R}_{\alpha,1}$ . The difference is bounded by $C\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{m})+C\varepsilon(1+|z|^{m})\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1}}$ . The terms with $\beta\neq\alpha$ are summed using Lemma 9.5. The cut-off terms, the operator terms, and the term involving $\mathbb{G}_{*}$ obey the same bound. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigl|\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl[\phi_{zz}-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})+\sum_{\beta}W^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\bigr]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\,dz\Bigr| \displaystyle\quad\leq C\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr). $$

Integrating the left-hand side of (9.30) by parts once gives

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl[\phi_{zz}-W^{\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})+\sum_{\beta}W^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\bigr]\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}\,dz \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}\,dz \displaystyle+(-1)^{\alpha}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\phi_{z}\,dz \displaystyle+\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}(-1)^{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\bigr)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}\,\partial_{z}(t_{\beta}-h_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\beta})\,dz \displaystyle-(-1)^{\alpha}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bar{\xi}_{1}^{\prime}\bigl((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\bigr)\phi_{z}\,dz. $$

Indeed,

$$ \partial_{z}\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}=(-1)^{\alpha}\Bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+\bar{\xi}_{1}^{\prime}\bigl((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha})\bigr)\Bigr), $$

$$ \partial_{z}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})=\phi_{z}+\sum_{\beta}(-1)^{\beta}\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}\partial_{z}(t_{\beta}-h_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\beta}). $$

The second and fourth lines on the right of (9.31) are $O(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{3/2})$ . In the third line, replacing $W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})$ by $W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{*})$ has the same cost. Moreover, by Proposition 4.26

$$ \partial_{z}(t_{\beta}-h_{\beta}\circ\Pi_{\beta})-1=O(\varepsilon^{1/3})+O(\varepsilon^{1/5})\|\nabla h_{\beta}\|_{C^{0}}. $$

Lemma 9.5 bounds the cost of removing this factor by $C(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A)$ . Since $(-1)^{\alpha+\beta}=-1$ for adjacent sheets, Lemma 9.6 yields

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}\,dz \displaystyle\quad=-2\bigl[A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|}+A_{(-1)^{\alpha}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)|}\bigr] \displaystyle\qquad+O\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\bigr). $$

It remains to restore $\mathbb{G}_{*}$ and $g_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ and to replace $\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)$ by $\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0)$ . Taylor expansion gives

$$ W^{\prime\prime}(u)=W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})+W^{\prime\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})\mathbb{G}_{*}+O(\varepsilon^{2}),\qquad(g_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}=(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}+2\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime}+(\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}. $$

After subtracting (9.32), the terms linear in the own-sheet correction are

$$ 2\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}^{\prime},\qquad\bigl(W^{\prime\prime\prime}(u-\mathbb{G}_{*})-W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\bigr)\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime})^{2}. $$

The subtraction of $W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\alpha})\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ in (9.21) is precisely what produces this cancellation. The part involving $\phi$ is $O(\varepsilon(\varepsilon^{2}+A))$ . Notice that

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|z|^{m})e^{-(1+\sigma)|z|}\min\{1,e^{z-t}\}\,dz\leq C_{m,\sigma}e^{-t}. $$

Taking $\sigma=7/8$ and using $\varepsilon A^{7/8}\leq(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{7/4})/2\leq(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{7/6})/2$ bounds all linear foreign-sheet terms. Terms containing two corrections are $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ . Finally, $|\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)-\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0)|\leq C\varepsilon(1+|z|^{m})\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0)$ , and the same estimate controls the density error. Multiplying by $\eta_{\alpha}^{2}$ and integrating in $y$ proves (9.28). ∎

#### 9.3. Cross terms

#### Lemma 9.8 (Cross terms).

For the ordered sum over $\alpha\neq\beta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigl|\sum_{\alpha\neq\beta}\int_{B^{+}_{r+20|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\bigl(\langle\nabla\varphi_{\alpha},\nabla\varphi_{\beta}\rangle+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\varphi_{\alpha}\varphi_{\beta}\bigr)\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g} \displaystyle\quad+2\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\beta=\alpha\pm 1}A_{(-1)^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}\eta_{\alpha}(y)\eta_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0))\,dA_{\alpha,0}\Bigr| \displaystyle\quad\leq C(N)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{1/4}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{1/2}\Bigr)\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0} \displaystyle\qquad+C(N)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\Bigr)\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

#### Proof.

For a fixed ordered pair, Green’s identity gives

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\bigl(\langle\nabla\varphi_{\alpha},\nabla\varphi_{\beta}\rangle+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\varphi_{\alpha}\varphi_{\beta}\bigr)={} \displaystyle\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}g_{\beta}^{\prime}\langle\nabla\eta_{\alpha},\nabla\eta_{\beta}\rangle \displaystyle+\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}\langle g_{\beta}^{\prime}\nabla g_{\alpha}^{\prime}-g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\nabla g_{\beta}^{\prime},\nabla\eta_{\beta}\rangle \displaystyle+\int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}(-\Delta+W^{\prime\prime}(u))g_{\beta}^{\prime} \displaystyle-\int_{\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}\partial_{\nu}g_{\beta}^{\prime}. $$

All unlabelled integrals in this proof are ambient integrals over the common support. Formula (9.34) follows by expanding both gradients and integrating only the derivative falling on $g_{\beta}^{\prime}$ . The decay estimates imply

$$ |g_{\alpha}^{\prime}|+|\nabla g_{\alpha}^{\prime}|\leq Ce^{-|t_{\alpha}|},\qquad|\nabla\eta_{\alpha}|\leq C|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|\circ\Pi_{\alpha}. $$

Lemma 9.5, applied in either sheet’s coordinates, gives

$$ \int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}e^{-|t_{\alpha}|-|t_{\beta}|}|\eta_{\alpha}\circ\Pi_{\alpha}|^{2}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}\leq CA^{11/12}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}, $$

$$ \int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}e^{-|t_{\alpha}|-|t_{\beta}|}|\nabla_{\beta,0}\eta_{\beta}|^{2}\circ\Pi_{\beta}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}\leq CA^{11/12}\int_{\Sigma_{\beta}}|\nabla_{\beta,0}\eta_{\beta}|^{2}\,dA_{\beta,0}, $$

where, in this proof, $A=A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)$ . These bounds also hold with fixed polynomial factors. The first line of (9.34) is therefore bounded by $CA^{11/12}$ times the two gradient energies. Cauchy’s inequality bounds its second line by

$$ CA^{1/2}\int_{\Sigma_{\beta}}|\nabla_{\beta,0}\eta_{\beta}|^{2}\,dA_{\beta,0}+CA^{4/3}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

Since $A^{11/12}\leq A^{1/2}$ and $A^{4/3}\leq A^{7/6}$ for $0\leq A\leq 1$ , these are allowed errors. Lemma 9.3 controls the boundary integral.

Substituting the $\beta$ -version of (9.12) and (9.1) in the third line of (9.34), its only principal part is

$$ \int_{B^{+}_{r+8|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}\bigl(W^{\prime\prime}(u)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\bigr)g_{\alpha}^{\prime}g_{\beta}^{\prime}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}. $$

The remaining scalar factors multiplying $\eta_{\alpha}\eta_{\beta}g_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ are

$$ -W^{\prime\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\beta})\mathbb{H}_{\beta}^{\prime}\mathbb{G}_{\beta},\quad-\mathbb{E}_{\beta}(\mathbb{H},h)-\mathbb{E}_{\beta}(\mathbb{G},h),\quad-(\Delta_{\beta,t_{\beta}}-\Delta_{\beta,0})g_{\beta}^{\prime},\quad H_{\beta}(\cdot,t_{\beta})\partial_{t_{\beta}}g_{\beta}^{\prime},\quad-\mathscr{E}_{\beta}g_{\beta}^{\prime}. $$

Equations (9.5)-(9.8), the coefficient bounds, Lemma 9.5, and Young’s inequality give the mass error in (9.33). For example,

$$ \varepsilon A^{11/12}\leq C(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{11/6}),\qquad\varepsilon^{3/4}A^{11/12}\leq C(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{22/15})\leq C(\varepsilon^{2}+A^{7/6}). $$

In (9.35), replace $u$ by $\mathbb{H}_{*}$ and both $g^{\prime}$ factors by the corresponding $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ factors. The preceding estimates control the error, and replacing $\lambda_{\alpha}(y,z)$ by $\lambda_{\alpha}(y,0)$ has the same bound. It remains to replace the transported test function by its value at height zero. The exact identity is

$$ \eta_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,z))-\eta_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0))=\int_{0}^{z}\sum_{j}(\partial_{y_{j}}\eta_{\beta})(\Pi_{\beta}(y,s))\partial_{s}\Pi_{\beta}^{j}(y,s)\,ds. $$

On the overlap, $|\partial_{s}\Pi_{\beta}|\leq C\varepsilon^{1/5}$ . The $s$ - and $z$ -intervals have length $O(|\log\varepsilon|)$ , and the maps $y\mapsto\Pi_{\beta}(y,s)$ have uniformly bounded Jacobians. Therefore, Cauchy’s inequality in $y$ , $s$ , and $z$ gives

$$ \displaystyle C\varepsilon^{1/5}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\left(\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}+\int_{\Sigma_{\beta}}|\nabla_{\beta,0}\eta_{\beta}|^{2}\,dA_{\beta,0}\right) \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\left(\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\eta_{\alpha}^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}+\int_{\Sigma_{\beta}}|\nabla_{\beta,0}\eta_{\beta}|^{2}\,dA_{\beta,0}\right), $$

where the last inequality holds for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ , since $\varepsilon^{2/35}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\leq C$ . Lemma 9.6 now gives the neighbouring principal terms in (9.33), and the nonadjacent terms satisfy the stated error estimate. Summing over the finitely many ordered pairs proves the lemma. ∎

#### Lemma 9.9 (Changing the base sheet).

In the terms involving a neighbouring pair $\{\alpha-1,\alpha\}$ , one may change the base from $\Sigma_{\alpha-1}$ to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , transport the exponential weight and the area measure, and replace $\eta_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha-1}(y,0),0))$ by $\eta_{\alpha}(y)$ . The sum of all resulting errors is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle C(N)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{1/4}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{1/2}\Bigr)\sum_{\gamma}\int_{\Sigma_{\gamma}}|\nabla_{\gamma,0}\eta_{\gamma}|^{2}\,dA_{\gamma,0} \displaystyle\quad+C(N)\Bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)^{7/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\Bigr)\sum_{\gamma}\int_{\Sigma_{\gamma}}\eta_{\gamma}^{2}\,dA_{\gamma,0}. $$

This applies to the squared factors in Lemma 9.7 and the mixed factors in Lemma 9.8.

#### Proof.

First suppose that the separation is at most $100|\log\varepsilon|$ . Use the inverse of $\Pi_{\alpha-1}|_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}$ for the change of variables. The first two estimates in (9.26) show that changing the exponential weight and the area measure has relative error $O(\varepsilon^{1/3})$ , hence absolute error $C\varepsilon^{1/3}A(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)$ times the two test-function masses.

The reverse projection need not be the inverse map. By (9.26), its composition with the first projection differs from the identity by $O(\varepsilon^{1/3})$ . Its derivative in graph coordinates differs from the identity by $O(\varepsilon^{1/5})$ . Therefore

$$ \int_{\{y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}:|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|\leq 100|\log\varepsilon|\}}\bigl|\eta_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha-1}(y,0),0))-\eta_{\alpha}(y)\bigr|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}\leq C\varepsilon^{2/3}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\eta_{\alpha}|^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

The integral on the left is over the logarithmic comparison region; the test function is zero outside its support. To compare squares, use $a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)$ ; for a mixed product, leave the other factor unchanged. Cauchy’s inequality, (9.38), and $e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}|}\leq CA(r+240|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)$ prove (9.37).

If the separation exceeds $100|\log\varepsilon|$ , the corresponding term is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ times the masses before and after the base change, by the coarse Jacobian bound in Lemma 9.5. Restricting the comparison to the logarithmic region differentiates no cut-off, because only the integrals are being compared. Summing over the finitely many pairs proves the lemma. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 9.1.

Since $\operatorname{supp}\varphi_{\alpha}\subset B^{+}_{r+20|\log\varepsilon|}(x)$ for every $\alpha$ , the stability assumption gives

$$ 0\leq\int_{B^{+}_{r+20|\log\varepsilon|}(x)}\bigl(|\nabla\varphi|^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(u)\varphi^{2}\bigr)\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g}. $$

If necessary, the compactly supported $C^{1}$ test is approximated in $H^{1}$ by smooth functions up to the boundary.

Expand the right-hand side of (9.39) into diagonal terms and the ordered cross sum. Apply Lemmas 9.4, 9.7, and 9.8. Before changing the base of a neighbouring term, the negative principal contribution is

$$ \displaystyle-2\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\beta=\alpha\pm 1}A_{(-1)^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}\eta_{\alpha}(y)^{2}\,dA_{\alpha,0} \displaystyle\quad-2\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\beta=\alpha\pm 1}A_{(-1)^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}\eta_{\alpha}(y)\eta_{\beta}(\Pi_{\beta}(y,0))\,dA_{\alpha,0}. $$

Fix the unordered neighbouring pair $\{\alpha-1,\alpha\}$ . By Lemma 9.9, all four terms may be written on $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Their common coefficient is $A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}$ . The two diagonal terms and the two ordered mixed terms then combine as

$$ -2A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(y,0)|}\bigl[\eta_{\alpha}(y)+\eta_{\alpha-1}(\Pi_{\alpha-1}(y,0))\bigr]^{2}. $$

Each unordered neighbouring pair is counted exactly once after this regrouping.

Choose the finitely many constants $\delta$ in Lemmas 9.3 and 9.4 so that the sum of their gradient contributions is at most $(\tau-1)\sigma_{0}$ times the total gradient energy. These choices are made after $N$ and $\tau$ are fixed and before $\varepsilon$ is decreased. Moving the negative square in (9.40) to the other side of (9.39), dividing by $\tau\sigma_{0}$ , and defining $Q(\eta)$ to be the sum of the two resulting nonnegative error terms give (9.1) and (9.2). ∎

### 10. A separation estimate from local bounds for the Emden equation

Recall that $R=\varepsilon^{-1}$ and

$$ A(r;x)=\max_{\alpha}\max_{y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r}^{+}(x)}e^{-D_{\alpha}(y)}. $$

We use the geometric and separation estimates of Section 4, the improved Toda equation in Corollary 8.3, and the stability inequality in Proposition 9.1. In particular, Lemma 4.32 implies

$$ A(5R/6;0)=o(1) $$

uniformly as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Fix once and for all a constant

$$ 0<\delta<\frac{1}{48}. $$

This value of $\delta$ remains fixed throughout this section.

#### Proposition 10.1 (Decay above the logarithmic comparison scale).

Suppose that $1\leq n\leq 9$ , where $n$ is the dimension of a sheet. There are fixed constants $M\gg K\gg 1$ such that the following holds for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ . Let $2R/3\leq r\leq 5R/6$ and $\kappa=A(r;0)$ . If

$$ \kappa\geq M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

then

$$ A(r-KR_{*};0)\leq\frac{\kappa}{2},\qquad R_{*}=\max\{\kappa^{-1/2},200|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\}. $$

#### Remark 10.2.

If the boundary is totally geodesic, the same conclusion holds under the weaker hypothesis

$$ \kappa\geq M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|. $$

The distinction between (10.1) and (10.3) occurs in the comparison between the signed Riemannian distance and the Euclidean distance in a coordinate chart. In a boundary Fermi chart, one has

$$ g-\mathrm{Id}=O(\varepsilon|y|+\varepsilon|z|). $$

On a base ball of radius $K\kappa^{-1/2}$ , replacing a distance of order $|\log\varepsilon|$ by the coordinate difference can therefore produce an error of order

$$ C(K)\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}|\log\varepsilon|. $$

Hypothesis (10.1) makes this error small. When the boundary is totally geodesic, all first derivatives of the normalised metric vanish at the centre of a boundary Fermi chart, and the corresponding metric error is quadratic. This yields (10.3).

The proof follows the reduction in [29, Section 9]: derive a scalar inequality for the gap between two adjacent graphs, transfer the stability inequality to the resulting exponential term, obtain an $L^{p}$ estimate with $p>n/2$ , and apply a local boundedness argument.

#### 10.1. The geometric reduction

To prove (10.2), suppose that $x\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r-KR_{*}}^{+}(0)$ satisfies

$$ e^{-D_{\alpha}(x)}>\frac{\kappa}{2}. $$

Choose a point on a neighbouring sheet that attains $D_{\alpha}(x)$ . Reversing the graphical ordering if necessary, denote it by $\Sigma_{\alpha+1}$ . Since $W$ is even, $A_{1}=A_{-1}$ , so this relabelling does not change the interaction coefficient. At this point,

$$ |t_{\alpha+1}(x)|<\log\frac{2}{\kappa}\leq 2|\log\varepsilon| $$

for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ .

The two sheets are the graphs of the functions $f_{\alpha}$ and $f_{\alpha+1}$ already introduced in Section 4, and $x=(x^{\prime},f_{\alpha}(x^{\prime}))$ . Recall that

$$ |\nabla f_{\alpha}|+|\nabla f_{\alpha+1}|\leq C,\qquad|\nabla^{2}f_{\alpha}|+|\nabla^{2}f_{\alpha+1}|\leq C\varepsilon. $$

In a boundary chart,

$$ \partial_{y_{1}}f_{\alpha}=\partial_{y_{1}}f_{\alpha+1}=0\qquad\text{on }\{y_{1}=0\}, $$

because $\partial_{y_{1}}$ is the ambient inward unit normal there. At the centre of the normalized chart,

$$ f_{\alpha}(0)=0,\qquad\nabla f_{\alpha}(0)=0,\qquad g(0)=\mathrm{Id}. $$

Consistently with Sections 3-5, $\mathbb{B}_{s}(x^{\prime})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ denotes the Euclidean ball, and $\mathbb{B}_{s}^{+}(x^{\prime})=\mathbb{B}_{s}(x^{\prime})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}$ in a boundary chart; in an interior chart we use $\mathbb{B}_{s}(x^{\prime})$ . We reserve $B_{s}^{+}(\cdot)$ for ambient Fermi coordinate balls, $B_{s}^{\alpha}(\cdot)$ for the sheet coordinate balls, and $B_{s}^{0,\alpha}(\cdot)$ for the boundary coordinate balls of Definition 5.4. In the graphical and scalar calculations, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$ denote Euclidean coordinate operations on the base; intrinsic derivatives on a sheet retain their earlier subscripts.

The estimates below are used on $\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ , together with a fixed multiple of $|\log\varepsilon|$ in the normal and tangential directions.

Set

$$ f_{\alpha}^{t}=(1-t)f_{\alpha}+tf_{\alpha+1},\qquad t_{\beta}(y)=t_{\beta}(y,f_{\alpha}(y)). $$

The vector $\nu=e_{1}$ denotes the inward normal to the boundary.

#### Lemma 10.3 (Riemannian gap inequality).

Under (10.1), for fixed $K$ , $M$ , and all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ , there is a symmetric matrix $B_{\alpha}$ such that

$$ |B_{\alpha}-\mathrm{Id}|\leq C(K)M^{-\delta},\qquad|\nabla B_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Id}\leq B_{\alpha}\leq 2\mathrm{Id}. $$

For every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ such that $f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)<4|\log\varepsilon|+1$ ,

$$ \operatorname{div}\!\left(B_{\alpha}\nabla(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})\right)\leq\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)e^{-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})}+C(K)M^{-\delta}\kappa. $$

On the boundary $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ , we have

$$ \left\langle B_{\alpha}\nabla(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha}),\nu\right\rangle=0. $$

For completeness, we record the matrix in Lemma 10.3. If $p=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})$ is the covector defining a graph, then

$$ \varpi(y,z,p)^{2}=g^{n+1,n+1}(y,z)-2\sum_{i}g^{i,n+1}(y,z)p_{i}+\sum_{i,j}g^{ij}(y,z)p_{i}p_{j}. $$

Thus the graph-area density relative to $dy$ is $\sqrt{\det g(y,z)}\,\varpi(y,z,p)$ , where the determinant is that of the ambient $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ metric matrix. Define

$$ B_{\alpha,ij}(y)=\int_{0}^{1}\left[\partial_{p_{i}p_{j}}^{2}\!\left(\sqrt{\det g}\,\varpi\right)\right]\bigl(y,f_{\alpha}^{t}(y),\nabla f_{\alpha}^{t}(y)\bigr)\,dt. $$

#### Remark 10.4.

At $y_{1}=0$ , boundary Fermi coordinates give $g^{1j}=0$ for $j\neq 1$ , $g^{11}=1$ , and $g^{1,n+1}=0$ . Equation (10.7) gives $p_{1}=0$ for $p=\nabla f_{\alpha}^{t}$ . Differentiating (10.11) therefore yields

$$ \partial_{p_{1}}\!\left(\sqrt{\det g}\,\varpi\right)=0,\qquad\partial_{p_{1}p_{j}}^{2}\!\left(\sqrt{\det g}\,\varpi\right)=0\quad(j\geq 2). $$

Consequently $B_{\alpha}\nu=B_{\alpha,11}\nu$ , and (10.7) gives the asserted conormal condition.

#### Proof of Lemma 10.3.

We begin with the two geometric estimates used in the proof.

#### Claim 10.5.

For every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}+20|\log\varepsilon|}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla f_{\alpha}| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}+C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|, \displaystyle|\nabla f_{\alpha+1}| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}+C\sqrt{\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|}+C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|, \displaystyle|g-\mathrm{Id}| \displaystyle\leq C(K)(\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|),\qquad|\partial g|\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad|\partial^{2}g|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

The first estimate follows from (10.8), (10.6), and the distance between 0 and $x^{\prime}$ . At $x^{\prime}$ , the uniform metric and graph bounds together with (10.5) first give $f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha}\leq C|\log\varepsilon|$ . The positive difference of two disjoint graphs whose Hessians are bounded by $C\varepsilon$ satisfies

$$ |\nabla(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})|\leq C\sqrt{\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|} $$

at that point. Indeed, Taylor’s inequality in a unit direction chosen to decrease the difference gives

$$ 0\leq(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)-s|\partial(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)|+C\varepsilon s^{2}. $$

Taking $s$ comparable to $\sqrt{|\log\varepsilon|/\varepsilon}$ gives (10.16).

Combining (10.16) with (10.13) at $x^{\prime}$ gives (10.14) there. Integrating (10.6) along base segments of length $O(K\kappa^{-1/2}+|\log\varepsilon|)$ proves (10.13)-(10.14) on $B_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}+20|\log\varepsilon|}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ . The graph values on this set remain in an ambient coordinate neighbourhood of radius $C(K)(\kappa^{-1/2}+|\log\varepsilon|)$ . Taylor’s theorem for the rescaled metric then gives (10.15). ∎

#### Claim 10.6.

For every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ satisfying $f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left||t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)\right|+\left||t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)\right| \displaystyle\quad\leq C(K)\left(\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}|\log\varepsilon|+\varepsilon^{2}\kappa^{-1}|\log\varepsilon|+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\right)\leq C(K)M^{-\delta}. $$

In particular,

$$ e^{-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})}=\bigl(1+O(C(K)M^{-\delta})\bigr)e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|}, $$

and the analogous formula holds with the two sheets interchanged. If $(y,f_{\alpha}(y))\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r}^{+}(0)$ and $(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))\in\Sigma_{\alpha+1}\cap B_{r}^{+}(0)$ , then

$$ e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|}\leq\kappa,\qquad e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}\leq\kappa. $$

#### Proof.

A vertical segment gives the upper distance bound

$$ |t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|\leq(1+C|g-\mathrm{Id}|)(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y), $$

and similarly from the upper sheet. For the reverse inequality, a Euclidean graph of slope at most $s$ has distance at least $d/\sqrt{1+s^{2}}$ from a point whose vertical gap is $d$ . Indeed, at horizontal displacement $a$ the vertical difference is at least $\max\{d-s|a|,0\}$ , and minimizing

$$ |a|^{2}+\max\{d-s|a|,0\}^{2} $$

gives $d^{2}/(1+s^{2})$ . The comparison applies to the extended graphs used in the definition of the signed distances in Section 4. The vertical upper bound confines every minimizing segment to a coordinate neighbourhood of radius $C|\log\varepsilon|$ .

By Claims 10.5, the squared slope and the metric error on this neighbourhood are bounded by

$$ C(K)(\varepsilon^{2}\kappa^{-1}+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|),\qquad C(K)(\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|), $$

respectively. Multiplying by a gap of order $|\log\varepsilon|$ proves the first inequality in (10.17). Under (10.1), its three terms are bounded by

$$ C(K)M^{-1/2},\qquad C(K)M^{-1}|\log\varepsilon|^{-1},\qquad C(K)\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Choose $M$ after $K$ and then choose $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small. Since $\delta<1/48$ , this proves the second inequality in (10.17); (10.18) follows by exponentiation. If $(y,f_{\alpha}(y))\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{r}^{+}(0)$ , then the definition of $A(r;0)$ gives $e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|}\leq e^{-D_{\alpha}(y)}\leq\kappa$ . At $(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))\in\Sigma_{\alpha+1}\cap B_{r}^{+}(0)$ , the definition of $A(r;0)$ gives $e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}\leq\kappa$ . ∎

We now need to compute the operator in (10.10). The proof of Lemma 4.22 in Appendix B already contains the essential computations to check that by Claims 10.5 for every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ ,

$$ |B_{\alpha}-\mathrm{Id}|\leq C(K)(\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}+\varepsilon^{2}\kappa^{-1}+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|),\qquad|\nabla B_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon. $$

After $M$ is fixed and $\varepsilon$ is decreased, these inequalities give (10.9). Remark 10.4 gives the boundary condition.

Fix

$$ y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})\quad\text{with}\quad f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)<4|\log\varepsilon|+1. $$

Apply Corollary 8.3 at $(y,f_{\alpha}(y))$ and $(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))$ . By the radius choice in the proof of Proposition 10.1,

$$ B_{300|\log\varepsilon|^{2}}^{+}\bigl((y,f_{\gamma}(y))\bigr)\subset B_{r}^{+}(0),\qquad\gamma\in\{\alpha,\alpha+1\}. $$

The remainder in each of the two Toda equations is

$$ C\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}+\kappa^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}\kappa\bigr). $$

In the equation for the lower sheet, discard the nonnegative interaction with its lower neighbour; in the equation for the upper sheet, discard the nonpositive interaction with its upper neighbour. Since $A_{1}=A_{-1}$ ,

$$ H_{\alpha}\geq-\frac{2A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha}(y))|}-C(\varepsilon^{2}+\kappa^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}\kappa), $$

while

$$ H_{\alpha+1}\leq\frac{2A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}+C(\varepsilon^{2}+\kappa^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}\kappa). $$

Multiply these inequalities by the corresponding positive densities and subtract the lower-sheet inequality from the upper-sheet inequality to obtain (10.10). Indeed, after division by $\kappa$ , all remaining terms are bounded by

$$ C(K)\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}(1+|\log\varepsilon|)}{\kappa}+\kappa^{1/2}+\varepsilon^{1/6}\right). $$

The first term is at most $C(K)/M$ under (10.1), and the other two tend to zero uniformly because $A(5R/6;0)=o(1)$ . This proves the lemma. ∎

#### 10.2. The rescaled inequality and its stability

Use the following rescaling:

$$ v_{\alpha}(y)=(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(\kappa^{-1/2}y)-|\log\kappa|,\qquad\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}(y)=B_{\alpha}(\kappa^{-1/2}y). $$

After rescaling, the base coordinate of $x$ is $\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime}$ . Then set

$$ V_{\alpha}(y)=\max\left\{e^{-v_{\alpha}(y)},\frac{\varepsilon^{4}}{\kappa}\right\}. $$

At every point

$$ y\in\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})\quad\text{such that}\quad(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(\kappa^{-1/2}y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|, $$

one has $V_{\alpha}(y)=e^{-v_{\alpha}(y)}$ . The proof of Proposition 10.1 shows that $(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(x^{\prime})<4|\log\varepsilon|$ , and hence $V_{\alpha}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})=e^{-v_{\alpha}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}$ .

For every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})$ satisfying $(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(\kappa^{-1/2}y)<4|\log\varepsilon|$ , rescaling (10.10) gives

$$ \operatorname{div}(\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla v_{\alpha})\leq\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)e^{-v_{\alpha}}+C(K)M^{-\delta}. $$

Consequently, $V_{\alpha}$ is a positive, continuous, locally Lipschitz weak subsolution of

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} -\operatorname{div}(\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha})&\leq\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)V_{\alpha}^{2}-V_{\alpha}^{-1}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle+C(K)M^{-\delta}V_{\alpha},\\
\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nu\right\rangle&=0\qquad\text{on }\{y_{1}=0\}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

The rescaled coefficient satisfies

$$ |\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}-\mathrm{Id}|\leq C(K)M^{-\delta},\qquad|\nabla\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2},\qquad\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Id}\leq\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\leq 2\mathrm{Id}. $$

#### Lemma 10.7 (Transfer of almost stability).

Fix $\tau\in(1,2)$ independently of $K$ , $M$ , and $\varepsilon$ . For every $\eta\in C^{1}(\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime}))$ supported away from $\partial_{+}\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}V_{\alpha}\eta^{2} \displaystyle\leq\bigl(\tau+C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla\eta,\nabla\eta\right\rangle \displaystyle\quad+C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\eta^{2}. $$

and similarly in a full ball in the interior.

#### Proof.

We put the same base test function on the two adjacent sheets, compare its projected values, and rescale, as in [29, Lemma 9.5 and (9.26)]. Throughout the proof, $\eta$ denotes the rescaled test function, extended by zero outside $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})$ . Set

$$ \eta_{\gamma}(y,f_{\gamma}(y))=\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)\quad(\gamma=\alpha,\alpha+1),\qquad\eta_{\gamma}=0\quad(\gamma\notin\{\alpha,\alpha+1\}). $$

Proposition 9.1, with $N=2$ , gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{2A_{1}^{2}}{\tau\sigma_{0}}\int_{\Sigma_{\alpha+1}}e^{-|t_{\alpha}|}(\eta_{\alpha+1}+\eta_{\alpha}\circ\Pi_{\alpha})^{2}\,dA_{\alpha+1,0}\leq{} \displaystyle\sum_{\gamma=\alpha,\alpha+1}\int_{\Sigma_{\gamma}}|\nabla_{\gamma,0}\eta_{\gamma}|^{2}\,dA_{\gamma,0}+Q((\eta_{\gamma})_{\gamma}), $$

Claim 10.5, Remark 4.16, and the coordinate-flow estimates used in the proof of Lemma 9.9 give, whenever $y\in\mathbb{B}_{K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ is such that $f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\Pi_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))-y| \displaystyle\leq C(K)\Bigl(\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}|\log\varepsilon|+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,|\log\varepsilon|^{3/2}+\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{3}\Bigr). $$

Claim: Let $\mathcal{S}\coloneqq\{y\in\mathbb{B}_{K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime}):f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|\}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}\left|\eta_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y)))-\eta_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))\right|^{2}\,dy \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\leq C(K)M^{-2\delta}\kappa^{1-n/2}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dy. $$

Proof of Claim. To obtain (10.23), let $\Pi_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))=(P(y),f_{\alpha}(P(y)))$ and notice that

$$ \displaystyle|\eta_{\alpha}(\Pi_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y)))- \displaystyle\eta_{\alpha+1}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|^{2}=|\eta(\kappa^{1/2}P(y))-\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\kappa|P(y)-y|^{2}\int_{0}^{1}|\nabla\eta(\kappa^{1/2}((1-s)y+sP(y)))|^{2}\,ds. $$

By (10.22),

$$ |P(y)-y|^{2}\leq C(K)\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}\kappa^{-1}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\varepsilon\kappa|\log\varepsilon|^{3}+\varepsilon^{2}\kappa|\log\varepsilon|^{6}\bigr), $$

so that, for fixed $K$ and $M$ , we can pick $\varepsilon$ small enough that

$$ C(K)\bigl(\varepsilon^{2}\kappa^{-1}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\varepsilon\kappa|\log\varepsilon|^{3}+\varepsilon^{2}\kappa|\log\varepsilon|^{6}\bigr)\leq C(K)M^{-2\delta} $$

Using $e^{-|t_{\alpha}|}\leq\kappa$ and integrating the left-hand side of (10.24) over $\mathcal{S}$ and the right-hand side over $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{K\kappa^{-1/2}(x^{\prime})}$ gives (10.23). ∎

Now notice that $(\eta_{\alpha+1}+\eta_{\alpha}\circ\Pi_{\alpha})^{2}\geq 4(1-M^{-\delta})\eta_{\alpha+1}^{2}-M^{\delta}|\eta_{\alpha+1}-\eta_{\alpha}\circ\Pi_{\alpha}|^{2}$ , so the previous claim gives

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}(\eta_{\alpha+1}+\eta_{\alpha}\circ\Pi_{\alpha})^{2}\,dy\geq{} \displaystyle 4(1-M^{-\delta})\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)^{2}\,dy \displaystyle\quad-C(K)M^{-\delta}\kappa^{1-n/2}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dy. $$

Under the graph parametrizations, Claim 10.5 gives

$$ dA_{\gamma,0}=\bigl(1+O(C(K)M^{-\delta})\bigr)\,dy\quad(\gamma=\alpha,\alpha+1), $$

and

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{\gamma}}|\nabla_{\gamma,0}\eta_{\gamma}|^{2}\,dA_{\gamma,0}\leq\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})}\left|\nabla_{y}[\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)]\right|^{2}\,dy. $$

The weight comparison in (10.18) and the formula immediately following it give

$$ e^{-|t_{\alpha}(y,f_{\alpha+1}(y))|}=\bigl(1+O(C(K)M^{-\delta})\bigr)e^{-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)} $$

when $f_{\alpha+1}(y)-f_{\alpha}(y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|$ . Now set $Y=\kappa^{1/2}y$ . On this set, $e^{-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)}=\kappa V_{\alpha}(Y)$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}}e^{-(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(y)}\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)^{2}\,dy=\kappa^{1-n/2}\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}V_{\alpha}(Y)\eta(Y)^{2}\,dY, $$

where $\mathcal{S^{\prime}}=\{Y\in\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime}):(f_{\alpha+1}-f_{\alpha})(\kappa^{-1/2}Y)\leq 4|\log\varepsilon|\}$ , whereas

$$ \int_{\mathbb{B}_{K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})}\left|\nabla_{y}[\eta(\kappa^{1/2}y)]\right|^{2}\,dy=\kappa^{1-n/2}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dY. $$

Substitute these comparisons and the lower bound for the square into the stability inequality, and cancel $\kappa^{1-n/2}$ . We obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{8A_{1}^{2}}{\tau\sigma_{0}}\bigl(1-C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}V_{\alpha}\eta^{2}\,dY\leq\bigl(2+C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dY+\kappa^{n/2-1}Q((\eta_{\gamma})_{\gamma}). $$

Moreover,

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{\gamma}}\eta_{\gamma}^{2}\,dA_{\gamma,0}\leq\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\kappa^{-n/2}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\eta^{2}\,dY\quad(\gamma=\alpha,\alpha+1). $$

Thus (9.2), with $N=2$ , gives

$$ \displaystyle\kappa^{n/2-1}Q((\eta_{\gamma})_{\gamma}) \displaystyle\leq C(2,\tau)(\varepsilon^{1/4}+\kappa^{1/2})\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dY \displaystyle\quad+C(2,\tau)\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa}+\kappa^{1/6}+\varepsilon^{1/7}\right)\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\eta^{2}\,dY \displaystyle\leq C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\left(\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dY+\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\eta^{2}\,dY\right). $$

Insert this bound for $Q$ into the inequality with coefficient $8A_{1}^{2}/(\tau\sigma_{0})$ . For $M$ sufficiently large, $C(K)M^{-\delta}\leq 1/2$ . Divide by $2$ and multiply by $\tau/(1-C(K)M^{-\delta})$ to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}V_{\alpha}\eta^{2}\,dY \displaystyle\qquad\leq\bigl(\tau+C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\,dY+C(K,\tau)M^{-\delta}\int_{\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})}\eta^{2}\,dY. $$

By (10.9),

$$ |\nabla\eta|^{2}\leq\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla\eta,\nabla\eta\rangle. $$

Moreover, on $\mathbb{B}^{+}_{K}(\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime})\setminus\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ , we have $V_{\alpha}=\varepsilon^{4}/\kappa$ . Adding the resulting contribution to (10.25) and using (10.27) gives (10.21). ∎

#### 10.3. Local bounds for the scalar inequality

We now state the scalar estimates for an arbitrary base-ball centre $y_{0}$ . In the application to the function $V_{\alpha}$ constructed above, take $y_{0}=\kappa^{1/2}x^{\prime}$ . We regard (10.20)–(10.21) as scalar weak inequalities on $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0})$ . If $\mathbb{B}_{K}(y_{0})\subset\{y_{1}>0\}$ , replace every $\mathbb{B}_{s}^{+}(y_{0})$ below by $\mathbb{B}_{s}(y_{0})$ and omit the conormal condition. The matrix $\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}$ is symmetric and has ellipticity constants between $1/2$ and $2$ . Test functions may meet $\mathbb{B}_{K}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}=0\}$ but have support disjoint from $\partial\mathbb{B}_{K}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}>0\}$ . All constants are uniform for every centre $y_{0}$ with $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0})\neq\varnothing$ . Once $\tau$ is fixed, its dependence is included in $C(K)$ .

#### Proposition 10.8 (Smallness from almost stability).

Suppose that $1\leq n\leq 9$ . Choose, once and for all,

$$ \frac{7}{4}<q<2,\qquad 1<\tau<\frac{2}{q},\qquad p=2q+1. $$

The only properties used below are

$$ p>\frac{n}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2q-\tau q^{2}>0. $$

For $K$ sufficiently large and then $M$ sufficiently large, every positive locally Lipschitz weak subsolution of (10.20) on $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0})$ that satisfies (10.21) obeys

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{1}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq\frac{1}{4}. $$

The proof is divided into the following three lemmas.

#### Lemma 10.9 (Bounded local subsolutions).

Suppose that $C(K)M^{-\delta}\leq 1$ , and let $V_{\alpha}$ satisfy (10.20) on $\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0})$ with $0<V_{\alpha}\leq\Lambda$ . For every $p\geq 2$ ,

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{1}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq c_{0}(n,p,W,\Lambda)\|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0}))}. $$

More generally, for every fixed $0<r_{1}<r_{2}\leq 2$ ,

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{r_{1}}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq c_{0}(n,p,W,\Lambda,r_{1},r_{2})\|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{r_{2}}^{+}(y_{0}))}. $$

#### Proof.

Discard the nonpositive quadratic-gradient term in (10.20). Since $C(K)M^{-\delta}\leq 1$ and $V_{\alpha}\leq\Lambda$ ,

$$ -\operatorname{div}(\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha})\leq\left(1+\frac{8A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\Lambda\right)V_{\alpha}. $$

For $s\geq 2$ and $\psi\in C^{1}(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0}))$ satisfying $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\bigl(\partial\mathbb{B}_{2}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}>0\}\bigr)=\emptyset$ , test this inequality with $\psi^{2}V_{\alpha}^{s-1}$ .

All integrals through (10.30) are over $\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0})$ . The conormal condition removes the integral over $\mathbb{B}_{2}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}=0\}$ . Uniform ellipticity and Young’s inequality give

$$ \displaystyle(s-1)\int\psi^{2}V_{\alpha}^{s-2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq C(W)(1+\Lambda)\int\psi^{2}V_{\alpha}^{s} \displaystyle\quad+2\,\Bigl|\int\psi V_{\alpha}^{s-1}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla\psi\right\rangle\Bigr| \displaystyle\leq C(W)(1+\Lambda)\int\psi^{2}V_{\alpha}^{s}+\frac{s-1}{2}\int\psi^{2}V_{\alpha}^{s-2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle \displaystyle\quad+\frac{C}{s-1}\int V_{\alpha}^{s}|\nabla\psi|^{2}. $$

Subtract the repeated gradient term and use $\nabla V_{\alpha}^{s/2}=(s/2)V_{\alpha}^{s/2-1}\nabla V_{\alpha}$ . It follows that

$$ \int\bigl|\nabla(\psi V_{\alpha}^{s/2})\bigr|^{2}\leq C(W)s^{2}\int V_{\alpha}^{s}\left((1+\Lambda)\psi^{2}+|\nabla\psi|^{2}\right). $$

Apply the Euclidean Sobolev inequality to $\psi V_{\alpha}^{s/2}$ after extending it by zero across $\partial\mathbb{B}_{2}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}>0\}$ . If $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\{y_{1}=0\}\neq\emptyset$ , take its even $H^{1}$ extension across $\{y_{1}=0\}$ . For $n>2$ use the exponent $2n/(n-2)$ ; for $n=1,2$ use exponent $4$ , including the $L^{2}$ term on the bounded support.

At the $j$ -th step, use the nested half-balls $\mathbb{B}_{1+2^{-j}}^{+}(y_{0})$ and $\mathbb{B}_{1+2^{-j-1}}^{+}(y_{0})$ , begin with exponent $s=p$ , and choose a cutoff supported in $\mathbb{B}_{1+2^{-j}}^{+}(y_{0})$ , equal to one on $\mathbb{B}_{1+2^{-j-1}}^{+}(y_{0})$ , with derivative bounded by $C2^{j}$ . Equation (10.30) multiplies the next norm by at most

$$ \bigl(C(W)s^{2}(1+\Lambda+4^{j})\bigr)^{1/s}. $$

The exponents grow geometrically, by $n/(n-2)$ when $n>2$ and by $2$ when $n=1,2$ . Hence the sums of $1/s$ and $j/s$ over the iteration are finite, and so is the product of the displayed factors. This proves (10.29). ∎

#### Lemma 10.10 ( $L^{p}$ estimate).

For the choices in (10.28), if $K$ is sufficiently large and then $M$ is sufficiently large, every subsolution satisfying (10.20) and (10.21) on $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0})$ satisfies

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0}))}^{p}\leq CK^{n-2p}+C(K)M^{-\delta p}K^{n}. $$

The constant in the first term is independent of $K$ and $M$ . Consequently, the left side can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $K$ first and then $M$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\psi\geq 0$ belong to $C^{1}(\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0}))$ and satisfy $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\bigl(\partial\mathbb{B}_{K}(y_{0})\cap\{y_{1}>0\}\bigr)=\emptyset.$ All integrals below are over $\mathbb{B}_{K}^{+}(y_{0})$ . Since $q$ and $\tau$ are fixed, the constants denoted by $C$ in this proof may depend on them, but not on $K$ or $M$ .

Test (10.20) with $V_{\alpha}^{2q-1}\psi^{2}$ . The conormal condition removes the boundary integral on $\{y_{1}=0\}$ , and the negative quadratic-gradient term changes the coefficient of the first integral from $2q-1$ to $2q$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle 2q\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-2}\psi^{2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle+2\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-1}\psi\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla\psi\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\bigl(1+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int V_{\alpha}^{2q+1}\psi^{2} \displaystyle\quad+C(K)M^{-\delta}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\psi^{2}. $$

Apply (10.21) with $\eta=V_{\alpha}^{q}\psi$ :

$$ \displaystyle\frac{4A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q+1}\psi^{2} \displaystyle\leq\bigl(\tau+C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\Big[q^{2}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-2}\psi^{2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle \displaystyle\qquad+2q\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-1}\psi\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla\psi\right\rangle+\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla\psi,\nabla\psi\right\rangle\Big] \displaystyle\quad+C(K)M^{-\delta}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\psi^{2}. $$

Substitute this estimate into (10.32). After increasing $C(K)$ , all perturbations of the fixed coefficients are bounded by $C(K)M^{-\delta}$ , and hence

$$ \displaystyle\bigl(2q-\tau q^{2}-C(K)M^{-\delta}\bigr)\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-2}\psi^{2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle \displaystyle\quad\leq C\left|\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-1}\psi\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla\psi\right\rangle\right|+C\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla\psi,\nabla\psi\right\rangle \displaystyle\qquad+C(K)M^{-\delta}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\psi^{2}. $$

The number $2q-\tau q^{2}$ is positive by (10.28). Choose $M$ so large that

$$ C(K)M^{-\delta}\leq\frac{1}{4}(2q-\tau q^{2}). $$

By Cauchy–Schwarz and Young’s inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle C\left|\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-1}\psi\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla\psi\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}(2q-\tau q^{2})\int V_{\alpha}^{2q-2}\psi^{2}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla V_{\alpha},\nabla V_{\alpha}\right\rangle \displaystyle\quad+C\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\left\langle\widetilde{B}_{\alpha}\nabla\psi,\nabla\psi\right\rangle. $$

Absorbing the first term and using uniform ellipticity yields

$$ \int V_{\alpha}^{2q-2}\psi^{2}|\nabla V_{\alpha}|^{2}\leq C\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+C(K)M^{-\delta}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\psi^{2}. $$

Insert this estimate into (10.33); the mixed term is handled by the same Cauchy–Schwarz and Young inequalities. We obtain

$$ \int V_{\alpha}^{2q+1}\psi^{2}\leq C\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+C(K)M^{-\delta}\int V_{\alpha}^{2q}\psi^{2}. $$

Now replace $\psi$ in (10.35) by $\psi^{p}$ , where $p=2q+1$ . The fixed factor $p^{2}$ is absorbed into $C$ . Hölder’s inequality gives

$$ \int V_{\alpha}^{p-1}\psi^{2p-2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}\leq\left(\int V_{\alpha}^{p}\psi^{2p}\right)^{(p-1)/p}\left(\int|\nabla\psi|^{2p}\right)^{1/p} $$

and

$$ \int V_{\alpha}^{p-1}\psi^{2p}\leq\left(\int V_{\alpha}^{p}\psi^{2p}\right)^{(p-1)/p}\left(\int\psi^{2p}\right)^{1/p}. $$

Dividing by the common factor, when it is nonzero, and raising to the power $p$ yields

$$ \int V_{\alpha}^{p}\psi^{2p}\leq C\int|\nabla\psi|^{2p}+C(K)M^{-\delta p}\int\psi^{2p}. $$

Finally, choose a radial cutoff about $y_{0}$ which is one on $\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0})$ , vanishes outside $\mathbb{B}_{K/2}^{+}(y_{0})$ , and satisfies $|\nabla\psi|\leq C/K$ . Its restriction to the half-space is admissible. Since $|\mathbb{B}_{K/2}^{+}(y_{0})|\leq CK^{n}$ , equation (10.36) gives (10.31). Finally,

$$ p=2q+1>\frac{9}{2}\geq\frac{n}{2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad n-2p<0. $$

Hence $CK^{n-2p}$ is made small by choosing $K$ large, and, after $K$ is fixed, $C(K)M^{-\delta p}K^{n}$ is made small by choosing $M$ large. This proves the lemma. ∎

#### Lemma 10.11 (Removal of the a priori upper bound).

Let $p>n/2$ , $p\geq 2$ , and suppose that $V_{\alpha}$ satisfies (10.20) on $\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0})$ , with $C(K)M^{-\delta}\leq 1$ and

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq 1. $$

There is a constant $C_{0}=C_{0}(n,p,W)$ such that

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq C_{0}. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose otherwise. Let $V_{i}$ be a sequence of subsolutions violating the conclusion. For the $i$ -th subsolution, $y_{0}$ denotes the centre of the half-ball $\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0})$ in the statement and may depend on $i$ . Choose $x_{i}\in\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0})$ such that $V_{i}(x_{i})\to\infty$ , and set

$$ r_{i}=V_{i}(x_{i})^{-1/4}. $$

For all large $i$ , $\overline{\mathbb{B}}_{r_{i}}(x_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}\subset\mathbb{B}_{3}^{+}(y_{0})$ . Let $y_{i}$ maximize

$$ (r_{i}-|y-x_{i}|)^{2}V_{i}(y) $$

on $\overline{\mathbb{B}}_{r_{i}}(x_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}$ . The maximum is positive and is not attained on $\partial\mathbb{B}_{r_{i}}(x_{i})\cap\{y_{1}>0\}$ , where $(r_{i}-|y-x_{i}|)^{2}=0$ . Put

$$ r_{i}^{\prime}=r_{i}-|y_{i}-x_{i}|>0,\qquad\lambda_{i}=V_{i}(y_{i}). $$

Maximality gives

$$ r_{i}^{\prime}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\geq r_{i}\sqrt{V_{i}(x_{i})}=V_{i}(x_{i})^{1/4}\to\infty. $$

Since $r_{i}^{\prime}\leq r_{i}\to 0$ , it follows that $\lambda_{i}\to\infty$ . If $|y-y_{i}|\leq r_{i}^{\prime}/2$ , then $r_{i}-|y-x_{i}|\geq r_{i}^{\prime}/2$ ; hence

$$ V_{i}(y)\leq 4\lambda_{i}\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{B}_{r_{i}^{\prime}/2}(y_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}. $$

Let $d_{i}$ be the Euclidean distance from $y_{i}$ to the boundary. First suppose that $d_{i}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\geq 4$ . Define

$$ \widetilde{V}_{i}(\widetilde{y})=\lambda_{i}^{-1}V_{i}(y_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y}). $$

By (10.37)–(10.38), this function is defined on $\mathbb{B}_{2}(0)$ for all large $i$ and satisfies

$$ \widetilde{V}_{i}(0)=1,\qquad 0<\widetilde{V}_{i}\leq 4. $$

The coefficient in the rescaled equation is

$$ \widetilde{B}_{i}(y_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y}), $$

not $\widetilde{B}_{i}(\widetilde{y})$ . After discarding the negative quadratic-gradient term and dividing the rescaled equation by $\lambda_{i}^{2}$ , we obtain

$$ -\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde{y}}\!\left(\widetilde{B}_{i}(y_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y})\nabla_{\widetilde{y}}\widetilde{V}_{i}\right)\leq\left(1+\frac{32A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\right)\widetilde{V}_{i}\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{B}_{2}(0). $$

Indeed, the term $C(K)M^{-\delta}V_{i}$ becomes $C(K)M^{-\delta}\lambda_{i}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_{i}$ after division by $\lambda_{i}^{2}$ , and its coefficient is at most one for all large $i$ ; ellipticity is unchanged. Lemma 10.9, or its proof applied to (10.39), now yields

$$ \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle\leq c_{0}(n,p,W,4)\|\widetilde{V}_{i}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{2}(0))} \displaystyle=c_{0}(n,p,W,4)\lambda_{i}^{n/(2p)-1}\|V_{i}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{2/\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}(y_{i}))} \displaystyle\leq c_{0}(n,p,W,4)\lambda_{i}^{n/(2p)-1}\to 0. $$

because $p>n/2$ . For all large $i$ ,

$$ \mathbb{B}_{2/\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}(y_{i})\subset\mathbb{B}_{r_{i}^{\prime}/2}(y_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}\subset\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0}), $$

which gives the last inequality. This is a contradiction.

Now suppose that $d_{i}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}<4$ . Let $y_{i}^{\prime}$ be the Euclidean projection of $y_{i}$ onto the boundary and retain the same value $\lambda_{i}=V_{i}(y_{i})$ . Define

$$ \widetilde{V}_{i}(\widetilde{y})=\lambda_{i}^{-1}V_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y}),\qquad\widetilde{y}_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}(y_{i}-y_{i}^{\prime}). $$

Then $|\widetilde{y}_{i}|<4$ and $\widetilde{V}_{i}(\widetilde{y}_{i})=1$ . By (10.37), $r_{i}^{\prime}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}>40$ for all large $i$ . The inclusion

$$ y_{i}^{\prime}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\mathbb{B}_{16}^{+}(0)\subset\mathbb{B}_{20/\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}(y_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\}\subset\mathbb{B}_{r_{i}^{\prime}/2}(y_{i})\cap\{y_{1}\geq 0\} $$

follows from $|\widetilde{y}_{i}|<4$ and $r_{i}^{\prime}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}>40$ . Thus (10.38) gives $\widetilde{V}_{i}\leq 4$ on $\mathbb{B}_{16}^{+}(0)$ . The coefficient is

$$ \widetilde{B}_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y}), $$

and

$$ -\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde{y}}\!\left(\widetilde{B}_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}+\lambda_{i}^{-1/2}\widetilde{y})\nabla_{\widetilde{y}}\widetilde{V}_{i}\right)\leq\left(1+\frac{32A_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}}\right)\widetilde{V}_{i}\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{B}_{16}^{+}(0), $$

with zero conormal derivative on $\mathbb{B}_{16}(0)\cap\{\widetilde{y}_{1}=0\}$ . The bounded Moser estimate on the radii $8$ and $16$ , followed by the exact scaling of the $L^{p}$ norm, gives

$$ 1\leq\|\widetilde{V}_{i}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{8}^{+}(0))}\leq C(n,p,W)\|\widetilde{V}_{i}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{16}^{+}(0))}\leq C(n,p,W)\lambda_{i}^{n/(2p)-1}\|V_{i}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0}))}\to 0. $$

This is again a contradiction. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 10.8.

Fix $q$ , $\tau$ , and $p$ as in (10.28). Lemma 10.10 allows us to choose $K$ and then $M$ so that

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{4}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq\min\left\{1,\bigl(4c_{0}(n,p,W,C_{0})\bigr)^{-1}\right\}. $$

By the first bound, we can apply Lemma 10.11; hence

$$ V_{\alpha}\leq C_{0}\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0}). $$

Apply Lemma 10.9 on the radii $1$ and $2$ with $\Lambda=C_{0}$ . Then

$$ \|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{B}_{1}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq c_{0}(n,p,W,C_{0})\|V_{\alpha}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{+}(y_{0}))}\leq\frac{1}{4}. $$

∎

#### 10.4. Completion of the separation estimate

#### Proof of Proposition 10.1.

We first assume (10.1). Fix any $q$ , $\tau$ , and $p$ satisfying (10.28). Choose the radius $K$ using (10.31), and then choose $M$ sufficiently large for (10.40), Claims 10.5–10.6, and Lemma 10.7. so Proposition 9.1 applies. For every $y\in\mathbb{B}_{2K\kappa^{-1/2}}^{+}(x^{\prime})$ and $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\alpha+1\}$ apply Corollary 8.3 on
