#### Corollary 10.12.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.3,

$$ A(2R/3;0)\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Increase $M$ in Proposition 10.1, while keeping its $K$ fixed, so that

$$ \frac{\sqrt{M}\log 2}{6K}>3. $$

This preserves Proposition 10.1. Suppose, to the contrary, that

$$ A(2R/3;0)>M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

By monotonicity,

$$ A(r;0)>M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\qquad\text{for every }r\in[2R/3,5R/6]. $$

Hence, for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ and every such $r$ ,

$$ \max\{A(r;0)^{-1/2},500|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\}\leq\frac{R}{\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|}. $$

Indeed,

$$ A(r;0)^{-1/2}\leq\frac{R}{\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|} $$

follows from $A(r;0)>M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ , while

$$ 500|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\leq\frac{R}{\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|} $$

holds after $\varepsilon$ is decreased.

Since $A(\,\cdot\,;0)$ is nondecreasing, Proposition 10.1 therefore implies

$$ A\!\left(r-\frac{KR}{\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|};0\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}A(r;0)\qquad\text{whenever }r\in[2R/3,5R/6] $$

provided that the radius on the left is at least $2R/3$ . Starting at $5R/6$ , this estimate can be iterated at least

$$ \left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|}{6K}\right\rfloor $$

times before reaching $2R/3$ . Since $A(5R/6;0)\leq 1$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle A(2R/3;0) \displaystyle\leq 2^{-\left\lfloor\sqrt{M}|\log\varepsilon|/(6K)\right\rfloor} \displaystyle\leq 2\varepsilon^{\sqrt{M}\log 2/(6K)}<M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2} $$

for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ . This contradicts $A(2R/3;0)>M\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ and proves (10.42). ∎

### 11. Final estimates and the boundary correction on nonzero levels

Throughout this section, $1\leq n\leq 9$ and $R=\varepsilon^{-1}$ . We use the geometric estimates of Section 4, the corrected approximate solution of Section 5, the estimates of Sections 7 and 8, and the separation estimate of Section 10. Constants depend only on the fixed data in Theorem 3.3; constants in statements concerning nonzero levels may also depend on $b^{\prime}$ .

There are two differences from the interior conclusion in [29, Proof of Theorem 1.1]. First, Proposition 10.1 gives a squared logarithm for a general boundary. Second, the correction $\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}$ constructed in Section 5 need not vanish at a nonzero value of the heteroclinic variable. The latter term enters the second derivatives of the graph of $\{u=t\}$ and therefore cannot be absorbed into the error.

#### 11.1. Separation and estimates on the zero level

#### Proposition 11.1 (Separation bounds).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.3,

$$ A(2R/3;0)\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Consequently, for every $y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{2R/3}^{+}(0)$ and every existing neighbouring sheet,

$$ D_{\alpha}(y)\geq 2|\log\varepsilon|-2\log|\log\varepsilon|-C. $$

#### Remark 11.2.

If $\partial_{0}B_{3R}^{+}(0)$ is totally geodesic, then

$$ A(2R/3;0)\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|. $$

#### Remark 11.3 (The boundary condition in the intrinsic separation equation).

The intrinsic improvement discussed in [29, Section 10.2 and Remarks 10.9–10.10] cannot be imported without a new boundary argument. To see the obstruction, let $\Sigma_{\alpha+1}$ be the upper neighbour of $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ and set

$$ \rho(y)=|t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)|=-t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)\qquad(y\in\Sigma_{\alpha}). $$

At a point of $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , the inward normal $\nu$ is tangent to $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ . Lemma 4.17, applied in the coordinates of $\Sigma_{\alpha+1}$ , gives the exact identity

$$ \begin{split}\partial_{\nu}\rho(y)&=-J_{\alpha+1}\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha+1}(y,0),t_{\alpha+1}(y,0)\bigr)\\
&=w_{\alpha+1}\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha+1}(y,0)\bigr)\rho(y)-\widetilde{J}_{\alpha+1}\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha+1}(y,0),-\rho(y)\bigr).\end{split} $$

The last term is bounded by

$$ C\varepsilon^{2}\rho(y)^{2}\bigl(1+\rho(y)^{3}\bigr), $$

whereas the first term is generally of order $\varepsilon\rho(y)$ . At the scale $\kappa\simeq\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|$ , the rescaling $y-y_{0}=\kappa^{-1/2}\widetilde{y}$ changes this boundary term into one of size $\varepsilon\kappa^{-1/2}\rho\simeq|\log\varepsilon|^{1/2}$ . It is therefore not a vanishing Neumann error. Nonnegative ambient Ricci curvature does not imply $w_{\alpha}=0$ .

#### Proof.

Equation (11.1) is Corollary 10.12. Since $e^{-D_{\alpha}(y)}\leq A(2R/3;0)$ , taking logarithms gives (11.2). If $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ has no neighbouring sheet, then $D_{\alpha}=+\infty$ and there is nothing to prove.

∎

#### Proposition 11.4 (Zero-level estimates).

On $B_{5R/8}^{+}(0)$ one has

$$ \displaystyle\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))}+\max_{\alpha}\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))} \displaystyle\qquad+\max_{\alpha}\|H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

$$ \max_{\alpha}\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

For every fixed $D>0$ ,

$$ \max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\\
1\leq i\leq n\end{subarray}}\|\phi_{y_{i}}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B_{5R/8}^{+}(0)\cap\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}^{0}\cap\{|t_{\alpha}|\leq D\})}\leq C(D)\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\alpha}\bigl\| \displaystyle H_{\alpha,0}+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}-\frac{2}{\sigma_{0}}\bigl(A_{(-1)^{\alpha-1}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha-1}(\cdot,0)|}-A_{(-1)^{\alpha}}^{2}e^{-|t_{\alpha+1}(\cdot,0)|}\bigr)\bigr\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))} \displaystyle\quad\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

In particular,

$$ \max_{\alpha}\|H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0))}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Let $H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ and $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ be the mean curvature and second fundamental form of the corresponding zero sheet in the original metric $\hat{g}$ . On $B_{1/2}^{+}(0)$ ,

$$ \|H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad[H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}]_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

and

$$ \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C. $$

If $n=1$ , then

$$ \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad[\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}]_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\varepsilon^{1-\theta}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

#### Remark 11.5.

If the boundary is totally geodesic, the factors $|\log\varepsilon|^{2}$ in (11.5), (11.10), and (11.11) may be replaced by $|\log\varepsilon|$ ; estimates (11.6) and (11.7) remain unchanged.

#### Proof.

Fix $x\in B_{5R/8}^{+}(0)$ . For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ ,

$$ B_{2+200|\log\varepsilon|^{2}}^{+}(x)\subset B_{2R/3}^{+}(0). $$

Apply Proposition 7.1, Corollary 8.2, and Proposition 8.1 with centre $x$ and radius $2$ . Every interaction quantity on their right-hand sides is bounded by

$$ A(2+200|\log\varepsilon|^{2};x)\leq A(2R/3;0). $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{2}^{+}(x))}+\max_{\alpha}\|h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{2}^{+}(x))} \displaystyle\qquad+\max_{\alpha}\|H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)+\Delta_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{2}^{+}(x))}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Moreover,

$$ (\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2})^{3/2}=\varepsilon^{3}|\log\varepsilon|^{3}\leq C\varepsilon^{2},\qquad\varepsilon^{1/6}(\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2})=\varepsilon^{13/6}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Since $D$ is fixed, $D<K|\log\varepsilon|$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ . Proposition 8.1 and Corollary 8.2 then give

$$ \max_{\alpha}\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}h_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{2}^{+}(x))}+\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\\
1\leq i\leq n\end{subarray}}\|\phi_{y_{i}}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B_{2}^{+}(x)\cap\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}^{0}\cap\{|t_{\alpha}|\leq D\})}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

This proves (11.6) and (11.7).

Assume now that $n=1$ . At every point of the original zero sheet, choose a unit tangent vector $\tau$ . Since the tangent space is one-dimensional,

$$ H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}=\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\tau,\tau),\qquad|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}|_{\hat{g}}=|H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}|. $$

In a graph coordinate, the covariant tensor $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ is $H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ times the induced tangent metric. The $C^{1,1}$ graph bound in (H2) and the fixed $C^{4}$ bound for $\hat{g}$ give a uniform $C^{\theta}$ bound for that induced metric. Hence

$$ [\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}]_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\left([H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}]_{C^{\theta}}+\|H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}}\right). $$

Corollary 8.3, together with (11.6) and the preceding two numerical estimates, gives (11.8). More precisely, for every $y_{0}\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{5R/8}^{+}(0)$ and every existing neighbour $\Sigma_{\alpha\pm 1}$ ,

$$ \|e^{-|t_{\alpha\pm 1}(\cdot,0)|}\|_{C^{\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0}))}\leq CA(2R/3;0). $$

Indeed, $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\subset\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{2R/3}^{+}(0)$ for small $\varepsilon$ , and the coordinate tangent derivatives of $t_{\alpha\pm 1}(\cdot,0)$ are uniformly bounded on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ . The mean value theorem controls pairs of points in $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ at base-coordinate distance less than one; pairs at distance at least one are controlled by the supremum $A(2R/3;0)$ . Equations (11.6), (11.8), and (11.1) prove (11.10).

Under the dilation $x\mapsto\varepsilon x$ ,

$$ H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\varepsilon y)=\varepsilon^{-1}H_{\alpha}(y,0),\qquad[H_{\alpha,\varepsilon}]_{C^{\theta}}=\varepsilon^{-1-\theta}[H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)]_{C^{\theta}}, $$

up to fixed equivalence constants for the graphical coordinates. This proves (11.11).

It remains to prove (11.12). In the graph coordinates from (H2), the mean-curvature equation for the original zero sheet is a uniformly elliptic quasilinear equation whose principal coefficient is the inverse graph metric divided by the graph area factor; see the computation in the proof of Lemma 4.22. The fixed slope and $C^{1,1}$ bounds in (H2) give uniform ellipticity and uniform $C^{\theta}$ bounds for the coefficients. The boundary condition is $\partial_{x_{1}}\hat{f}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}=0$ . Since (11.11) gives a uniform $C^{\theta}$ bound for the right-hand side, the local interior and Neumann Schauder estimates of Appendix E, applied on coordinate neighbourhoods contained in $B_{5/8}^{+}(0)$ , give a uniform $C^{2,\theta}$ bound for the graph on $B_{1/2}^{+}(0)$ . This is equivalent to (11.12). This last step is the boundary version of the closing elliptic argument in [29, Proof of Theorem 1.1, equations (11.1)–(11.2)].

If the boundary is totally geodesic, use (11.3) in the same argument. The two error terms from Section 8 are still $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ . ∎

Notice that this concludes the proof of Theorem 3.3.

#### 11.2. Nonzero levels

For the remainder of the section, fix $t\in[-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime}]$ and set

$$ s(t)=\mathbb{H}^{-1}(t). $$

We orient every level graph by the normal having positive $z$ -component. This orientation agrees with the one used for $H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)$ at $t=0$ ; the normal $\nabla u/|\nabla u|$ differs from it by the constant sign $(-1)^{\alpha}$ near $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ .

$$ Y_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}\bigl(B_{2}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D]\bigr)\subset\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}^{0}. $$

For every $(y,z)\in B_{2}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D]$ , the cutoff used in the definition of $\mathbb{H}_{\alpha}(y,z;h_{\alpha})$ equals one. Lemma 4.30, Corollary 5.10, and the distance and projection estimates of Section 4 give

$$ \displaystyle\Bigl\|\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}\Bigl(\mathbb{H}_{\beta}+(-1)^{\beta}\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)\Bigr)\Bigr\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])}\leq C(b^{\prime})A(2R/3;0), \displaystyle\Bigl\|\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}\mathbb{G}_{\beta}\Bigr\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon A(2R/3;0)^{3/4}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}. $$

The first estimate follows by differentiating the exponentially decaying tails on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D]$ and summing with Lemma 4.30. The second follows from (5.12) with any fixed exponential weight larger than $3/4$ . On $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D]$ , the distance and projection estimates control the maps $t_{\beta}$ and $\Pi_{\beta}$ that occur in every summand $\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,z)$ and $\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(y,z)$ , together with their derivatives and $C^{\theta}$ seminorms.

Equations (11.5), (5.12), and (11.17) yield

$$ \left\|u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}\bigl((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))\bigr)\right\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon. $$

Moreover,

$$ \min_{|\tau|\leq 1-b^{\prime}}\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}^{-1}(\tau))>0. $$

The intermediate value theorem and the implicit function theorem therefore give a unique root $z=\ell(y,t)$ for every $y\in B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ . Uniqueness makes the locally defined roots agree on overlaps as $y_{0}$ varies, producing the graph (11.14) over $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ . For every $y\in B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ , evaluation at $(y,\ell(y,t))$ gives

$$ \ell_{i}=-\frac{u_{i}}{u_{z}},\qquad\ell_{ij}=-\frac{u_{ij}+u_{iz}\ell_{j}+u_{jz}\ell_{i}+u_{zz}\ell_{i}\ell_{j}}{u_{z}}. $$

The estimate

$$ \left\|u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}\bigl((-1)^{\alpha}(z-h_{\alpha}(y))\bigr)\right\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon, $$

together with the product and composition estimates in (11.18), gives (11.15) on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ . Taking the supremum over $y_{0}\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ gives the $C^{0}$ bounds on $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ . If $p,q\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ have base-coordinate distance less than one, apply the estimate on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(p)$ ; if their base-coordinate distance is at least one, bound the Hölder quotient by twice the $C^{0}$ norm on $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ . This gives the full $C^{2,\theta}$ norm in (11.15).

At the root (11.14), the exact identity $u=\mathbb{H}_{*}+\mathbb{G}_{*}+\phi$ becomes

$$ \displaystyle 0={} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}\bigl(s(t)+(-1)^{\alpha}\eta\bigr)-\mathbb{H}(s(t))+\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}\bigl(y,s(t)+(-1)^{\alpha}\eta\bigr)+\phi(y,\ell) \displaystyle+\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}\left(\mathbb{H}_{\beta}(y,\ell)+(-1)^{\beta}\operatorname{sgn}(\beta-\alpha)+\mathbb{G}_{\beta}(y,\ell)\right). $$

Taylor’s theorem and the higher-order version of (5.12) give, with $s=s(t)$ ,

$$ \left\|\mathbb{H}\bigl(s+(-1)^{\alpha}\eta\bigr)-\mathbb{H}(s)-(-1)^{\alpha}\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)\eta\right\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0}))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\|\eta\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0}))}^{2}, $$

$$ \left\|\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}\bigl(\cdot,s+(-1)^{\alpha}\eta\bigr)-\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(\cdot,s)\right\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0}))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon\|\eta\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0}))}. $$

Substituting (11.15), (11.5), and (11.17) into (11.19), and dividing by $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s(t))$ , gives (11.16) on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})$ . Taking the supremum over $y_{0}\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ gives the $C^{0}$ part on $\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ . If $p,q\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ have base-coordinate distance less than one, apply the estimate on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(p)$ ; if their base-coordinate distance is at least one, bound the Hölder quotient by twice that $C^{0}$ norm. This proves (11.16).

For $t=0$ , $s(0)=0$ , $\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(y,0)=0$ , and the zero sheet is $z=0$ ; hence $\eta=-h_{\alpha}$ . Finally, let $p\in B_{R/2}^{+}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ . The rescaled form of (H1) is $|\nabla u|\geq c_{0}$ on $\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ . The integral curve of $-\operatorname{sign}(u(p))\nabla u/|\nabla u|$ starting at $p$ reaches a zero of $u$ after length at most $(1-b^{\prime})/c_{0}$ . Let $q$ be the zero of $u$ reached by this integral curve and let $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ be the zero sheet containing $q$ . For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ , one has

$$ q\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0),\qquad\Pi_{\alpha}(p)\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0). $$

The uniqueness in (11.14), applied with $t=u(p)$ and base point $\Pi_{\alpha}(p)$ , therefore gives $p\in\Sigma_{\alpha}(u(p))$ . ∎

#### Proposition 11.7 (Mean curvature of a nonzero level).

Let $H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}$ be the mean curvature of the graph (11.14), with the orientation fixed above. Uniformly for $t\in[-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime}]$ ,

$$ \left\|H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}-H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)+\frac{(-1)^{\alpha}}{\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s(t))}\Delta_{\alpha,0}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(\cdot,s(t))\right\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \|H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon. $$

#### Remark 11.8.

Recall if $|\nabla u(x)|\neq 0$ , then

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u)|^{2}=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\{u=u(x)\}}|^{2}+|\nabla^{T}\log|\nabla u||^{2}. $$

If in addition $x\in\partial_{0}B^{+}_{3R}(0)$ ,

$$ \partial_{\nu}\log|\nabla u|=\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3R}^{+}(0)}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|},\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|}\right). $$

In particular, on $\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha}$ , we have $\partial_{\nu}\log|\nabla u|=-w_{\alpha}$ , and

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u)|^{2}\geq|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|^{2}+|w_{\alpha}|^{2}. $$

If $n=1$ , then at every regular boundary point, in the original metric,

$$ |\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|_{\hat{g}}^{2}=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\{u_{\varepsilon}=u_{\varepsilon}(x)\}}|_{\hat{g}}^{2}+|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}|_{\hat{g}}^{2}. $$

Thus, in ambient dimension two, a decay estimate for $|\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|$ at boundary points in the transition layer requires the curvature of the boundary to vanish at the same rate.

#### Remark 11.9.

If $\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)$ is totally geodesic, then $\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}=0$ for every sheet $\Sigma_{\alpha}$ meeting $B_{2R/3}^{+}(0)$ . Then uniformly for $t\in[-1+b^{\prime},1-b^{\prime}]$ ,

$$ \|H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}-H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}, $$

$$ \|H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}\|_{C^{\theta}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|. $$

and its second fundamental form satisfies

$$ \|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{R/2}^{+}(0))}+\varepsilon^{-\theta}[\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}]_{C^{\theta}(B_{R/2}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon. $$

If, in addition, $n=1$ , then each level set is a curve, so its second fundamental form has one component and its norm equals the absolute value of its mean curvature. Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{p\in B_{R/2}^{+}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}}|\mathcal{A}(u)(p)| \displaystyle\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|. $$

Unlike the dimension-one conclusion in Proposition 11.4, this estimate still requires total geodesicity of the boundary, as noticed in Remark 11.8.

#### Proof of Proposition 11.7.

The graph in Lemma 11.6 is a regular level contained in $\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ . Hence (H3), together with the uniformly controlled twisted-coordinate map, gives $|\nabla_{\alpha,0}\ell|\leq C\eta_{0}$ and $|\nabla_{\alpha,0}^{2}\ell|\leq C\Lambda_{0}\varepsilon$ . The smallness of $\eta_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ is chosen so that Lemma 4.22 applies to $\ell(\cdot,t)$ . Since the operator in that lemma annihilates constants,

$$ \displaystyle H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}(t)}-H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)={} \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\ell]}(h_{\alpha}+\eta)+\bigl(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}})\bigr)\ell+\mathcal{Q}(y,\ell,d\ell). $$

On the bounded strip containing the graph, the coefficient estimates of Proposition 4.19, together with (11.15), imply

$$ \|\mathcal{L}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\ell]}(h_{\alpha}+\eta)-\Delta_{\alpha,0}(h_{\alpha}+\eta)\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon\|\nabla_{\alpha,0}(h_{\alpha}+\eta)\|_{C^{1,\theta}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}. $$

The curvature coefficient in (11.30) is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ in $C^{\theta}$ by Proposition 4.1 and the rescaled metric bounds. The estimate for $\mathcal{Q}$ in Lemma 4.22, its differentiated form supplied by Proposition 4.19 and Appendix B, and (11.15) likewise give

$$ \left\|\bigl(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}})\bigr)\ell+\mathcal{Q}(y,\ell,d\ell)\right\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Finally, (11.16) and (11.6) give

$$ \left\|\Delta_{\alpha,0}(h_{\alpha}+\eta)+\frac{(-1)^{\alpha}}{\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s(t))}\Delta_{\alpha,0}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(\cdot,s(t))\right\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Combining (11.30)–(11.33) proves (11.20). Equation (5.12) gives $\|\Delta_{\alpha,0}\overline{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}(\cdot,s(t))\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\varepsilon$ ; together with (11.10), this proves (11.21). ∎

We conclude by making the dependence of the curvature estimates on the second fundamental form of the boundary explicit. The following remark compares the enhanced second fundamental form throughout the transition region with the second fundamental forms of the zero sheets.

#### Remark 11.10 (Dependence on the boundary geometry).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.3, fix $b<b^{\prime}<1$ . Applying (F.4) to (5.10), with $\mathsf{f}=0$ and $\psi(y,\tau)=-w_{\alpha}(y)\tau\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(\tau)$ and using the identity for $w_{\alpha}$ in Lemma 4.17 gives, for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ and uniformly for $|t|\leq 1-b^{\prime}$ ,

$$ \|H_{\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\hat{g}}(\{u_{\varepsilon}=t\}\cap B_{1/2}^{+}(0))}\leq C(b^{\prime})\left(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}\|_{C^{2}_{\hat{g}}(\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0))}\right), $$

and

$$ \sup_{B_{1/2}^{+}(0)\cap\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}}|\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|_{\hat{g}}\leq C\max_{\alpha}\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\hat{g}}(\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3/5}^{+}(0))}+C(b^{\prime})\left(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}\|_{C^{2}_{\hat{g}}(\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0))}\right), $$

where the metric $\hat{g}$ is as in Theorem 3.3.

If $n=1$ , Proposition 11.4 and (11.35) give

$$ \sup_{B_{1/2}^{+}(0)\cap\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}}|\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|_{\hat{g}}\leq C(b^{\prime})\left(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}\|_{C^{2}_{\hat{g}}(\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0))}\right). $$

The boundary second fundamental form term cannot in general be omitted because of (11.25). Thus, as we pointed out in Remark 1.2, unlike the interior decay estimates in [28, Theorem 3.6] and [6, Proposition C.4], no uniform $o(1)$ estimate for $|\mathcal{A}(u_{\varepsilon})|$ is possible where $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}|_{\hat{g}}$ stays bounded away from zero. This applies even on $\{u_{\varepsilon}=0\}$ , although the ordinary curvature of its components tends to zero by Proposition 11.4.

Indeed, if we choose $D$ as in the proof of Lemma 11.6 and $y_{0}\in\Sigma_{\alpha}\cap B_{3R/5}^{+}(0)$ , and note that $-w_{\alpha}(y)\tau\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(\tau)$ is odd in $\tau$ , then the product estimate and (F.4), with $\mathsf{f}=0$ , give

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{\mathbb{G}}_{\alpha}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])} \displaystyle\leq C_{D}\|w_{\alpha}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(\partial_{0}\Sigma_{\alpha})} \displaystyle\leq C_{D}\varepsilon\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}\|_{C^{2}_{\hat{g}}(\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0))}, $$

where the second inequality follows by differentiating the identity for $w_{\alpha}$ in Lemma 4.17 and using Proposition 4.1 and (4.5). The cutoff equals one for $|z|\leq D$ , hence, (11.20) and (11.10), followed by rescaling, give (11.34).

For (11.35), use $u=\mathbb{H}_{*}+\mathbb{G}_{*}+\phi$ , (11.5), (11.17), and the estimate

$$ \displaystyle\|u(y,z)-\mathbb{H}((-1)^{\alpha}z)\|_{C^{2}(B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D])}\leq C_{D}\left(\varepsilon^{2}|\log\varepsilon|^{2}+\varepsilon\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0)}\|_{C^{2}_{\hat{g}}(\partial_{0}B_{3}^{+}(0))}\right). $$

Since $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ is bounded below on $[-D,D]$ , this controls the difference between $\nabla(\nabla u/|\nabla u|)$ and $(-1)^{\alpha}\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}$ . By (B.4) and Lemmas 4.11 and 4.15, $|\nabla_{Z}\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}|\leq C_{D}\varepsilon^{2}$ on $B_{1}^{\alpha}(y_{0})\times[-D,D]$ . Comparing with the value at $z=0$ and rescaling proves (11.35).

## Part III Appendices

### Appendix A Proof of derivative estimates for enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}$ in Proposition 4.1

In this appendix we prove derivative estimates for the enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}$ in Proposition 4.1.

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

We prove the estimates on $B^{+}_{3R-1}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ , using (H1) and (H3) of Theorem 3.3 on the larger set $\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ , as in [28, proof of Lemma 8.1].

Fix $x_{0}\in B^{+}_{3R-1}(0)\cap\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ . By the uniform local gradient upper bound and $b^{\prime}>b$ , there is a small ball (if $x_{0}$ is an interior point) or half-ball (if $x_{0}$ is a boundary point) centred at $x_{0}$ , denoted by $B$ , which lies in $\{|u|<1-b\}$ . The radius of $B$ is uniform in $x_{0}\in\{|u|\leq 1-b^{\prime}\}$ and $\varepsilon$ . On $B$ , by (H1), (H3), and the metric rescaling, we have $|\nabla u|\geq c_{0}>0$ .

Let $(x_{1},\dots,x_{n+1})$ be the Fermi coordinates of Section 3.1, and recall that $u$ satisfies $|u|\leq 1$ and the equation $\Delta_{g}u=W^{\prime}(u)$ , with boundary condition $\partial_{1}u=0$ on $\{x_{1}=0\}$ , so that by interior/Neumann elliptic regularity (see Appendix E),

$$ \|u\|_{C^{m+2,\theta}}\leq C_{m}\bigl(\|u\|_{C^{0}}+\|W^{\prime}(u)\|_{C^{m,\theta}}\bigr)\leq C_{m} $$

for $m\geq 0$ on a ball/half-ball $B^{\prime}\Subset B$ centred at $x_{0}$ of, say, half the radius.

Set $w=|\nabla u|^{2}$ , $N=w^{-1/2}\nabla u$ , so that $\mathcal{A}=\nabla N$ , and let $N_{q}=g(N,\partial_{x_{q}})=w^{-1/2}u_{q}$ . Since $w\geq c_{0}^{2}$ on $B^{\prime}$ , then, by the product rule and the chain rule, by (A.1), we obtain

$$ \|w^{-1}\|_{C^{m,\theta}}+\|N\|_{C^{m,\theta}}\leq C_{m}\quad\text{on }B^{\prime}. $$

Notice that this implies $\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C$ on $B^{\prime}$ .

Since $\partial_{i}N_{q}=\mathcal{A}_{iq}+\Gamma^{k}_{iq}N_{k}$ and $|\Gamma|\leq C\varepsilon$ , together with the assumption $|\mathcal{A}|\leq C\varepsilon$ , we conclude that

$$ |DN|\leq C\varepsilon\quad\text{ on $B^{\prime}$.} $$

As in [28, Lemma 8.1], Bochner’s formula gives

$$ \operatorname{div}(w\nabla N)=-w|\mathcal{A}|^{2}N-w\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(N,N)N+w\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(N,\cdot)^{\#}. $$

Let us differentiate the Allen–Cahn equation satisfied by $u$ , and use (A.4) to obtain the following scalar equation for $N_{q}=w^{-1/2}u_{q}$

$$ \Delta_{g}N_{q}+\langle\nabla\log w,\nabla N_{q}\rangle=F_{q}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle F_{q}={} \displaystyle-|\mathcal{A}|^{2}N_{q}-\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(N,N)N_{q}+R_{q}{}^{k}N_{k}+2g^{ij}\Gamma^{k}_{iq}\partial_{j}N_{k} \displaystyle+g^{ij}\bigl(\partial_{i}\Gamma^{k}_{jq}-\Gamma^{\ell}_{ij}\Gamma^{k}_{\ell q}-\Gamma^{\ell}_{iq}\Gamma^{k}_{j\ell}+(\partial_{i}\log w)\Gamma^{k}_{jq}\bigr)N_{k}. $$

Here, repeated coordinate indices are summed and $q$ is fixed.

By the bounds on curvature and the Christoffel coefficients in Theorem 3.3, (A.2), and (A.3),

$$ \||\mathcal{A}|^{2}N_{q}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{0}}\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\varepsilon. $$

Thus $\|F\|_{C^{\theta}}\leq C\bigl(\varepsilon+\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{0}}\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{\theta}}\bigr)\leq C\varepsilon$ .

Now, on $B^{\prime}$ , the oscillation of $N_{q}$ is $O(\varepsilon)$ because $|DN|\leq C\varepsilon$ . If $x_{0}$ is on the boundary $\partial_{0}B^{+}_{3R-1}$ , then $u_{1}=u_{1q}=0$ for $q\geq 2$ , so we have

$$ w_{1}=(\partial_{1}g^{ij})u_{i}u_{j},\quad N_{1}=0,\quad\partial_{1}N_{q}=-\frac{(\partial_{1}g^{ij})u_{i}u_{j}}{2w}N_{q}\quad(q\geq 2). $$

In either case, if we let $v_{q}=N_{q}-N_{q}(x_{0})$ , then by the interior/Neumann elliptic estimates (see Appendix E) for $q\geq 2$ , and the interior/Dirichlet elliptic estimates for $v_{1}$ , then

$$ \|v_{q}\|_{C^{2,\theta}(B^{\prime\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon $$

on a ball $B^{\prime\prime}\Subset B^{\prime}\Subset B$ of, say, half the radius of $B^{\prime}$ . This gives $\|\mathcal{A}\|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{\prime\prime})}\leq C\varepsilon$ . The result then comes from differentiating (A.5) and iterating this argument. ∎

### Appendix B Proof of geometric approximation estimates and mean curvature expansion in Proposition 4.19

We collect in this appendix the various geometric approximation estimates in Proposition 4.19 that we obtain in twisted Fermi coordinates and the mean curvature expansion under twisted Fermi coordinates in Lemma 4.22.

Throughout, $|z|\leq K|\log\varepsilon|$ . Tensors on $\Sigma_{\alpha,z}$ are pulled back by $y\mapsto Y_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}(y,z)$ and measured using $g_{\alpha,0}$ .

#### Proof of Proposition 4.19.

Notice that by definition $Z=\partial_{z}$ . Since $\{\partial_{y_{1}},\dots,\partial_{y_{n}},\partial_{z}\}$ are coordinate vector fields, then $0=[\partial_{z},\partial_{y_{i}}]=[Z,\partial_{y_{i}}]$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$ .

By definition $\{\partial_{y_{1}}|_{(y,z)},\dots,\partial_{y_{n}}|_{(y,z)}\}$ are tangent to $\Sigma_{\alpha,z}$ at $(y,z)$ . Therefore, $g_{\alpha,ij}(y,z)=g_{ij}(y,z)$ , and

$$ \partial_{z}g_{\alpha,ij}=Z(g(\partial_{y_{i}},\partial_{y_{j}}))=g(\nabla_{Z}\partial_{y_{i}},\partial_{y_{j}})+g(\partial_{y_{i}},\nabla_{Z}\partial_{y_{j}})=g(\nabla_{\partial_{y_{i}}}Z,\partial_{y_{j}})+g(\partial_{y_{i}},\nabla_{\partial_{y_{j}}}Z). $$

By (4.24) and (4.42), then $|\partial_{z}g_{\alpha,ij}(y,\tau)|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|\tau|)$ for $|\tau|<K|\log\varepsilon|$ . Therefore, after integrating between $0$ and $|z|$ , we obtain the first half of (4.56).

By the chain rule

$$ \partial_{z}g_{\alpha}^{ij}=-\sum_{l,k=1}^{n}g_{\alpha}^{li}g_{\alpha}^{jk}\partial_{z}g_{\alpha,lk}, $$

and by definition,

$$ \Gamma_{\alpha,ij}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{n}g_{\alpha}^{kl}(\partial_{y_{i}}g_{\alpha,lj}+\partial_{y_{j}}g_{\alpha,il}-\partial_{y_{l}}g_{\alpha,ij}). $$

The coordinate-field bounds in Section 4.2.1 give

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{z}g_{\alpha,ij}|+|\partial_{z}\partial_{y_{\ell}}g_{\alpha,ij}|+|\partial_{z}\Gamma^{k}_{\alpha,ij}| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon(1+|z|), \displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{2}\bigl(|\partial_{y}^{m}g_{\alpha,ij}|+|\partial_{y}^{m}g_{\alpha}^{ij}|\bigr)+|\partial_{y_{\ell}}\Gamma^{k}_{\alpha,ij}| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon(1+|z|^{2}), $$

which completes the proof of (4.56), and proves (4.57), (4.58), (4.59).

For the estimates involving the second fundamental form, recall that, by the Riccati equation in [5, Appendix A], we have

$$ \nabla_{\widetilde{Z}}\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}=-(\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha})^{2}-g(R(\cdot,\widetilde{Z})\widetilde{Z},\cdot),\qquad\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}(\widetilde{Z},\cdot)=0. $$

The initial bounds and $|\operatorname{Rm}_{g}|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}$ give $|\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon$ , and $|\nabla_{\widetilde{Z}}\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}$ . Then, tangential differentiation gives

$$ \big|(\nabla^{4}t_{\alpha})(\widetilde{Z},\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)\big|\leq C|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|\,|\nabla_{\alpha,z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|+C|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}_{g}|+C|\operatorname{Rm}_{g}|\,|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|, $$

with the remaining slots tangent and normally parallel transported. Since

$$ \nabla_{\alpha,z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}=-(\nabla^{3}t_{\alpha})|_{T\Sigma_{\alpha,z}^{\otimes 3}}, $$

an ODE argument using Gronwall’s inequality for vector valued functions, together with Appendix A, yields

$$ |\nabla_{\alpha,z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad\big|(\nabla^{4}t_{\alpha})(\widetilde{Z},\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)\big|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Now recall that by definition

$$ \partial_{z}=\widetilde{Z}+T,\qquad\nabla_{Z}\partial_{y_{i}}=\nabla_{\partial_{y_{i}}}Z,\qquad\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,ij}=-(\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha})(\partial_{y_{i}},\partial_{y_{j}}), $$

so that by Lemmas 4.11 and 4.15, we finally obtain the following estimates:

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,ij}|+|\partial_{z}(\nabla_{\alpha,z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z})_{kij}| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{2}+C|T|\bigl(|\nabla^{3}t_{\alpha}|+|\nabla^{4}t_{\alpha}|\bigr)+C|\nabla Z|\bigl(|\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}|+|\nabla^{3}t_{\alpha}|\bigr) \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{3}), $$

and

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{z}H_{\alpha}| \displaystyle=\big|(\partial_{z}g_{\alpha}^{ij})\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,ij}+g_{\alpha}^{ij}\partial_{z}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,ij}\big|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}(1+|z|^{3}). $$

Integration between 0 and $|z|$ completes the proof of (4.60),(4.61), and (4.62).

Finally, for the volume form

$$ \partial_{z}\lambda_{\alpha}=\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}^{ij}\partial_{z}g_{\alpha,ij}=\lambda_{\alpha}(-H_{\alpha}+\operatorname{div}_{\alpha,z}T), $$

so that $|\partial_{z}\lambda_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon(1+|z|)$ by (4.47) and (4.61). ∎

We shall now give an expansion for the mean curvature of the graph of a function $\varphi\in C^{2}(\Sigma_{\alpha},)$ . This is analogous to [5, Lemma 2.9].

#### Proof of Lemma 4.22.

By Proposition 4.19 and (B.4), $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|+|H_{\alpha}|+|\nabla^{2}t_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon$ and

$$ \widetilde{Z}H_{\alpha}=|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,z}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(\widetilde{Z},\widetilde{Z}),\qquad|\widetilde{Z}^{2}H_{\alpha}|\leq C\varepsilon^{3}. $$

By the definition of $Z_{2}$ and $Z$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla Z_{2}|\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad\langle\widetilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle(y,0)=0,\qquad|\partial_{z}\langle\widetilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle|\leq C\varepsilon, \displaystyle|\langle\widetilde{Z},Z_{2}\rangle(y,z)|\leq C\varepsilon|z|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|T(y,z)|\leq C\varepsilon|z|. $$

For $\widetilde{y}=\widetilde{\Pi}_{\alpha}(Y_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}(y,z))$ , Lemma 4.4 yields

$$ \frac{d\widetilde{y}}{dz}=D\widetilde{\Pi}_{\alpha}(T)(Y_{\Sigma_{\alpha}}(y,z)),\qquad|\widetilde{y}-y|\leq C\varepsilon z^{2}. $$

Taylor expansion along the normal geodesic from $\widetilde{y}$ gives

$$ H_{\alpha}(y,z)=H_{\alpha}(\widetilde{y},0)+z(\widetilde{Z}H_{\alpha})(\widetilde{y},0)+O(\varepsilon^{3}z^{2}). $$

By Appendix A and the rescaled metric bounds,

$$ |\nabla_{\alpha,0}^{2}H_{\alpha}(\cdot,0)|\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad|\nabla_{\alpha,0}(\widetilde{Z}H_{\alpha})(\cdot,0)|\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle|H_{\alpha}(\widetilde{y},0)-H_{\alpha}(y,0)| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon z^{2}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}H_{\alpha}(y,0)|+C\varepsilon^{3}z^{4}, \displaystyle|z|\,|(\widetilde{Z}H_{\alpha})(\widetilde{y},0)-(\widetilde{Z}H_{\alpha})(y,0)| \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{3}|z|^{3}, $$

and therefore

$$ \begin{split}&\Big|H_{\alpha}(y,z)-H_{\alpha}(y,0)-\bigl(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,0}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{g}(\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}},\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}})\bigr)(y)z\Big|\\
&\qquad\leq C\varepsilon z^{2}|\nabla_{\alpha,0}H_{\alpha}(y,0)|+C\varepsilon^{3}z^{2}(1+z^{2}).\end{split} $$

Write $\varphi_{i}=\partial_{y_{i}}\varphi$ and evaluate coefficients at $(y,\varphi(y))$ . The defining function $t_{\alpha}-\varphi\circ\Pi_{\alpha}$ gives

$$ \varpi^{2}=(1+T^{i}\varphi_{i})^{2}+|d\varphi|_{g_{\alpha,\varphi}}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}=\frac{(1+T^{i}\varphi_{i})\widetilde{Z}-\nabla_{\alpha,\varphi}\varphi}{\varpi}, $$

where $\nabla_{\alpha,z}\varphi=\nabla_{\alpha,z}(\varphi\circ\Pi_{\alpha})$ and repeated indices are summed. Since

$$ |T|\,|d\varphi|=o(1),\qquad\langle\mathbf{n}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]},\widetilde{Z}\rangle=\frac{1+T^{i}\varphi_{i}}{\varpi}\geq C^{-1}, $$

the graph metric is uniformly equivalent to $g_{\alpha,0}$ . The stated properties of $\mathcal{L}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}$ follow from its definition. Since $t_{\alpha}=\varphi\circ\Pi_{\alpha}$ on the graph, the restriction formula for the Laplacian gives

$$ H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}-\mathcal{L}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}\varphi=\frac{\varpi}{1+T^{i}\varphi_{i}}H_{\alpha}(y,\varphi)-\frac{\mathrm{I\!I}_{\alpha,\varphi}(\nabla_{\alpha,\varphi}\varphi,\nabla_{\alpha,\varphi}\varphi)}{(1+T^{i}\varphi_{i})\varpi}. $$

Since

$$ \frac{\varpi}{1+T^{i}\varphi_{i}}-1=\frac{|d\varphi|_{g_{\alpha,\varphi}}^{2}}{(1+T^{i}\varphi_{i})(\varpi+1+T^{i}\varphi_{i})}, $$

we obtain

$$ \big|H_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}-\mathcal{L}_{\Sigma_{\alpha}[\varphi]}\varphi-H_{\alpha}(y,\varphi)\big|\leq C\varepsilon|d\varphi|_{g_{\alpha,0}}^{2}. $$

Together with (B.7), this proves the expansion. ∎

### Appendix C The one-dimensional heteroclinic solution $\mathbb{H}$

We summarize in this appendix the results on the one-dimensional heteroclinic solution needed in this work.

Let $W$ be the even double-well potential fixed in Section 2. There is a unique increasing solution $\mathbb{H}:\mathbb{R}\to(-1,1)$ of

$$ \mathbb{H}^{\prime\prime}=W^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}),\qquad\mathbb{H}(0)=0,\qquad\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}\mathbb{H}(t)=\pm 1. $$

This is called the heteroclinic solution. Since $W$ is even and the normalization fixes the translation, $\mathbb{H}$ is odd and $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ is positive and even. Multiplying the equation by $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ and using the limits at infinity gives

$$ \mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)=\sqrt{2W(\mathbb{H}(t))},\quad\text{for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$}. $$

It is not difficult to check that, as $t\rightarrow\pm\infty$ , the function $\mathbb{H}(t)$ converges exponentially to $\pm 1$ . More precisely, as $t\rightarrow+\infty$ , we have the following asymptotic expansions: there exists a constant $A_{1}$ , depending on $W$ , such that for all $t>0$ large enough, there holds

$$ \displaystyle\quad\,\,\mathbb{H}(t) \displaystyle=1-A_{1}e^{-t}+O(e^{-2t}),\qquad\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)=A_{1}e^{-t}+O(e^{-2t}),\qquad\mathbb{H}^{\prime\prime}(t)=-A_{1}e^{-t}+O(e^{-2t}). $$

Likewise, as $t\to-\infty$ , the analogous expansion holds with a positive constant $A_{-1}$ . Since $W$ is even and $\mathbb{H}$ is odd, in the present paper $A_{-1}=A_{1}$ .

The correctly rescaled heteroclinic is $\mathbb{H}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\mathbb{H}(t/\varepsilon)$ ; it satisfies $\varepsilon^{2}\mathbb{H}_{\varepsilon}^{\prime\prime}=W^{\prime}(\mathbb{H}_{\varepsilon})$ . Finally,

$$ \sigma_{0}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t))^{2}+W(\mathbb{H}(t))\right)dt=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t))^{2}dt\in(0,+\infty). $$

#### Lemma C.1.

For all $T>0$ large, we have the following expansions.

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t))-1\right)\left(\mathbb{H}(-t-T)+1\right)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)dt=-2A_{-1}^{2}e^{-T}+O(e^{-4T/3}), $$

and

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t))-1\right)\left(\mathbb{H}(T-t)-1\right)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)dt=2A_{1}^{2}e^{-T}+O(e^{-4T/3}), $$

as well as

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t)+\mathbb{H}(-t-T)+1)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(-t-T))\right)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(-t-T)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)dt=-2A_{-1}^{2}e^{-T}+O(e^{-7T/6}), $$

together with

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t)+\mathbb{H}(T-t)-1)-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(T-t))\right)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(T-t)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)dt=-2A_{1}^{2}e^{-T}+O(e^{-7T/6}). $$

#### Proof.

The proof of the first two estimates can be found in [28, Lemma A.1], while for the last two we refer the reader to [29, Lemma A.2]. ∎

We conclude by discussing the spectrum of the linearized operator at $\mathbb{H}$ , i.e.

$$ \mathcal{L}=-\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t)). $$

A direct computation shows that $\mathbb{H}^{\prime}$ is an eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$ corresponding to the 0 eigenvalue. One can prove that this is the lowest eigenvalue. On the other hand, we have the following result, which can be proven via a contradiction argument.

#### Theorem C.2.

There exists a constant $\mu>0$ such that for any $\varphi\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the orthogonality $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(t)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(t)\,dt=0$ , we have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left((\varphi^{\prime}(t))^{2}+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(t))\varphi^{2}(t)\right)dt\geq\mu\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left((\varphi^{\prime}(t))^{2}+\varphi^{2}(t)\right)dt. $$

### Appendix D Proofs of exponential interaction decay estimates in Lemmas 5.2 and Lemma 5.3

In this appendix we prove Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

On the interval of integration, Proposition 4.26 gives

$$ |t_{\beta}(y,z)-t_{\beta}(y,0)-z|\leq C\varepsilon^{1/3}. $$

The harmless error in (D.1) may be absorbed in the implicit constant. The elementary one-dimensional estimate

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|z|)^{k}e^{-\sigma|T+z|-\varsigma|z|}\,dz\leq C(1+|T|)^{k+1}e^{-\min\{\sigma,\varsigma\}|T|} $$

holds when $\sigma,\varsigma>0$ . Since $|t_{\beta}(y,z)|\leq|t_{\beta}(y,0)|+|z|+C\varepsilon^{1/3}$ , this estimate proves both (5.29) and (5.30). ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.3.

Assume first that $\beta>\alpha$ ; the other case follows by reflection. Then $t_{\beta}(y,0)<0$ . The truncated heteroclinic satisfies

$$ |\overline{\mathbb{H}}(s)+1|\leq C\min\{1,e^{s}\},\qquad|\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)|\leq Ce^{-|z|}. $$

Using (D.1) and splitting at $z=0$ and $z=|t_{\beta}(y,0)|$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\overline{\mathbb{H}}(t_{\beta}(y,z))+1|\,|\overline{\mathbb{H}}^{\prime}(z)|\,dz\leq C\int_{\mathbb{R}}\min\{1,e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|+z}\}e^{-|z|}\,dz\leq C(1+|t_{\beta}(y,0)|)e^{-|t_{\beta}(y,0)|}. $$

This proves (5.31). The estimate $(1+s)e^{-s}\leq C_{\sigma}e^{-\sigma s}$ for $s\geq 0$ gives (5.32). ∎

### Appendix E Some classical elliptic regularity estimates

In this section, we state the Schauder estimate for the linear elliptic equation

$$ L\mathsf{u}=a^{ij}D_{ij}\mathsf{u}+b^{i}D_{i}\mathsf{u}+c\mathsf{u}=\mathsf{f}+\operatorname{div}\mathsf{G},\quad\lambda\left|\xi\right|^{2}\leq a^{ij}\xi_{i}\xi_{j}\leq\Lambda|\xi|^{2}. $$

Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and assume the $C^{0,\alpha}$ norms of the coefficients $a^{ij},\;b^{i},\;c$ are bounded by $\Lambda$ .

#### Proposition E.1 (Schauder estimate).

Then the following estimates hold, with $C=C(n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda)$ .

(a) Interior estimate [15, Theorems 8.32, 6.2], [27, Theorem 1.2]. Suppose $\mathsf{u}$ satisfies (E.1) on $B_{2}=B_{2}(0)$ . Then on $B_{1}=B_{1}(0)$

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{1})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2})}\right), \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{1})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{2})}\right). $$

(b) Boundary estimate for the Dirichlet condition [15, Corollary 6.7], [27, Theorem 1.2]. Suppose $\mathsf{u}$ satisfies (E.1) on $B_{2}^{+}=B_{2}^{+}(0)$ and $\mathsf{u}=\phi$ on $\partial_{0}B_{2}^{+}(0)$ . Then on $B_{1}^{+}=B_{1}^{+}(0)$

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{1}^{+})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2})}+\|\phi\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{2}^{+})}\right), \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{1}^{+})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{2})}+\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{2}^{+})}\right). $$

(c) Boundary estimate for the Neumann condition [15, Lemma 6.29], [27, Theorem 1.2]. Suppose $u$ satisfies (E.1) on $B_{2}^{+}=B_{2}^{+}(0)$ and $\partial_{1}\mathsf{u}=\phi$ on $\partial_{0}B_{2}^{+}(0)$ . Then on $B_{1}^{+}=B_{1}^{+}(0)$

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{1}^{+})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2})}+\|\phi\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\partial_{0}B_{2}^{+})}\right), \displaystyle\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{1}^{+})}\leq C\left(\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{0}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{2}^{+})}+\|\mathsf{G}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{2})}+\|\phi\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\partial_{0}B_{2}^{+})}\right). $$

#### Remark E.2.

In the estimates stated in [15, Corollary 6.7] and [15, Lemma 6.29], there are $\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}$ on the left-hand side and $\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$ on the right-hand side. However, from the proofs of these two results, it follows that to estimate $\|\mathsf{u}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}}$ , it is enough to have $\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0}}$ on the right hand side (see also equation 4.46 and Theorem 8.33 in [15]); therefore we have the estimates (E.4) and (E.6).

The $C^{1,\theta}$ estimates with a scalar source merely in $C^{0}$ and a divergence source in $C^{\theta}$ follow from the corresponding first-order Campanato estimates, or from the boundary estimates in [27, Theorem 1.2]. Equivalently, one first takes an exponent $p>(n+1)/(1-\theta)$ in the local $W^{1,p}$ estimate for the divergence source and then applies Morrey’s inequality.

### Appendix F Liouville theorems and a priori estimates in gluing procedure

#### Lemma F.1.

Let $L\varphi=\Delta_{y}\varphi+\partial_{ss}\varphi-W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H})\varphi$ , where $(y,s)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, smooth solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi(y,s)=c\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, smooth solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ and $\varphi=0$ on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi(y,s)=c\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, smooth solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ and $\partial_{\nu}\varphi=0$ on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi(y,s)=c\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ .

We omit the proof of this lemma since it is similar to [7, Proof of Lemma 4.1].

#### Lemma F.2.

Given an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ , $a^{i}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)$ , $b:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\inf_{\Omega}b=b_{0}>0$ , define $L\varphi=\Delta\varphi+a^{i}\partial_{i}\varphi-b\varphi$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, $C^{2}$ solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi\equiv 0$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, $C^{2}$ solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ and $\varphi=0$ on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi\equiv 0$ .

- • If $\varphi$ is a bounded, $C^{2}$ solution of $L\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ and $\partial_{\nu}\varphi=0$ on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}$ , then $\varphi\equiv 0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi_{\pm}=\exp(\pm\lambda|x|)$ , where $\lambda$ is to be specified later. Let $\max_{i}\|a^{i}\|_{L^{\infty}}=a_{0}$ . Then, for $|x|\neq 0$ ,

$$ L\varphi_{\pm}\leq\big(\lambda^{2}\pm\frac{n\lambda}{|x|}+a_{0}\lambda-b_{0}\big)\varphi_{\pm}. $$

We choose $\lambda>0$ such that $\lambda^{2}+a_{0}\lambda\leq\frac{b_{0}}{4}$ and define $r=\frac{4n\lambda}{b_{0}}$ . Then for $|x|\geq r$ , $L\varphi_{\pm}<0$ . For $\epsilon>0$ , let

$$ \varphi_{\epsilon}=\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}e^{\lambda(r-|x|)}+\epsilon e^{\lambda|x|}. $$

By the maximum principle, $|\varphi(x)|\leq\varphi_{\epsilon}(x)$ on $\{|x|\geq r\}$ ; letting $\epsilon\to 0$ , we obtain $|\varphi(x)|\leq\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}e^{\lambda(r-|x|)}$ Again applying the maximum principle, we conclude that $\varphi\equiv 0.$ ∎

Let us introduce some notation, which will be used in Proposition F.3. Suppose $r>0$ , $\Sigma\subset\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{r}(0)\times\mathbb{R}$ is a hypersurface equipped with a Riemannian metric and $\Sigma$ is the graph of a smooth function defined on $\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{r}(0)$ . Then $\partial_{0}\Sigma$ (resp. $\partial_{+}\Sigma$ ) denotes the portion of $\Sigma$ lying over $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(0)$ (resp. $\partial_{+}\mathbb{B}^{+}_{r}(0)$ ), $\partial_{*}\Sigma=\overline{\partial_{0}\Sigma}\cap\overline{\partial_{+}\Sigma}$ , $\hat{\Sigma}=\Sigma\setminus\partial_{*}\Sigma$ . For $\Sigma^{\prime}\subset\Sigma$ , $\partial_{0}\Sigma^{\prime}:=\partial\Sigma^{\prime}\cap\partial_{0}\Sigma$ . For $\delta\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \Sigma_{(-\delta r)}=\Sigma\setminus\{p\in\Sigma:d(p,\partial_{0}\Sigma),\;d(p,\partial_{+}\Sigma)<\delta r\}. $$

For $\mathsf{f}\in L^{1}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})$ , $c_{\mathsf{f}}(y)=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathsf{f}(y,s)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)ds$ .

Suppose $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{l}$ (for some integer $l$ ) is the closure of an open set with smooth boundary, $m\geq 0$ , $\theta,\sigma\in(0,1)$ and $\mathsf{u}\in C^{m,\theta}(\Omega\times\mathbb{R})$ . Then

$$ \left\|\mathsf{u}\right\|_{C^{m,\theta}_{\sigma}(\Omega)}:=\sup\left\{e^{\sigma|s|}\sum_{i=0}^{m}(|\mathsf{u}|_{i}+|\mathsf{u}|_{i,\theta})(y,s):(y,s)\in\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\right\}. $$

#### Proposition F.3.

Given $\eta>0$ sufficiently small and $\sigma,\delta\in(0,1)$ , there exist two constants $\hat{\varepsilon},C>0$ such that the following holds. Suppose

- (i) $0<\varepsilon\leq\hat{\varepsilon}$ , $R=\varepsilon^{-1}$ , $\mathsf{h}\in C^{\infty}(\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{R}(0),(-R,R))$ , $\Sigma\subset\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{R}(0)\times(-R,R)$ is the graph of $\mathsf{h}$ , $|\mathsf{h}|_{1}\leq\eta$ , $|\mathsf{h}|_{i}=O(\varepsilon)$ for $i\geq 2$ ; $\Sigma$ is parametrized by $(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\mapsto(y_{1},\dots,y_{n},\mathsf{h}(y_{1},\dots,y_{n}))$ ;

- (ii) $\hat{\mathtt{g}}$ is a Riemannian metric on $\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{1}(0)\times(-1,1)$ , $\|\hat{\mathtt{g}}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\|_{C^{3}}\leq\eta$ ;

- (iii) the Riemannian metric $\mathtt{g}$ on $\bar{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{R}(0)\times(-R,R)$ is defined by $\mathtt{g}(x)=\hat{\mathtt{g}}(\varepsilon x)$ and we restrict $\mathtt{g}$ on $\Sigma$ .

Then, for all $\mathsf{f}\in C_{c}^{m-2,\theta}(\hat{\Sigma}\times\mathbb{R})$ and $\psi\in C_{c}^{m-1,\theta}(\partial_{0}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})$ ( $m\geq 2$ ), there exists a unique solution $\varphi\in C^{0,\theta^{\prime}}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})\cap C^{m,\theta}(\hat{\Sigma}\times\mathbb{R})$ (for some $\theta^{\prime}\in(0,1)$ ) to the following mixed boundary value problem:

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} -\Delta_{\Sigma}\phi-\partial_{ss}\phi+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H}(s))\phi&=\mathsf{f}-c_{\mathsf{f}}(y)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)&&\text{in }\operatorname{int}(\Sigma)\times\mathbb{R},\\
\partial_{\nu_{\Sigma}}\phi&=\psi&&\text{on }\partial_{0}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R},\\
\phi&=0&&\text{on }\partial_{+}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R},\\
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(y,s)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)\,ds&=0&&\text{for every }y\in\Sigma.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Moreover, $\|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}\right)}<\infty$ and

$$ \|\varphi\|_{C^{m,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma_{(-3\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}\leq C\left(\|\psi\|_{C^{m-1,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\partial_{0}\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{m-2,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}\right). $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to [7, Proof of Proposition 4.1]. Let $T_{0}:W^{1,2}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})\to L^{2}(\partial_{0}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})$ and $T_{+}:W^{1,2}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})\to L^{2}(\partial_{+}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})$ denote the trace maps. $\mathcal{H}_{0}:=\{\mathsf{u}\in W^{1,2}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}):T_{+}\mathsf{u}=0\}.$ Then $\mathcal{H}_{0}$ is the completion of $C^{1}_{c}\left((\text{int}(\Sigma)\cup\partial_{0}\Sigma)\times\mathbb{R}\right)$ with respect to the $W^{1,2}$ norm. $\mathcal{H}:=\left\{\mathsf{u}\in\mathcal{H}_{0}:\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathsf{u}(y,s)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)ds=0\;\forall\;y\in\Sigma\right\}$ . Let the bilinear form $\mathbf{a}$ on $\mathcal{H}$ be defined by

$$ \mathbf{a}(\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2})=\int_{\Sigma}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\partial_{s}\varphi_{1}\partial_{s}\varphi_{2}+\langle\nabla_{y}\varphi_{1},\nabla_{y}\phi_{2}\rangle+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H})\varphi_{1}\varphi_{2}\right)ds\>d\mathcal{H}^{n}(y). $$

Then $\varphi$ is a weak solution of (F.3) iff

$$ \mathbf{a}(\varphi,\varphi^{\prime})=\int_{\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{f}\varphi^{\prime}ds\>d\mathcal{H}^{n}(y)+\int_{\partial_{0}\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}}\psi T_{0}(\varphi^{\prime})ds\>d\mathcal{H}^{n}(y)\quad\forall\;\varphi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}. $$

Theorem C.2 implies $\mathbf{a}$ is coercive; hence by the Lax-Milgram theorem, there exists a unique weak solution $\varphi$ of (F.3). By standard elliptic regularity [26, Theorem 7.1], $\varphi\in C^{0,\theta^{\prime}}(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R})\cap C^{m,\theta}(\hat{\Sigma}\times\mathbb{R})$ (for some $\theta^{\prime}\in(0,1)$ ).

Next, we show that the solution $\varphi$ satisfies $\|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}\right)}<\infty$ . Since $\mathsf{f},\psi$ are compactly supported, there exists $s_{0}$ such that (using the notation $I=\{s\in\mathbb{R}:|s|>s_{0}\}$ )

$$ \displaystyle- \displaystyle\Delta_{y}\varphi-\partial_{ss}\varphi+W^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{H})\varphi=c_{\mathsf{f}}(y)\mathbb{H}^{\prime}(s)\text{ on }\Sigma\times I, \displaystyle\partial_{y_{1}}\varphi=0\text{ on }\partial_{0}\Sigma\times I,\quad\varphi=0\text{ on }\partial_{+}\Sigma\times I. $$

Using the barrier function

$$ \varphi_{\epsilon}=\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}\left(e^{-\sigma(|s|-s_{0})}+\epsilon\cosh\sigma s+\epsilon\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cosh\sigma y_{i}\right), $$

one can show that $|\varphi|\leq\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}e^{-\sigma(|s|-s_{0})}$ on $\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}$ , hence $\|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}\right)}<\infty$ .

Lastly, we show that if $\varphi\in C^{m,\theta}(\hat{\Sigma}\times\mathbb{R})$ is a solution of (F.3) and $\|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}\right)}<\infty$ then (F.4) holds. To prove this, without loss of generality we can assume that $c_{\mathsf{f}}=0$ and (because of Theorem E.1) it is enough to establish the following estimate

$$ \|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma_{(-2\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}\leq C\left(\|\psi\|_{C^{1,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\partial_{0}\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}\right). $$

Let us assume by contradiction that the estimate in (F.7) does not hold. So, there exist sequences $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ , $R_{k}=\varepsilon_{k}^{-1}$ , $\mathsf{h}_{k},\Sigma^{k},\hat{\mathtt{g}}^{k},\mathtt{g}^{k},\varphi_{k},\mathsf{f}_{k},\psi_{k}$ such that the assumptions (i)–(iii) in Proposition F.3 are satisfied for $(\varepsilon,R,\mathsf{h},\Sigma,\hat{\mathtt{g}},\mathtt{g})=(\varepsilon_{k},R_{k},\mathsf{h}_{k},\Sigma^{k},\hat{\mathtt{g}}^{k},\mathtt{g}^{k})$ , (F.3) is satisfied for $(\varphi,\mathsf{f},\psi)=(\varphi_{k},\mathsf{f}_{k},\psi_{k})$ , and

$$ \|\varphi\|_{C^{0}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma^{k}_{(-2\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}=1,\left(\|\psi\|_{C^{1,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\partial_{0}\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}+\|\mathsf{f}\|_{C^{0,\theta}_{\sigma}\left(\Sigma_{(-\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}\right)}\right)\to 0. $$

Hence there exists $(p_{k},s_{k})\in\Sigma^{k}_{(-2\delta R)}\times\mathbb{R}$ and $c>0$ such that

$$ e^{\sigma s_{k}}|\varphi(p_{k},s_{k})|\geq c. $$

If $q\in\text{int}(\Sigma^{k}_{(-2\delta R)})$ , using a normal coordinate system (cf. Lemmas 4.2, 4.4) of $\Sigma^{k}$ centreed at $q$ , we can find $Y_{q}:\mathbb{B}_{r}(0)\to\text{int}(\Sigma_{k})$ , where $r=\min\{R_{k}^{1/2},d(q,\partial\Sigma^{k}),\delta R_{k}\}$ , such that $Y_{q}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image, $Y_{q}(0)=q$ , $\|(Y_{q}^{*}\mathtt{g}^{k})_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\|_{C^{2}}=o(1)$ uniformly as $k\to\infty$ . Similarly, if $q\in\partial\Sigma^{k}_{(-2\delta R)}$ , using a Fermi coordinate system (cf. #### Lemma F.4.

Let us fix $\delta_{i}>0$ , $i=0,1,2,3$ , satisfying $\delta_{0}+\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}<\delta_{3}$ and $a,b>0$ . Let $r\in(0,\delta_{1}R)$ , $\rho\in(1,\delta_{2}R)$ , $p\in B^{+}_{\delta_{0}R}(0)$ , $B^{+}_{s}(p)=B_{s}(p)\cap B^{+}_{2R}(0)$ , $U\in C^{2,\theta}(B^{+}_{\delta_{3}R}(0))$ with the uniform estimates

$$ U\geq a>0,\quad U+|\nabla U|\leq b\text{ on }B^{+}_{\delta_{3}R}(0). $$

Then there exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $r,\>\rho,\>p,\>U,\>\varepsilon$ with the following significance.

- (i) If $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small11 1 The metric $g$ in (F.14) depends on $\varepsilon$ . and $\varphi\in C^{2}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))$ satisfies (F.14)

$$ \begin{cases}\Delta_{g}\varphi-U\varphi=E+\operatorname{div}(F)\text{ on }B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p),\\ \partial_{\nu}\varphi=\psi\text{ on }\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p),\\ \end{cases} $$

there holds (F.15)

$$ \left|\varphi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r}(p))}\leq C\left(\left|E\right|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\left|F\right|_{C^{\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\left|\psi\right|_{C^{0,\theta}(\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\rho^{-1}\left|\varphi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}\right). $$

- (ii) If $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small and $\varphi\in C^{2}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))$ satisfies (F.16)

$$ \begin{cases}\Delta_{g}\varphi-U\varphi=E+\operatorname{div}(F)\text{ on }B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p),\\ \varphi=\psi\text{ on }\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p),\\ \end{cases} $$

there holds (F.17)

$$ \left|\varphi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r}(p))}\leq C\left(\left|E\right|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\left|F\right|_{C^{\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\left|\psi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\rho^{-1}\left|\varphi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}\right). $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to [9, proof of Lemma 8.1]. Since the proofs of (i) and (ii) are very similar, we will prove only (i). Let us first prove the following claim.

#### Claim F.5.

There exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $r,\>\rho,\>p,\>U,\>\varepsilon$ such that if $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small, $\tilde{\varphi},\tilde{E},\tilde{F},\tilde{\psi}$ are compactly supported in $B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p)$ and (F.14) is satisfied for $(\varphi,E,F,\psi)=(\tilde{\varphi},\tilde{E},\tilde{F},\tilde{\psi})$ , there holds

$$ |\tilde{\varphi}|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}\leq C\left(|\tilde{E}|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+|\tilde{F}|_{C^{\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+|\tilde{\psi}|_{C^{0,\theta}(\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}\right). $$

To prove this claim, we assume by contradiction that the estimate (F.18) does not hold. Then there exist sequences $\tilde{U}_{i},\tilde{\varphi}_{i},\tilde{E}_{i},\tilde{F}_{i},\tilde{\psi}_{i}$ , $r_{i},\>\rho_{i},\>p_{i},\>\varepsilon_{i}$ such that $\varepsilon_{i}\rightarrow 0$ , $\tilde{\varphi}_{i},\tilde{E}_{i},\tilde{F}_{i},\tilde{\psi}_{i}$ are compactly supported in $B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i})$ ,

$$ |\tilde{\varphi}_{i}|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}))}=1,\quad\left(|\tilde{E}_{i}|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}))}+|\tilde{F}_{i}|_{C^{\theta}(B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}))}+|\tilde{\psi}_{i}|_{C^{0,\theta}(\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}))}\right)\rightarrow 0 $$

and (F.14) is satisfied for $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{i}$ and

$$ (U,\varphi,E,F,\psi,r,\rho,p)=(\tilde{U}_{i},\tilde{\varphi}_{i},\tilde{E}_{i},\tilde{F}_{i},\tilde{\psi}_{i},r_{i},\rho_{i},p_{i}). $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\hat{g}^{jk}(\varepsilon_{i}\cdot)\partial_{jk}\tilde{\varphi}_{i}-\varepsilon_{i}\hat{g}^{jk}(\varepsilon_{i}\cdot)\hat{\Gamma}_{jk}^{l}(\varepsilon_{i}\cdot)\partial_{l}\tilde{\varphi}_{i}-\tilde{U}_{i}\tilde{\varphi}_{i}=\tilde{E}_{i}+\operatorname{div}\tilde{F}_{i}\text{ on }B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}); \displaystyle\partial_{\nu}\tilde{\varphi}_{i}=\tilde{\psi}_{i}\text{ on }\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r_{i}+\rho_{i}}(p_{i}). $$

Since $\tilde{\varphi}_{i},\tilde{E}_{i},\tilde{F}_{i},\tilde{\psi}_{i}$ are compactly supported, we can assume that (F.20) holds on $B^{+}_{\delta_{3}R}(0)$ . Let $\delta^{\prime}_{3}=\delta_{0}+\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}$ . There exists $\tilde{x}_{i}\in B^{+}_{\delta^{\prime}_{3}R}(0)$ such that $|\tilde{\varphi}(\tilde{x}_{i})|\geq 1/2$ .

Suppose $\limsup_{i\to\infty}\tilde{x}_{i,1}=\infty$ . We define $\bar{\varphi}_{i}(x)=\tilde{\varphi}_{i}(\tilde{x}_{i}+x)$ . Then $|\bar{\varphi}_{i}(0)|\geq 1/2$ and (by Theorem E.1) the $C^{1,\theta}$ norm of $\bar{\varphi}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded on $B(0,s_{i})$ where

$$ s_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\min\left\{\tilde{x}_{i,1},(\delta_{3}-\delta^{\prime}_{3})R_{i}\right\}. $$

Therefore there exist $\varphi_{\infty},U_{\infty}:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that up to a subsequence, $\bar{\varphi}_{i}\to\varphi_{\infty}$ in $C^{1}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ ,

$$ \Delta_{g_{E}}\varphi_{\infty}-U_{\infty}\varphi_{\infty}=0\text{ on }\mathbb{R}^{n+1} $$

and $|\varphi_{\infty}(0)|\geq 1/2$ . However, this contradicts Lemma F.2(i).

On the other hand, if $\limsup_{i\to\infty}\tilde{x}_{i,1}<\infty$ , we define $\bar{x}_{i}=(0,\tilde{x}_{i,2},\dots,\tilde{x}_{i,n+1})$ and $\bar{\varphi}_{i}(x)=\tilde{\varphi}_{i}(\bar{x}_{i}+x)$ . The $C^{1,\theta}$ norm of $\bar{\varphi}_{i}$ is uniformly bounded on $B(0,\frac{1}{2}(\delta_{3}-\delta^{\prime}_{3})R_{i})$ . Therefore there exist $\varphi_{\infty},U_{\infty}:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{g_{E}}\varphi_{\infty}-U_{\infty}\varphi_{\infty}=0\text{ on }\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}, \displaystyle\partial_{\nu}\varphi_{\infty}=0\text{ on }\partial\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}. $$

Moreover, $|\varphi_{\infty}(x_{\infty})|\geq 1/2$ for some $x_{\infty}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{+}$ , which contradicts Lemma F.2(iii). This finishes the proof of the claim.

To prove the lemma, we choose a cut-off function $0\leq\chi\leq 1$ such that $\chi=1$ on $B^{+}_{r}(p)$ , $\text{spt}(\chi)\subset B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p)$ , $\left|\nabla\chi\right|+\left|\nabla^{2}\chi\right|\lesssim\rho^{-1}$ and apply the above claim to $\tilde{\varphi}=\chi\varphi$ . Indeed, $\Delta_{g}\tilde{\varphi}-U\tilde{\varphi}=\tilde{E}+\textrm{div}(\tilde{F})\text{ on }B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p)$ , where $\tilde{E}=\chi E+2\langle\nabla\varphi,\nabla\chi\rangle+\varphi\Delta\chi-\langle F,\nabla\chi\rangle$ , $\tilde{F}=\chi F$ and $\partial_{\nu}\tilde{\varphi}=\tilde{\psi}\quad\text{on }\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p)$ where $\tilde{\psi}=\chi\psi+\varphi\partial_{1}\chi$ . Therefore, the lemma follows from above claim and elliptic estimate

$$ \displaystyle\left|\varphi\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r}(p))} \displaystyle=\left|\tilde{\varphi}\right|_{C^{1,\theta}(B^{+}_{r}(p))}\lesssim\left(|\tilde{E}|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+|\tilde{F}|_{C^{\theta}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+|\tilde{\psi}|_{C^{0,\theta}(\partial_{0}B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}+\left|\tilde{\varphi}\right|_{C^{0}(B^{+}_{r+\rho}(p))}\right). $$
